From back pain to cancer, how the interstitium could transform medicine

New Scientist August 24, 2026

In the 17th century, physician Samuel Collins observed a mesh around each organ, which he called a “common Vest” made of “curious well-spun Threads… wonderfully interwoven with each other”. The “remanent spaces”, he noted, were filled with a “concreted Animal Liquor”.

Over the following centuries, the purpose of these structures was thought to be purely architectural. The vest, known today as fascia, offers a kind of girding that holds our organs in place; the gaps filled with that “animal liquor” – called interstitial fluid – provide a kind of shock absorber that allows our organs to slide freely as we move, without bruising.

We now know that those pockets of fluid are far more important than this. Emerging research suggests they form an interconnected network called the interstitium that provides an important channel of communication between and inside our tissues. And that is set to cause a quiet revolution in medicine, changing how we think about everything from muscle pain and the microbiome to the spread of cancerous tumours across the body.

Advertisement

According to some scientists, it may even offer a modern explanation for concepts in traditional Chinese medicine, including the fundamental life force “qi”.

The interstitium’s basic anatomy certainly suggests some structural role. The extracellular matrix within it provides structural support for pockets of fluid, with threads made of collagen, which create a strong scaffold, and elastin, which act like tiny bungee cords and offer flexibility. The interstitial fluid coursing through gaps in this matrix comprises around 12 per cent of our body weight and contains hyaluronic acid, a large molecule that forms a gel in water, perfect for cushioning delicate tissue.

The mainstream view was that each organ and muscle is sealed off in its own compartment, with its own, isolated interstitium. While a few researchers, such as molecular engineer Melody Swartz at the University of Chicago, have long been interested in how the fluid flows within the different compartments, there was little evidence that they were interconnected.

That was partly due to a serious practical limitation: when you take tissue samples to study under a microscope, the interstitial fluid drains away and the collagen fibres that give the cavities their structure collapse in on themselves. This made it very hard to characterise the space.

Fascia: The long-overlooked tissue that shapes your health

That changed with a groundbreaking study in 2018, using a new procedure that combines a laser with an endoscope to build microscopic images of tissue in a living body. This enabled Neil Theise, professor of pathology at the New York University Grossman School of Medicine, and his colleagues to follow the movement of a fluorescent dye injected during pancreatic surgery. This revealed a series of channels and cavities where they had expected to find dense connective tissue, suggesting that the interstitium was larger and more intricate than previously recognised. Widening their search to other organs, their detailed images provided the strongest evidence yet that it comprised a network spanning the whole body.

“If this organ is present in every tissue and other organ the way the cardiovascular and lymphatic systems are, then we have an incomplete understanding of the entire body,” Theise said at the time. “I don’t think there’s anything that doesn’t get changed by this.”

Building on these results, Theise and his colleagues later examined biopsies of people with tattooed skin. They found that some of the ink had crept from the skin into the interstitial spaces around other organs, proving that the interstitial compartments are interconnected.

Such discoveries paint the interstitium as a tidal marsh, streaming in nutrients and washing out waste. The main drift comes from high-pressure arteries, which supply much of the interstitial fluid, to low-pressure lymphatic vessels where the trash is deposited. But the motion of the fluid is also strongly affected by body movement, with every muscle in the body contributing a squeeze. Even in repose, there is flow from the peristaltic motion of the digestive tract, overlaid with the tremolo of arterial pulsing throughout the body.

This may have immediate implications for fast-moving infections like necrotising fasciitis, which destroys the tissue beneath the skin, including fascia and muscles, and cellulitis, a deep infection that leaves the skin red and swollen. “Appreciating the interstitial location of these infections may give us important information about their spread,” says Rebecca Wells, professor of gastroenterology at the University of Pennsylvania and part of the team behind the 2018 study. “On the flip side, the patterns of spread in fasciitis and cellulitis may tell us about interstitial structure and flow.”

More profoundly, a closer study of the interstitium could offer new insights into basic biological systems.

We know, for instance, that immune cells called T-cells pursue pathogens throughout the extracellular matrix. Peter Friedl, director of the Microscopic Imaging Centre at Radboud University in the Netherlands, who has studied cellular transport through the interstitium since 2007, compares them to “little monkeys” swinging through the “jungle” of collagen. Investigations into the interstitium might therefore reveal overlooked but essential elements of the immune response.

Presiding over the interstitial tissues are multi-tentacled cells called telocytes, first named in 2010 by Laurentiu Popescu at the Carol Davila University of Medicine and Pharmacy in Romania and Maria-Simonetta Faussone-Pellegrini at the University of Florence in Italy. Using electron microscopy, they found that the arms of these cells have an impressive reach, which they use to create junctions with distant cells. The junctions are similar to neural synapses, except they connect with all types of body cells, including blood vessels, nerve fibres, muscle cells, glands, stem cells and other telocytes.

Like neurons, telocytes have electric properties that allow them to stimulate those neighbouring cells. In this way, the interstitium complements the nervous system as a body-wide sensory tissue, responding to stretching, tension, pressure, vibration and movement. The resulting input provides us with proprioception – the sense of where our body is – and much of what we feel as muscle pain and stiffness may originate in the interstitium.

Telocytes also play a crucial role in healing. Popescu and Faussone-Pellegrini observed them controlling the release of heart stem cells in the myocardial interstitium, for instance.

The interstitial fluid is also awash with extracellular vesicles, tiny packets filled with bits of RNA, proteins and lipids. These interstitial messengers bud off from sender cells and drift to a recipient. Extracellular vesicles include potent regulatory microRNAs that can make epigenetic changes to the receiving cell, altering its behaviour or even changing its identity.

This may have particularly important implications for the treatment of cancer. In 2015, David Lyden at Weill Cornell Medical College in New York and his colleagues discovered that tumour cells continuously launch extracellular vesicles into the interstitium, complete with a chemical “address” directing them to specific target tissues.

Because they are tiny, they can easily sail through the interstitium, leaving a trail of chemical breadcrumbs behind them. When they hit their target, they promote the growth of new blood vessels, preparing the ground for the metastatic cells to follow.

To make that journey, the cancer cell reaches out a sticky appendage and attaches to a fibre in the matrix of collagen. It isn’t an easy trek; it must pull its cell body along until its chunky nucleus gets jammed in the webbing. At that point, the cell releases chemicals that break down the collagen around the nucleus, freeing the cell to continue hacking its way through the interstitial undergrowth.

In this way, rogue cancer cells create tunnels throughout the interstitium, making it easier for subsequent metastatic cells to slide through.

Free newsletter

With time, researchers may find ways to interfere with interstitial metastasis before the tumours embed. Because the tumour extracellular vesicles are addressed to specific organs, Lyden’s goal is to create personalised treatments that direct therapeutic payloads to specific tissues, avoiding damage to healthy organs.

Swartz, meanwhile, has been developing a vaccine that induces the growth of lymphatic vessels in the interstitium around melanomas. The idea is that these would attract cancer-killing T-cells. The research is still in its early stages, but her tests on mice suggest it can limit the spread of the disease.

Beyond cancer, the interstitium and its contents may shed light on endometriosis, in which tissue similar to the lining of the womb starts to grow outside the uterus, leading to pain, fatigue and fertility problems. Some experts have therefore proposed that malfunctioning telocytes may support the growth of new blood vessels that help the endometrial tissue to implant and survive.

The all-encompassing continuity of the interstitium, including organs, blood, lymph cells and nerves, is astonishing. But there is an exception: the brain, which has its own private interstitium.

This is largely to avoid friendly fire from our immune system, which could take out memories, cognitive function and motor control. The brain is therefore separated from the rest of the body by the blood-brain barrier. It keeps out most microbes most of the time, but if they do manage to sneak in, they alert the brain’s more delicate immune cells, the microglia, that must avoid too much collateral damage.

In the brain, the interstitial liquid is called cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). It provides the fuel for brain tissue and picks up the waste afterwards. The flow of CSF runs through the glymphatic system, first discovered by Maiken Nedergaard, a neuroscientist at the University of Rochester Medical Center in New York state. Arteries and veins normally run alongside lymphatic vessels, but in the brain, they run inside the glymphatic vessels. The pulsing of arteries drives the surrounding CSF into the brain interstitium, pushing its fluid towards returning veins, helping to flush out detritus.

Crucially, the glymphatic system ultimately drains into ordinary lymphatic vessels, meaning there is still a connection to the body’s interstitium – and this may affect the famous gut-brain axis.

Restoring the brain’s mitochondria could slow ageing and end dementia

The communication between the gut and the brain is important enough to have at least three other conduits, including the bloodstream, the vagus nerve and hormonal signalling. But the interstitium may provide a new corridor.

“A continuous interstitial pathway means that gut-derived signals might find a more direct anatomical back door into the central nervous system’s fluid compartments,” says Theise, possibly via interstitial fluid surrounding arteries and nerve bundles.

This would a good reason to avoid a leaky gut, where the lining of the gut becomes too porous to properly contain microbes and their toxins. The best advice here is to add fibre and fermented food to your diet. These encourage your gut microbes to produce substances like butyrate that both heal and maintain your gut lining.

One of the most provocative claims about the interstitium concerns its relationship to the ancient concept in traditional Chinese medicine known as qi, the flow of energy that is supposed to underlie our physical health.

Researchers like Wei-Bo Zhang at the China Academy of Chinese Medical Sciences suggest there are anatomical analogies between six of the bodies named in traditional Chinese medicine – the Fu organs – and six tissues integrated with the interstitium: epidermis, dermis, deep fascia, joints, visceral fascia and the rest of the inter-organ interstitium. In ancient Chinese texts, the largest of these organs, the Sanjiao, is described as “the official in charge of drainage, from which waterways emerge”, an apt description of the interstitium.

Traditional Chinese medicine posits that energy flows through the body in a system of pathways called meridians. This is the basis for acupuncture and acupressure, which have been shown in several studies to be better than placebo for back pain, knee pain and headaches.

Could these pathways represent the movement of liquid in the interstitium? Some evidence of this arrived in 2021, when Andrew Ahn at Harvard University used fluorescent dyes to track interstitial flow from the wrist to the elbow. The path, he found, followed the accepted meridian line.

Intriguingly, Nedergaard has shown that gently rotating acupuncture needles releases adenosine, which acts like an analgesic, into the interstitium – offering one potential mechanism for the pain relief achieved through traditional Chinese medicine.

Qi is sometimes interpreted as an electric phenomenon, which makes sense in the context of the interstitium. The interstitial framework of stiff collagen fibres is piezoelectric, meaning it generates a small charge of electricity when the fibres bend. The hyaluronic acid that fills the interstitium is negatively charged, so there is electric potential throughout. Bioelectric fields are known to alter epigenetics and shape cell development, as well as attracting immune cells to the site of injury. The charges created by interstitial activity could therefore influence these processes.

These ideas remain to be proven, though. Swartz suspects the interstitial flow is too sluggish and local to explain the long-distance effects of meridians. If anything, the meridian lines show lymphatic flow, she suggests, which is quicker. “You don’t walk from Minneapolis to Chicago – you take a bus and then you walk from the bus stop to your home,” she says.

Low on energy? A new understanding of rest could help revitalise you

For her part, Wells is sceptical of the idea that interstitial fluid moves along well-defined channels akin to the meridians. “An ocean, or a bath, may be a more useful way to think of the interstitium than something like a river delta,” she says.

Wells is also doubtful of the role of electrical energy. “Although it sounds very promising as a physical, Western explanation for qi, it’s still not clear that elastin [or] collagen piezoelectricity could support flow of the magnitude of qi,” she says, although she is planning new studies to better determine the actual voltages that can be generated in this wet environment.

There may be other mechanisms. Helene Langevin at the University of Vermont has shown that when you rotate an acupuncture needle, it grips fascial tissue. This causes fibroblast cells, whose primary job is to maintain the interstitium’s collagen, to move and reorganise. “In mice, we were able to demonstrate propagation of the mechanical signal from acupuncture needle rotation several centimetres away from the needle,” says Langevin, who is also the former director of the US Center for Complementary and Integrative Health. “That is a very large distance – nearly the whole mouse.” Such changes to the connective tissue may have knock-on effects for the interstitial flow.

Whether or not the interstitium offers a point of contact between traditional and Western medicine, this unifying tissue promises to revolutionise our understanding of our bodies. Four hundred years since Samuel Collins made his observations, we may have just seen a glimpse of what the “animal liquor” means to our health.

Plastic bottles can be turned into edible, vanilla-flavour cookies

New Scientist August 24, 2026

Plastic bottles and agricultural waste can be converted into consumable cookies via genetically engineered yeast. The team members behind the initiative are currently awaiting institutional approval so they can taste the product.

Plastic pollution and food scarcity are two of society’s thorniest problems. Sandhya Jayasekara and her colleagues from Southern Illinois University Carbondale hope to use the former to solve the latter – potentially eliminating both in the process.

The first stage of the process is to take used plastic bottles – sourced from a supermarket – and discarded sweetcorn plant stalks and leaves, and put them through a process called oxidative hydrothermal dissolution. This uses heat to break down the materials into components that microbes can digest.

Advertisement

Plastic can be programmed to have a lifespan of days, months or years

Those components are then fed to yeast that has been genetically altered using CRISPR gene-editing technology. This allows the yeast to convert the components into a variety of useful ingredients, including proteins, fats and acids, as well as vanilla flavouring and beta-carotene, which the body can convert into vitamin A.

Finally, fibre, starch and sweetener are added to the mix, and the paste is extruded through a 3D printer into any desired shape. The resulting cookies have been dubbed µBites, pronounced microbites.

The researchers, who are presenting the work at the fall meeting of the American Chemical Society (ACS) in Chicago on Friday, are eager to try µBites for themselves as soon as their university approves the experiment. But they are confident that the cookies are both safe and tasty.

Subscriber-only newsletter

“I think it has a pleasant, appealing aroma,” says Jayasekara. “And it will taste good, too. We’ve not tasted it, but it smells good – that’s for sure – like a real cookie.”

Team member Lahiru Jayakody, also at Southern Illinois University Carbondale, says it will take 20 years of additional research before plastic waste can be pulled from oceans or landfills and converted to safe and appetising food, but that he hopes the process alone can inspire others to tackle the problem of plastic waste in innovative ways, leading to “a social shift” in the way we think about the problem.

But not everyone is convinced that µBites can make a meaningful impact on plastic pollution. Jason Hallett at Imperial College London says the research is fun and interesting, but also, in all likelihood, a practical dead end.

Making all shampoo or detergent bottles look the same isn’t anti-capitalist, and it’s the only way to make a truly circular economy for plastics, says Saabira Chaudhuri

“We produce 400 million tons a year of plastic waste. You’re not going to turn it all into cookies,” says Hallet. “So it’s not a solution to the plastic-waste crisis. There’s no way you could do this commercially. We’re not gonna be eating plastic cookies.”

The concept certainly faces challenges. In a time when there is growing concern about the amount of microplastics in our environment, food and even our brains, it could be difficult to sell the idea of food that is actually made from plastic. Add the stigma of genetic engineering to the mix, and manufacturers may find a limited appetite for µBites.

Hallett says the best solution to the plastic crisis is recycling through processes we already understand, but logistical problems with gathering such widely cast waste and the low cost of virgin plastic mean it isn’t being done on a large enough scale.

‘Off the charts’ El Niño is already the strongest since records began

New Scientist August 21, 2026

“The El Niño has blossomed. It is off the charts. Usual measures of El Niño have blown past prior record levels in the period with good data, even though maximum effects are still several months in the future.”

So writes renowned climate scientist James Hansen at Columbia University in New York in a newsletter sent today.

There are different ways of measuring El Niños, which occur when warm surface waters spread eastwards along the equator across the surface of the tropical Pacific Ocean. Hansen thinks the best measure is how much warmer than usual the upper 300 metres of the eastern tropical Pacific becomes.

Advertisement

This El Niño will be the hottest by a huge margin

“Our preferred metric, the heat anomaly in the upper 300 meters of the Equatorial Pacific Ocean… already exceeds the 1997-98 super El Niño,” he writes.

A more common measure, called the Niño3.4 index, is based on how much warmer than usual the sea surface temperature is in the Pacific in the long rectangle between 5 degrees north and south of the equator, and between 120 and 170 degrees west.

“The more common Niño3.4 metric, sea surface temperature… in the equatorial Pacific, also far exceeds prior values,” Hansen writes.

But Adam Scaife at the Met Office, the UK’s national weather service, says the Niño3.4 index has not yet exceeded previous super El Niños. “The anomaly in Niño3.4 is currently about 2 degrees above the norm which is very high for this time of year but not quite as high as the anomaly at the peak of the 1997/1998 El Niño which was around 2.5 degrees,” Scaife told New Scientist.

Free newsletter

The disagreement on the Niño3.4 index might partly be because this index is usually expressed as a three or five-month running mean. By contrast, the daily Niño3.4 value hit 2.75°C earlier this month before dropping back slightly.

“In this case, I would agree with Jim,” says Daniel Swain at the California Institute for Water Resources. “Niño3.4 values are clearly now the highest on record for the time of year, and are expected to remain so for the rest of the calendar year.”

Using a running mean with a long lag is misleading in a rapidly evolving situation like this, says Swain.

The looming El Niño could be bad – but much worse is to come

However, during November 2015 the daily Niño3.4 reached nearly 3.1°C, so the current event is not yet as strong as the 2015 one on this measure, either. It appears Hansen meant to say the Niño3.4 index exceeds values for this time of year, as Swain says. New Scientist has asked Hansen for clarification, but had no response at the time of publication.

“Under the standard El Niño metric region it’s still currently the third strongest event on record,” says Zeke Hausfather at Berkeley Earth. “But upper 300m heat is generally a leading indicator of what we will see at the surface.”

“I agree that this El Nino is the biggest on record,” says Kevin Trenberth at the National Center of Atmospheric Research.

What’s clear is that this developing super El Niño will soon exceed previous events on all measures. “I have never seen an El Niño signal this intense in our forecasts,” Scaife said in a statement released today. “If the forecast is accurate… then 2026 will far exceed our recent experience of El Niño and its worldwide climate influences.”

While Hansen is comparing the developing super El Niño to other modern events for which we have direct temperature records, Hayley Fowler at Newcastle University in the UK thinks it could also exceed historical events suspected to be even larger.

“The super El Niño evolving in the Pacific will likely be the biggest ever recorded, reaching or exceeding the levels of the 1877-1878 El Niño which caused widespread impacts, including famines and around 50 million deaths (3-4 percent of the global population at the time), mostly across Asia and South America,” Fowler said in a statement.

Greenland meltwater is intensifying European heatwaves

New Scientist August 21, 2026

The melting of the Greenland ice sheet is causing more extreme heat in Europe, contributing to the major heatwaves experienced there so far this year.

The surge of cold meltwater into the North Atlantic is altering ocean temperatures and shifting the jet stream to favour heatwaves in western Europe and the Mediterranean, a study undergoing peer review has found. As Greenland ice loss accelerates, Europe may suffer more frequent and intense heatwaves than climate models currently predict.

This newly discovered “atmospheric bridge” played a major role in the unprecedented heatwaves this summer, according to Marilena Oltmanns at the UK’s National Oceanography Centre, who is one of the study’s authors.

Advertisement

Drought and heat push Europe’s power grid to breaking point

“Europe heats up faster. This is because of the jet stream shift,” she says. “In future years… it will be even more extreme. In the future we will think this [year’s heatwave] was not a heatwave; this was nice.”

The steady rise in global temperature has increased heatwaves. But it’s still debated whether changes in prevailing weather patterns are also contributing.

In the past 30 years, high-pressure ridges – large areas of elevated air pressure that look like a ridge or upside-down U on weather maps – have been forming more frequently over Europe, the study finds, leading to sunny skies and extreme heat. These ridges are caused by waviness in the jet stream, the band of strong winds that circles the northern hemisphere. When the more or less straight-flowing jet stream meanders northward around western Europe, it allows warm air from the central Atlantic and Sahara desert to pour into the ridge that’s been created.

Years with extensive high-pressure ridges over Europe have resulted in heatwaves like the one that killed 70,000 people in 2003.

Free newsletter

The researchers say the formation of the ridges can be traced back to Greenland through a cascade of climate events. In the summer before years of extensive ridging, an average of 81 billion tonnes more meltwater rushes off the ice sheet, they found. The cold meltwater lowers sea surface temperatures as it spreads through the North Atlantic in the autumn and winter. Its freshness inhibits mixing with saltier, warmer deep layers, further cooling the surface.

These pulses of meltwater cooling come on top of the “cold blob,” a long-term decline in ocean temperatures in the North Atlantic that some scientists blame on the weakening of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) system of currents. Together, they create a sharp temperature front between the cold waters and the warmer surface waters further south in the Atlantic.

As warm air masses rise to the south of the front and cold masses descend to the north of it, they begin to swirl and generate cyclones. This makes the jet stream wavier. It tends to meander southward of these cyclones, then back northward over western Europe, creating the persistent, high-pressure ridges and heatwaves there.

The critical current could remain stable beyond 5°C of warming, but only if the warming happens very slowly

Most worryingly, climate models don’t fully capture this process, according to Oltmanns.

“This is a big problem,” she says. “It’s going to be even more intense in terms of heatwaves and droughts, in particular in the Mediterranean region, so the weather extremes are likely underestimated.”

A study in July found that the jet stream has shifted southward in the Atlantic in recent decades, similar to the pattern shown in the study. But it concluded that this was due to natural fluctuations in the climate and would eventually reverse.

Meltwater from Greenland could be forcing the jet stream to meander, according to John Methven at the University of Reading, UK, who was one of the authors of the July study. But the weakening of the AMOC or changes in atmospheric circulation over the North Atlantic could also be causing this shift.

“That’s the weak link as far as I’m concerned, the link between the cold blob and whatever’s melting in Greenland is not established, and there might be other things going on,” he says.

If North Atlantic cooling continues to affect the jet stream, it could cause not just heatwaves but also other extreme weather, according to Oltmanns. The research linked it to an unprecedented derecho, a stream of thunderstorms and strong winds, in the Mediterranean in 2022. Winds reached more than 60 metres per second, and fist-sized hail killed 12 people.

“We [will] have more droughts at some locations, flooding events at others, and the variability on top of this increases,” she says.

Research Square DOI: 10.21203/rs.3. rs-10342381/v1

Burns improve more rapidly after treatment with fish skin

New Scientist August 21, 2026

Fish skin may be the safest and most effective way of treating severe burns. Exposing burns to the skin of Atlantic cod seems to result in patients spending less time in hospital and experiencing fewer complications compared with other treatments. This may be due to cod skin containing omega-3 fatty acids that trigger just the right amount of inflammation to assist the healing process.

“Fish skin actually looks a lot like human skin when you look at it with a microscope, so maybe it works like [our] skin,” says John Lantis at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York. “[It] offers a faster, possibly slightly cleaner way of rebuilding your skin than some other options.”

Every day, more than 30,000 people worldwide develop burns that require medical attention. Severe cases are often treated with grafts, where healthy skin is taken from one part of the body and moved to cover or replace skin that is damaged or missing.

Advertisement

Humans evolved to survive mild burns at the expense of severe ones

Prior to graft surgery, many patients undergo temporary wound coverage to prepare the area and manage infection risk. This can involve applying synthetic or biosynthetic scaffolds made up of collagen, the most abundant protein in skin. But an Icelandic company called Kerecis manufactures products made from wild Atlantic cod (Gadus morhua), which are approved to treat burns and other wounds in the US and the UK.

To compare these approaches, Lantis and his colleagues used data from 465 adults who attended 49 burn centres between 2019 and 2025.

All the adults had moderately sized burns affecting 13 per cent of their body, on average. Most of the burns were either mixed – affecting multiple layers of the skin – or third-degree, in which the outer and middle layers of the skin are destroyed, with no sensation in the area. The underlying bones, muscles and tendons are sometimes also affected.

Free newsletter

Prior to undergoing a skin graft, 93 of these patients were treated with GraftGuide, a minimally processed intact fish skin from Kerecis, which funded the study but didn’t analyse the data. The remaining patients received approved synthetic substitutes. The two groups were matched for factors like age, sex, burn severity and size, and any other complications from the injury.

The researchers found that the individuals treated with GraftGuide spent 12 fewer days in hospital, on average, than those who got synthetic substitutes, with the former group being discharged after an average of 23 days and the latter after an average of 35.

What’s more, rates of complications were twice as high in the synthetic-substitute group, with 16 per cent experiencing issues like sepsis, compared with 8 per cent who received GraftGuide.

How much sunscreen should you be using, when should you apply it, and are there any downsides to doing so? Skin cancer expert Rachel Neale is here to answer all of these questions and more

Atlantic cod naturally contains collagen and omega-3 fatty acids. Unpublished data suggests that putting omega-3 on burns causes an initial spike in inflammation, which helps stop any bleeding, says Lantis. This inflammation then quickly fades, assisting healing, he says. “If you had a wish list, you’d say, we want a lot of inflammation [initially], but you don’t want to keep inflammation going.”

Very few fish viruses are thought to affect people, which means the skin doesn’t have to be treated with harsh detergents that could wash away the omega-3, says Lantis. An advantage of Atlantic cod over other fishes is that it has a relatively large body size, so you can get a lot of skin from each fish, he says.

Comparing equivalent patients who received different treatments is always difficult, says Fiona Wood at the University of Western Australia. Formal head-to-head trials directly comparing the approaches are needed, she says.

One such ongoing trial is assessing whether Kerecis’s fish-skin product reduces the need for grafts in second-degree burns, which affect just the outer and middle layers of the skin. Each participant will receive fish skin to part of their burn, while the rest of it will be treated with a graft. “Every patient’s their own control,” says Lantis. This should eliminate the risk of discrepancies between participants affecting the results, he says.

National MP Chris Penk is refusing to confirm or deny whether Prime Minister Christopher Luxon was right when he alleged Penk launched a leadership challenge against him.

Arriving at Parliament for the first time since he was accused of launching a leadership challenge against Luxon, Penk said he was “looking forward, not backwards” and wouldn’t comment on the events of two weeks ago which led to his sacking as a minister.

When the Herald put to Penk that the Prime Minister had accused him of launching a leadership challenge and he was not addressing that, Penk responded: “I don’t need to address anything because I’ve been open about the fact that I’m looking forward, not backwards”.

He repeatedly wouldn’t answer questions about whether it was true he had launched a challenge, if he was working alone on a challenge or with others, or about what had led to his sacking.

“If the Prime Minister makes appointments and the reverse in terms of ministerial roles, he’s perfectly entitled to do that. He’s explained that he’s done that and his reasons for it. ”

Asked again by the Herald why he not willing to confirm or deny whether the Prime Minister was correct to say one of his National ministers had tried to challenge him, Penk said: “I’m perfectly happy where I am now”.

“I’m going to be a good local Member of Parliament.”

Speaking moments later, Luxon said he was aware Penk was back at Parliament but didn’t believe New Zealanders would be interested in the matter. He believed Kiwis would be more interested in what taxes Opposition parties were proposing.

Luxon said it was “sad” Penk was out of Cabinet, but “we’re moving on”. He wouldn’t say when he last spoke with Penk.

Discontent amongst National MPs with the party’s leadership was reported by the Herald two weeks ago, with Luxon subsequently calling an urgent caucus meeting to address the matter.

During that meeting, Luxon won a vote of confidence. Afterwards, he released a statement accusing Penk of launching a leadership challenge and sacking Penk from his ministerial roles. Penk announced he would not seek re-election in his seat of Kaipara Ki Mahurangi.

While some National MPs have claimed Penk was acting alone, there has been speculation he was working alongside another potential leadership contender. One outsider linked to National told the Herald that Penk was engaging MPs to see whether Erica Stanford had the numbers to roll Luxon.

Both Stanford and Chris Bishop, another National MP suspected of wanting the leadership, have denied asking Penk to work on their behalf.

“I didn’t ask anybody to act on my behalf,” Stanford said. “I didn’t ask anybody to challenge for the leadership. I didn’t challenge for the leadership because I’ve always supported the Prime Minister 100%.”

Free-range hens may move in and out of lockdown as bird flu persists. Photo / RNZ, Sally Round

By RNZ Digital reporters, RNZ Checkpoint of RNZ

While the threat of bird flu still hangs over the egg industry, the Egg Producers Federation says it’s likely free-range chickens will be going in and out of lockdown in the coming months.

Hundreds of thousands of hens have been in lockdown as the third case of bird flu was confirmed in a wild bird in Aotearoa.

But Egg Producers Federation chairperson and Mainland Poultry chief executive John McKay told RNZ’s Checkpoint they would let half a million of their hens back outside on Wednesday.

McKay said there was now good data available for farmers to decide the risk level for their birds and whether to let their hens out of temporary lockdown.

Many egg suppliers that are able to have put their hens into lockdown, restricting their roaming to protect them from bird flu, meaning free-ranging was not always possible.

The most recent data McKay had seen showed there was a low risk for chickens, he said, even with the third detection.

“It’s in a petrel, and it’s likely we will continue to find those ocean-going birds occasionally washed up on our shores.”

He said Mainland Poultry had decided to prepare its farms on Tuesday for the hens to be let outside on Wednesday morning.

“This is an evolving situation so we will continue to look at it and judge the risk. The welfare of our birds is paramount, and the risk is likely to change in the future.

“As the risk level changes, it might be time to bring those birds back in again.”

McKay warned it might be something Aotearoa had to get used to in free-range farming.

“We are free-range farmers because we want our birds roaming outside and we value that highly, and people who buy free-range eggs care deeply about welfare.”

For consumers who were worried about whether their eggs were still free-range, McKay said stickers would be put on Mainland Poultry cartons, next time the birds went into lockdown, alerting potential buyers to the fact the birds were temporarily kept inside.

He said the stickers would very clearly state the eggs had been laid by birds temporarily housed for their own welfare.

“It will be very clear communication... we’re also explaining to consumers around New Zealand how we as farmers are looking to manage this risk going forward.”

A traveller faces the next eight years in prison after attempting to smuggle more than $1 million of methamphetamine into New Zealand by concealing it in a kitchen stock pot.

The 59-year-old man was sentenced to seven years and eight months’ imprisonment in the Manukau District Court on Friday for attempting to import around 3.5kg of the Class A substance.

Last year, the man was referred to Customs for questioning and examination after arriving at Auckland International Airport on a flight from Shanghai, China, on September 27.

Officers searched his suitcase, revealing packaged food, personal items, cooking paraphernalia and a notably heavy stockpot.

With glue indicating the pot had been tampered with, Customs officers X-rayed it and discovered further inconsistencies.

The base of the pot was drilled into, revealing a white crystal-like substance that tested positive for methamphetamine.

Officers identified 3.58kg of the substance inside the pot, equivalent to approximately 179,000 doses and with a street value of $1.074m. The man was arrested and charged with importing a Class A-controlled drug.

At the time of his arrest, Customs estimated the seizure prevented up to $3.7m in harm to New Zealand communities and the economy.

“Customs is continually evolving its tradecraft, data, and technology to combat all forms of illicit drug smuggling,” said chief customs officer of compliance and enforcement Ben Wells.

“Full credit to our frontline officers for lifting the lid on this concealment.”

Prominent business leader Dame Therese Walsh has set up a Givealittle page for the family of a young Manawatū police officer left fighting for his life after being struck by a stolen car driven by fleeing teenagers.

The Air New Zealand chairwoman started the page yesterday with an open goal to help the officer’s family with any financial support they needed.

“My heart just went out to them and so I got in touch with the family and they are a wonderful family,” she told the Herald.

“It’s a deeply emotional time for them, but they’re at his bedside and they are just dedicated to being there for him. He has a little one, a very little one and a partner, so, you know, that’s really, really difficult when you’re a very young police officer.”

The family have also passed on a message through Walsh, thanking the public “for all the support and messages they have been receiving as they focus on being at their loved one’s side”, she said.

The constable remains in the intensive care unit in Wellington Hospital after being critically injured while laying road spikes in the early hours of Saturday. Two teens, 14 and 15 years old, have been charged over the incident.

Walsh was a wing patron for police in late 2023, and had become “quite close” to the recruits during that time.

“I thought, ‘oh gosh, I hope it’s not one of my recruits,’ and then I realised it wasn’t but then I thought ‘I don’t want anyone to be in that situation’,” she said.

“These guys, they go out and risk their lives for us, keeping us safe.”

She had joined in some of the training with the recruits when she was wing patron, and said the situations they dealt with were “really tough”.

“I’m a desk job person really, I chair boards and things like that and I never have to put myself in that sort of danger, you know? So I just think we have to be really clear to support those that are helping us out in the community.”

Walsh said she only started the Givealittle page yesterday but was pleased at the “really phenomenal response”.

“The police do a great wraparound job with their injured officers but, you know, there’s always a whole lot of unintended expenses in these situations and so providing some support is really important.

“I just feel really strongly about it and I’m hoping to get even more people involved.”

The page has raised at least $8000 at the time of updating this article.

According to police, the officer had been deploying road spikes on Kairanga Bunnythorpe Rd about 2am on Saturday when a car carrying two youths crashed into the police car he was standing behind, sending him flying several metres into another vehicle.

He was airlifted to Wellington Hospital in a critical condition, while a second officer was treated for minor injuries.

The teens were arrested and charged with a raft of offences, with the older of the two facing a charge of reckless driving causing injury.

Central District Commander Superintendent Dion Bennett earlier described the officer as a “great family man”.

“In his mum’s words, he’s a good bloke – and we think so too.

“There is no shortage of love and support pouring in for him; his family are by his side and staying incredibly strong for him, and we’re also doing everything we can to support them as they navigate this awful situation.”

Police said the investigation into the crash is ongoing; however, the alleged driver, the older of the two teenagers, now faces charges relating to theft, failing to stop, dangerous driving and reckless driving causing injury.

The second teenager has been charged with unlawfully getting into a motor vehicle.

Both are due to appear in the Youth Court on Thursday.

Police said the teenagers had fled after failing to stop for officers on Amberley Ave, but police were not pursuing them when they later encountered the road spikes.

The vehicle swerved to avoid the spikes, struck the police car and then hit the two officers.

The car involved appeared to be stolen but Bennett said he did not know where from.

“We had discovered a stolen vehicle and police followed the stolen vehicle initially. As that vehicle sped away, police withdrew from that pursuit.”

The Independent Police Conduct Authority has been notified, as is standard in such circumstances.

Police Association president Steve Watt said his organisation had contacted the police welfare section and, alongside police, would provide wraparound support for the officer and his family.

The incident again highlighted the “unpredictable and dangerous nature of policing”, Watt said.

“It’s a traumatic event that cuts deep for our whole membership ... it really resonates with everyone and our thoughts and prayers go out to the family and to our member involved.”

Melissa Nightingale is a Wellington-based reporter who covers crime, justice, and news in the capital. She joined the Herald in 2016 and has worked as a journalist for 12 years.

Disruptive behaviour in classrooms on the rise

New Zealand Herald August 24, 2026

A recent survey of secondary teachers has found that 67% of respondents' classroom time was sometimes or often disrupted by students' bad behaviour. Photo / 123rf

By Charlyse Tansey of RNZ

Another report has highlighted the struggles teachers face because of bad behaviour in the classroom.

The New Zealand Council for Educational Research recently released a survey of secondary teachers, which found 67% of respondents’ classroom time was sometimes or often disrupted by students’ bad behaviour.

RNZ’s education correspondent John Gerritsen says that figure is higher than in previous surveys.

“That’s up quite a lot from 2021, when the figure was 61%. But if you go back to 2015 to 2018, it was only around half of teachers [who] said that they were experiencing that sort of disruption.”

Gerritsen says one respondent was “quite shocked by what they were experiencing”.

“One of them was a new teacher who said, ‘Look, I’ve only been teaching for three years, I’ve been assaulted three times by students physically, you know, breaking up physical fights’.”

He says that increasingly disruptive behaviour in classrooms is not just an issue in secondary schools.

“In 2024, the Council for Educational Research published a survey of primary teachers, and it found that the percentage in that sector reporting disruption by bad student behaviour sometimes or often had jumped from 68% in 2019 to 82% in 2024.”

This is only the most recent report to spell out how bad the situation is.

In 2023, the OECD Programme for International Students survey found that either New Zealand students were the worst-behaved in the OECD and/or more likely to report disruptive behaviour.

In 2024, a report from the Education Review Office found that half of teachers surveyed said that bad behaviour in schools had got worse in the two previous years.

“[Education Review Office] called for national action on this. They said this is really, really serious. It said that violence and disruption had reached really critical levels, and half of teachers were spending an hour a day just responding to bad behaviour,” Gerritsen says.

The Act Party has put forward a proposal to help deal with the problem. As part of its election promise, the party says it will give teachers the clear legal power to remove seriously or persistently disruptive students and send them to a supervised space.

It says that teachers will be protected when they use “reasonable and proportionate intervention” to prevent harm or destruction of property. It also proposes fines for parents and firmer consequences for assaulting staff or other students.

But there are doubts among teachers that this proposed policy would make a difference in classrooms.

Post Primary Teachers’ Association president Chris Abercrombie says the policy is not what teachers have been asking for.

“The vast majority of teachers that said there was disruption in the class [were referring to] students talking when they shouldn’t have been.

“So, you’ve got that level of disruption and all the way to, you know, quite serious disruption in the class – and I’ve had to deal with these once or twice over my 20-year career.

“At not one point did I think, ‘Hey, you know what will solve this? Me physically manhandling this child out of the classroom’.

“The policy is just – to be frank – it’s stupid.

“It doesn’t solve the issue and [is] actually going to create way more issues.”

Teachers currently have the ability to physically restrain a child, but the incident must meet three requirements: it is necessary to prevent imminent harm, including emotional distress, to another student or person; there are no other options; and the physical restraint is “reasonable and proportionate” to the situation.

All teachers and staff must complete mandatory training around the rules and guidelines.

Abercrombie says there are big questions to be answered about the practical side of Act’s proposed policy.

“If I asked a hundred people what reasonable force looked like, I’m sure I’d get a hundred different answers. I’m a bloke in his 40s – what, am I meant to drag a 14-year-old out of the class? You know, wrestle a 17-year-old boy out of the class? The practicalities of it are just ridiculous.”

He says there are better solutions to deal with the ongoing issue.

“We know that a lot of these students who are creating this disruption have specific learning needs. They have other things going on in their life and we need to make sure that they are supported fully and resourced fully to meet those needs.

“It could be something as simple as really making sure our alternative education system’s working properly ... beefing up these other things so kids have options, schools have options to support these kids, be it learning support, be it mental health, be it alternative education, all of these things.

“We need to get solutions and not just ... these cheap politics that seem to exist.”

NZ star track: A watch on space from Beijing to Tehran, Paris to Somalia

New Zealand Herald August 24, 2026

A satellite, seen in orbit around the globe, with the black of space behind it. Photo / University of Auckland Space Institute

By Phil Pennington of RNZ

New Zealand is helping track satellites, including from Iran and the Chinese military, in a network that also watched over the Paris Olympics, United States and New Zealand government documents show.

The Auckland space-watching hub – set up in 2023 and largely funded by the US Pentagon – tracked an Iranian TV broadcasting satellite in February during a launch from Russia the hub called “a significant milestone for Iran’s space [programme] and continued Russian-Iranian co-operation in space activities”.

Iran also has some military satellites.

That same month the hub at Whenuapai Air Force base tracked a Chinese satellite as it moved close to a French satellite. Beijing said it was an experimental spacecraft but the West suspects it was a “military test satellite” that has in the past manoeuvred near US satellites to get a look.

The satellite operations are revealed in reports from the New Zealand Defence Force released under the Official Information Act.

They were generated within a US-led global space-and-ground-based network that makes up to 800,000 observations of space every day.

Other operations over Paris and Somalia have been revealed in US Space Force reports that show how the network has been “rapidly expanding into new mission areas”.

New Zealand, the US and United Kingdom host one hub each of the Joint Commercial Operations or JCO network, which co-ordinates 24 countries to give 24-hour round-the-world coverage.

The network has been pulling in more and more data from more than 400 ground-based and space sensors operated by private companies.

While most of it is non-classified, the US documents show the JCO also had “secret” and “top secret” channels and was increasing what it shared with military commands and with the US spy agency, the National Reconnaissance Office.

There had been a “significant increase in successful tracking” of Chinese and Russian launches, one network report in April said.

Its civilian-side work was vital, tracking solar flares and space debris, and helping rescue missions.

But the network’s core task was clear: “Adversary satellite tracking”, “manoeuvre detection” and “predict adversary behaviour”, an August 2025 US report said.

The network’s operators – local military personnel in their home countries – hone their proficiency by practising “kill-chains” and rehearsing “realistic threat scenarios”.

The JCO network guarded the Paris Olympics in 2024 from GPS disruptions, a US Space Force report titled ‘Watch, Warn, Win’ said. A small map showed two “jammers” near Rouen.

The Olympics task came within days of the network getting new powers for positioning, navigation and timing for situational awareness (PNT-SA) powers on July 1, 2024.

Around the same time the network took over a big US Tactical Surveillance, Reconnaissance, and Tracking (TacSRT) programme, as well as taking on board electromagnetic spectrum operations which could be used against people trying to interfere with GPS location data.

The New Zealand Defence Force last year denied taking part in this broad expansion of JCO activity, saying New Zealand had sovereignty over what its hub did. RNZ has asked again about that.

Cabinet papers said the Defence Minister must be in the loop on any change to what the JCO did.

The new tactical and electromagnetic powers were used in Somalia, the April report said.

US military commanders had asked the network to find where radio-frequency interference was coming from. They used electro-optical imagery, synthetic aperture radar from satellites that could see at night and through clouds, and radio frequency scans to find a jammer near Mogadishu International Airport.

Space-watching is only becoming more important as space traffic and dual military-commercial use of it ramps up.

US President Donald Trump last week signed a memo aiming to boost rocket launches by more than five times, to a thousand a year by 2030. Last year he signed an order for integrating commercial space capabilities with US national security much more.

The first confirmation of the US-Israel operation Epic Fury against Tehran in February was from commercial not government spacecraft.

New laws required the US military to “buy before build ... requiring agency heads to search for commercial solutions before building their own”.

“Modern warfare depends heavily on these kinds of commercial, dual-use space systems,” a local expert said.

The JCO network uses commercial sources to augment the monitoring done by the much older US Space Surveillance Network that makes 800,000 observations of 45,000 objects a day.

The goal is higher still: the Pentagon wants its new Space-Watch programme to track every object in low earth orbit by tapping an “enormous volume” of cheap sensors in space; the JCO document mentioned Elon Musk’s Starlink and 24,000 sensors.

The US space commander who had oversight of 2026’s ‘Year of Integration’ with allies, Lieutenant-General Dennis Bythewood, said recently, “Space as a warfighting domain has been established”.

He also noted that the US could not do it without the teamwork of the JCO, and it was fed from at least 17 companies.

One such tracker is in New Zealand, a ground-based radar in central Otago run by US company Leolabs. It tracked almost 100% of satellites and over 98% of space debris, and recently signed a JCO contract to feed the central repository, the UDL.

The UDL served thousands of users across more than two dozen countries.

A new project called Atlas aims to expand and speed up access to UDL using technology from data-crunching firm Palantir.

The deal to set up the Auckland hub with eight personnel in 2023 was celebrated by defence for the “operational and diplomatic benefits it provides at a small operating cost” – just $180,000 last year for New Zealand.

It co-ordinated and trained operators in Australia, South Korea and Japan to US standard.

The hub was cemented last year as a core part of the NZDF Space Squadron. Cabinet papers have stressed the aim was to help keep space safe and secure.

The JCO was an extension of the National Space Defence Centre set up in 2018 to improve collaboration between military and intelligence communities to respond to attacks in space.

An NZDF spokesperson on Monday said its involvement in the JCO network was focused on understanding the space environment and contributing to collective awareness, “consistent with our policy settings”.

Its role in the space domain was centred on awareness, information sharing, and co-operation with partners.

“This includes participation in selected multinational activities and exercises, and partner-led engagements for learning, planning, and interoperability purposes.

“Future participation in exercises or initiatives referenced by partners remains subject to government approval and resource considerations, and future NZDF contributions are expected to remain modest in scale and focused on capability development.”

It did not directly address whether it was now involved in the network’s expanded range of operations, such as tactical reconnaissance, or not.

RNZ-Reid Research poll: Did National make the wrong call in keeping Luxon?

New Zealand Herald August 24, 2026

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon speaking to media after he foiled a bid to replace him as National Party leader. Photo / Mark Mitchell

By Craig McCulloch of RNZ

National’s decision to stick with Christopher Luxon as leader appears at odds with the wider public, with more voters saying the caucus got it wrong than right.

The latest RNZ-Reid Research poll gauged voters’ views on the National Party’s emergency caucus meeting two weeks ago, where a majority of MPs opted to keep Luxon as leader, foiling a bid to replace him.

Asked whether that was the right call, 45.4% of respondents said no, compared with 36.8% who said yes.

Another 17.8% were unsure.

National supporters were the most likely to support Luxon, with 78% endorsing his continued leadership, against just 11.5% who disagreed.

Act voters were less emphatic – with 54.2% in support of the decision to keep Luxon and 28.7% opposed.

In contrast, a majority of New Zealand First voters were against Luxon staying, with 52.4% saying National MPs made the wrong decision, compared with 31.6% who backed them.

Labour and Green supporters were much more likely to say National got it wrong, with 64.6% and 69.8% respectively registering their disapproval.

The poll also asked those who wanted Luxon gone who they would have picked to take over from a selection of names discussed during the recent leadership turmoil.

Erica Stanford was the most popular name, at 16.6%, narrowly ahead of Chris Bishop on 15.2%.

Nicola Willis was third on 9%, followed by Chris Penk on 7.6%.

But the largest share by far went to “none of the above”, selected by 39.6%.

A further 13.3% said they did not know.

Following the failed leadership coup, Luxon sacked Chris Penk from Cabinet, declaring that the rogue MP had acted alone in challenging the prime ministership.

But sources within and close to the party connected Stanford to the failed bid.

In the aftermath, Stanford denied any involvement, but before the meeting, she stayed silent when repeatedly asked by reporters if she had confidence in Luxon.

Bishop and Willis were also believed to be positioning themselves if the party leadership was vacated.

Both declared loyalty to Luxon before and after the caucus meeting.

This poll of 1000 people was conducted by Reid Research, using quota sampling and weighting to ensure a representative cross-section by age, gender and geography. The poll was conducted through online interviews between August 14-21, 2026 and has a maximum margin of error of +/- 3.1% at a 95% confidence level.

New Zealand Herald August 24, 2026

A charity was facing possible deregistration for its failure to file annual returns on time when it was awarded a $1 million Government tender to open a mental health support cafe in Gisborne.

Te Kupenga Net Trust’s chief executive says the charity has been working constructively with the Department of Internal Affairs to complete the outstanding reports and the issue was “not a reflection of the organisation’s services, governance commitment, or use of funding”.

Health New Zealand Te Whatu Ora awarded the trust a tender for $500,000 a year over two years at the start of 2026 to open a Peer Support Crisis Recovery Cafe, also known as a “resilience cafe”, in Tairāwhiti. It was part of a $61.6m investment into mental health support services nationwide.

The trust was required to file an annual return for its year ended June 30, 2024, before December 31, 2024 and its year ended June 30, 2025, before December 31, 2025.

Department of Internal Affairs (DIA) director of charities services Charlotte Stanley said these returns were now overdue after the charity had initially received extensions.

“Charities Services has engaged with the charity regarding its outstanding returns and has commenced regulatory action,” Stanley said.

Formal deregistration action for Te Kupenga Net Trust started on March 24, 2025, when a Notice of Intention to Deregister was issued. The annual return for the year ended June 30, 2023, was still outstanding at the time.

Charities Services agreed to allow the trust more time to meet its reporting obligations.

The annual return for the year ended June 30, 2023, was subsequently filed but the next two years remain outstanding – one year on from the extended deadlines.

Te Kupenga Net Trust chief executive officer Hine Moeke-Murray said the charity was working constructively with the DIA to complete the outstanding filings.

“That process is well advanced and the issue is an administrative reporting matter – not a reflection of the organisation’s services, governance commitment or use of funding,” Moeke-Murray said.

“Te Kupenga remains focused on delivering safe, effective support for whānau in the region. Any contracting decisions are properly a matter for the relevant funder, but Te Kupenga is engaging transparently and in good faith with all appropriate agencies while the reporting process is finalised.”

When asked if Charities Services’ decision to commence regulatory action would affect the trust’s charitable work and ability to deliver the tender, she said the trust “would not characterise an active compliance process as regulatory action”.

“Te Kupenga is co-operating fully to resolve the outstanding filings, as it has throughout. For more than 30 years, Te Kupenga has provided trusted support to some of our region’s most vulnerable people and its priority remains protecting that work and the people who rely on it.”

The charity’s most recently published audit report said the charity aims to improve the health and wellbeing of all people with mental health and addictions in Tairāwhiti. It offers education, peer support and advocacy.

Its purpose, according to the register, is to “cast its net to ensure that the potential of people is realised through committed advocacy, peer support and consumer leadership”.

Cath Cronin, executive regional director for Midland Te Manawa Taki, said Health NZ would assess the process associated with awarding the cafe tender to ensure appropriate processes and due diligence requirements were followed.

Minister for Mental Health Matt Doocey attended an event at Te Kāuta cafe in July, although the space has not opened to the public yet.

A sign on the door of the venue on Gisborne’s Gladstone Rd says it expects to be operational in two months.

Doocey, in a statement, said he was not involved in the operational details or individual procurement decisions made by Health NZ.

“I expect Health New Zealand to follow the appropriate procurement processes and undertake the necessary scrutiny and due diligence when assessing organisations and negotiating contracts with providers,” he said.

“The decision to award this contract was a matter for Health New Zealand, and I would expect it to have considered all relevant information as part of that process.”

All charities are required to file an annual return, including financial statements, within six months of their balance date at the end of the financial year.

Stanley said the publication of annual returns on the Charities Register provided transparency to the public on a charity’s use of its resources for its charitable purpose.

Depending on the circumstances, regulatory action could include removal from the register, imposing administrative penalties and referring matters to the Charities Registration Board for consideration.

The trust employed 31 fulltime staff and two part-time staff as of the year ended June 30, 2023.

It commissioned an evaluative review of itself this year, conducted by Pūrēhua consultancy. It found Te Kupenga Net Trust supported 5565 unique whānau through direct engagement and case co-ordination between July 2019 and December 2024, 64% of which were Māori.

The report said the trust had a “funding envelope” of about $3.5m.

US supreme court rules Trump can proceed with crackdown on mail-in voting

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 21:53:38 GMT

Justices’ ruling comes after lower courts had blocked president’s election order ahead of November midterms

The US supreme court has sided with Donald Trump in his effort to crack down on mail-in voting, though it remains unclear if his administration can take action ahead of the midterm elections in November.

Justices on the court voted 6-3 along ideological lines to lift an injunction from June that a judge in Massachusetts placed on an executive order issued by the president. But a second injunction remains in place and the ruling leaves room for legal challenges.

Trump has repeatedly likened voting by mail to cheating, despite his own use of it and overwhelming evidence that the system is secure.

In March he ordered the government to create a “state citizenship list” of eligible voters, requiring that mail-in ballots only be delivered to people on that list. He also directed the justice department to prioritise investigations and prosecutions of state and local election officials who issue ballots to people deemed ineligible to vote in federal elections.

Democratic officials in 23 states and the District of Columbia sued over Trump’s March order, saying the US constitution gives states and Congress the authority to set election rules, not the president. They argued that imposing sweeping changes so close to the election risked disenfranchising voters and disrupting preparations already under way.

A judge in Massachusetts, Indira Talwani, sided with the plaintiff states – nearly half the country – and ruled that Trump lacked authority to dictate how states administer federal elections. She also questioned whether federal agencies could compile accurate citizenship lists.

An appeals court upheld her decision. Talwani later issued a second injunction with nationwide effect.

The justice department had argued that the states’ lawsuit was premature because the administration had not yet taken concrete actions that harmed them and they therefore lacked legal standing to sue. The administration said the Massachusetts injunction prevented it from finalising and implementing policies intended to promote “election integrity” before November.

Republican-led states backed the administration before the supreme court, arguing that states would have an opportunity to provide input on the final lists of eligible voters.

The supreme court, in a 6-3 decision, has now lifted the first injunction, allowing the administration to move forward while litigation continues. The three liberal justices dissented. The ruling does not finally resolve the underlying legal questions and leaves the door open to further challenges as the midterms approach.

The wrangling over how US voters can cast their ballots comes less than 100 days until November’s midterm elections, which will decide the balance of power in the US Senate and House of Representatives.

Democratic voters are deemed more likely to cast their ballots by mail than Republicans: about one in four registered Democrats did so in 2024, according to the States United Democracy Center, alongside one in five registered Republicans.

About 30% of all ballots were cast by mail in the 2024 presidential election, according to federal data. A 2025 Brookings Institution study found roughly four cases of fraud for every 10m mail ballots cast.

Trump’s executive order forms part of a wider effort to reshape the electoral system. He has repeatedly made false claims of widespread fraud in American elections, including his defeat by Joe Biden in 2020, and has pressed the Republican-controlled Congress to pass the Save America Act, a contentious package of voting restrictions.

US strikes a vessel in the eastern Pacific, killing 2 people in first attack in months

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 21:40:48 GMT

US Southern Command has struck another vessel in the eastern Pacific, killing two accused of trafficking drugs

The US military has launched a deadly strike on a vessel in the Pacific Ocean, killing two people accused of drug trafficking.

On Monday, US Southern Command (SouthCom) announced it “executed a lethal kinetic strike on a low-profile vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Eastern Pacific”.

“Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel’s active involvement in narco-trafficking. The operation killed two narco-terrorists,” SouthCom added.

Southern Command did not provide evidence for the vessel’s alleged involvement in drug trafficking.

In a statement on the strikes, Francis L Donovan, SouthCom’s commander general, said: “We are committed to imposing total systemic friction on narco-terrorists – disrupting their operations, dismantling their leadership and eliminating cartel terror across the region.”

“This operation is a powerful demonstration of our lethal precision, overwhelming capability, and absolute resolve to protect the US homeland,” Donovan added.

A pixelated black-and-white video posted to SouthCom’s X account on Monday showed a vessel moving through the water before it was struck by an explosion that produced a large flash of light.

Monday’s strike marks the latest in a series of US military strikes since the Donald Trump administration launched what it described as a campaign targeting “narco-terrorists” smuggling drugs into the US, despite numerous reports indicating that the strikes have done little to stem the flow of drugs into the country.

It brings the overall death toll to 223 people killed in 67 strikes during the nearly year-long US campaign of bombing alleged drug boats off Latin America’s Caribbean coast and in the eastern Pacific Ocean. US Southern Command says the campaign has resulted in the destruction of 64 speedboats, three “low-profile” ships and a semisubmersible craft.

The latest strike comes as the Trump administration pursues deals with allied nations to extend its offensive to land across multiple Latin American countries. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said during a visit to Panama this month that Colombia, Guatemala and Honduras had agreed to allow the US to carry out joint military operations against criminal groups on their soil. Guatemala denied reaching such a deal.

Ecuador launched similar missions with the US in March.

The Trump administration’s boat bombing campaign began in early September and has left numerous survivors, but most of them have never been recovered.

US Southern Command said in a separate statement on Monday that there have been more than 20 search and rescue efforts overall, almost all of which were unsuccessful.

According to data compiled from the command’s social media posts, the strikes have generated 28 survivors with only three people ever being rescued – one person during a strike in March who was transferred to the Costa Rican Coast Guard, and two wounded people who were later repatriated to their home countries of Ecuador and Colombia.

The very first strike in September 2025 left two survivors who were killed in a second, follow-up strike. When that became public, it drew concern from some lawmakers and those who study military law. The White House insisted it was done “in self-defense” to ensure the boat was destroyed and in accordance with armed conflict laws.

Despite the defense department framing the strikes as attacks against “narco-terrorism”, it has provided little evidence on whether the vessels were actually transporting drugs. The attacks have been condemned as extrajudicial killings by the United Nations and other humanitarian organizations.

According to a 2020 report by the US Drug Enforcement Administration, 74% of the cocaine reaching the US arrived through the Pacific while only 8% came from fast boats from the Caribbean.

Critics have questioned the overall legality of the boat strikes as well as their effectiveness, in part because the fentanyl behind many fatal overdoses is typically trafficked to the US over land from Mexico, where it is produced with chemicals imported from China and India.

The Pentagon’s watchdog said in May that it plans to look into whether the US military followed an established targeting framework when carrying out the strikes. However, the evaluation is focused specifically on what’s known as the six-phase Joint Targeting Cycle and not on the legality of the strikes, the inspector general’s office said.

Meanwhile, an investigation by the Latin American Center for Investigative Journalism (Clip) this year identified 13 previously unidentified victims of US vessel attacks. All came from impoverished communities across Latin America and the Caribbean and several were fishers with no indication of involvement in the drug trade, it found.

“There are communities where they stopped fishing for several weeks – and if they do that, people go hungry – because they were terrified of being bombed,” María Teresa Ronderos, Clip director, said at the time of the report’s release.

Other families continue to grieve as they seek answers about their relatives killed in US airstrikes.

“If the boat was carrying so much cocaine and then exploded and caught fire, where is the evidence? Where is the cocaine? That is what I want to know. I know Ricky. He was a fisherman. That was his life,” Titus, the brother of Ricky Joseph, one of the 13 people identified in the CLIP investigation, said in June from the Carribean island of St Lucia.

Burnham backtracks on spending housing fund only on building social homes

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 21:30:39 GMT

About 40% of £10bn from Affordable Homes Programme will now go on types of housing such as sheltered and shared ownership

Andy Burnham has backtracked on his proposal to rip up the government’s housing plans and boost social home building.

Ministers laid out plans on Monday to spend an initial £10bn from the 10-year Affordable Homes Programme on a mix of subsidised housing types in England, in line with the Starmer government’s policy.

Burnham previously called for the programme to be spent entirely on social homes, which are more heavily subsidised and therefore more affordable than other types of government-funded housing.

He said when launching his campaign to become MP for Makerfield: “There’s £39bn allocated over a 10-year period … I’m saying that should be dedicated to council homes. Let’s not be coy any more … I’m saying council homes because control matters.”

Under the plans announced on Monday, however, £10bn will be spent helping to build 70,000 homes outside London, about 60% of which will be social rented houses. The rest will be other types of accommodation such as shared ownership schemes and sheltered housing.

London will get another £6bn, which will be allocated at a later date.

Ministers said the investment would help bring the government closer to its promise of building 300,000 affordable homes over the next 10 years. It will be spent by 33 “strategic partners”, who will be guaranteed funding for the next decade to help deliver their plans.

The Guardian has learned that for the first time in the history of the scheme, three of those partners will be local councils, as the government looks to deliver what Burnham has promised will be “the biggest council housebuilding programme since the postwar period”.

Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, said: “Growing up on a council estate and raising children as a young working mum, I know firsthand that access to a secure, affordable home can be a lifeline for families up and down the country.

“Guardian readers will know just how important council housing is too. You will know it’s so much more than just a roof over your head – it gives working parents a safe place to raise their family, offers kids the stability needed to thrive in school and wraps a community around those who need it most.”

She added: “This once-in-a-generation investment will help rewrite these stories, delivering the genuinely affordable homes our country needs, getting people off waiting lists and helping families put down roots so they can get on in life.”

Officials say that another £16bn is yet to be allocated, and that social rent homes and council houses will be prioritised in future funding rounds.

Sarah Elliott, the chief executive of the charity Shelter, said: “Today’s announcement puts councils back on the pitch in the fight to end homelessness. By giving local authorities some of the funding and support they need to start delivering social homes at scale again and ramping up the percentage of funds allocated to social homes, the government has laid the foundations for its council housing revolution.

“But there are still underlying obstacles which hold councils back from building. The government must use the autumn budget to finally remove these barriers, like unsustainable housing debt that councils are saddled with, to make the prime minister’s vision of a new generation of social homes a reality.”

The plans contrast with those announced by Reform UK on Monday, which is promising to boost the supply of social homes by evicting foreign tenants and allowing housing associations to borrow more.
