Chelsea’s front three dazzle as they edge out Fulham in derby thriller

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 21:05:48 GMT

This was a crash course for Xabi Alonso in life at Chelsea. His new side thrilled in possession at Craven Cottage. The front three of João Pedro, Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers combined to devastating effect and there was even an assist for the new £52m centre-back, Maxence Lacroix.

At times the only issue was the two No 10s both laying claim to the ice cold celebration. Palmer had a point to prove after missing out on England’s World Cup squad and Rogers scored on his debut after his £117m move from Aston Villa. Yet victory in Alonso’s first competitive game as Chelsea’s manager was far from straightforward. He saw that he needs a better goalkeeper than Robert Sánchez and will worry about his side’s lack of smarts. Fulham, who will hope this bright start under Alvaro Arbeloa shows there is life after Marco Silva, were unfortunate not to rescue a point.

There were tactical conundrums for Alonso to solve. Chelsea were without Moisés Caicedo in midfield, where there was a rare start for Roméo Lavia alongside Reece James, while Marco Palestra was unable to make his debut because of a minor knock meant there was also an adjustment on the flanks.

However, while Malo Gusto and Jorrel Hato seemed cautious picks as the wing-backs in the 3-4-2-1 system Alonso used when winning the Bundesliga with Bayer Leverkusen in 2024, the early concern belonged to Fulham. They have also had a summer of change, Silva departing for Benfica, and it is hard to work out Arbeloa’s level given his managerial experience is limited to his spell in charge of Real Madrid after Alonso’s firing last season.

The nerves deepened when Chelsea led after 31 seconds. Fulham’s defensive shape was wrong when a clearance came back at them and Palmer exacted the punishment. The playmaker looked refreshed after a first summer off in four years and he was alert when the ball reached him, a deft flick exposing the hole left by Jorge Cuenca in the middle and sending João Pedro through to build on his scorching pre-season form by lifting a calm dink over Bernd Leno.

The positive for Arbeloa is that Fulham responded by playing their football, rattling the visitors. Old failings flared, bookings for Levi Colwill and Lavia inside the first 12 minutes a reminder of Chelsea’s rashness. Alonso saw little control and he was provided with immediate evidence that an upgrade is required in goal.

Sánchez was shaky. He let a backpass from Josh Acheampong run for a corner and his handling was unconvincing. Josh King was close with one shot and the teenager’s luck was in when he had another go, a low drive from a tight angle exposing Sánchez at his near post and somehow squirming under the Chelsea goalkeeper.

Fulham have looked to lower the age of their squad this summer. King is a homegrown gem and was aided by two former Madrid youngsters. César Palacios looked smooth in midfield and there was a chance for Gonzalo García as Fulham pressed after the equaliser, only for Acheampong to deny the striker with a vital block.

Chelsea realised they were in a game. Lavia tested Leno. Palmer flickered again, drifting down the right and crossing for João Pedro to volley wide.

Fulham took too many risks. They did not have a handle on Palmer, although the assist went to Lacroix when Chelsea regained their lead. The centre-back made an ambitious overlapping run to reach a pass from Palmer, then stormed past a weak challenge, drew Leno and pulled the ball back for Rogers to make it 2-1.

Post-Pep Premier League era begins with blast of hyper-managed shock and awe

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 19:30:15 GMT

Possession numbers, the intense physicality and the pure rhythm of games all felt noticeably new as the season began

There has been something oddly narcotic and moreish about the drip‑drip of fresh Pep Guardiola content either side of the start of the new Premier League season. Eras come and go. Everything dies, baby, that’s a fact. But four‑part Amazon Prime documentaries make angels of us all.

So we have continued to feast on the Pep-at-City visuals: dead jeopardy, reheated beefs, the uplifting team talks of a departed manager to the departed players of a departed team, and moments that often feel far more gripping than the daily churn of what we must, out of habit, call the real world.

The thought occurred watching all this: has the Premier League found its Tupac? Is Pep just going to keep on doing this, dropping new material, fresh hits, posthumous platinum albums? A bald, thin charismatic man who keeps on releasing his lost tapes. We have exactly the thing, sir. Is he even actually dead?

Probably this won’t happen. But a profound absence is still a profound presence at moments like these. The ghosts continue to pull the strings. This weekend was the first of the new Premier League season. More significantly, it was also the first of the post‑Pep era.

And this has been a genuine era, 10 years in the game and an entire tactical culture shift in the making. Unsurprisingly, there was an odd sense of lightness across those nine fixtures on Friday through to Sunday, of old bonds cast aside, even a little giddiness. Suddenly dad isn’t home. The chair by the door is empty. Let’s all just rip it up a bit, shall we?

This relies on a slightly out‑of‑date notion of what Guardiola‑ism became in its later years. But the fact is, something interesting did happen in those Friday‑to‑Sunday games. Think of pure Pep-ball and what are you seeing? Possession. Cold, high‑craft control. This is a coach who famously said: “My desire is to have 100% possession,” after a 5-1 thrashing of Arsenal in Munich during which Thiago Alcântara complete 122 passes.

Admittedly, Guardiola was speaking out of frustration that day, talking more about not losing the ball at key moments, possession as defence. But these ideas did have a profound mimetic effect in England. During Guardiola’s decade at Manchester City the team that had the least possession in the Premier League would win, on average, only 30%-35% of games, a figure that fell as low as 28% in 2021‑22 but which had begun to pick up in the last two seasons as even City’s own version of Pep‑ball became more mixed and next‑gen.

But this weekend the opposite thing happened. In six of nine games played from Friday to Sunday one team took significantly more possession while failing to win. Liverpool had 60% possession plus 27 shots but still just scrambled a draw and looked, frankly, pretty wild. Manchester United had 71% possession and were well beaten by Hull. Tottenham had 60 % possession and lost 3-0. Nottingham Forest had 56% and lost. Sunderland had 62%, Crystal Palace 58%, and both lost.

There were three exceptions to this, all outliers in their own way. Manchester City had 66% possession and won at home against Bournemouth, but spent 84 minutes looking like they were losing. Brighton had 73% possession and beat an Aston Villa team that had made a collective decision to play with their eyes closed and their legs on the wrong way round. Arsenal dominated every metric against a promoted Coventry team that looked, frankly, a little spooked by their first sight of that fresh Everest.

So, a tiny sample size. It may mean absolutely nothing. It could get flipped on its head before we hit September. Also, it is important to note that pure possession stats have rarely dictated with any certainty who will win a game. The top teams always tend to have most of the ball, thus skewing the overall stats.

Otherwise, possession has been a far less reliable guide to victory than, say, expected goals, which speaks clearly to the effectiveness of a system. Whereas simply keeping the ball is often a sign of the opposite of good health, of football as a collective anxiety attack, out there playing with your worry beads, tramping a horseshoe shape into the grass while your opponents mass for the decisive blitzkrieg.

The Guardian's daily football game, On the ball, is now live in the app for both iOS and Android. Can you identify the Premier League star from the clues?

But it wasn’t just the possession numbers that were notable this weekend. The rhythms of the matches were striking. All three Sunday games featured nine or 10 substitutes in the last 40 minutes or so, and a sense of two separate halves, of finishers brought into play, of a broken, episodic tactical to‑and‑fro in response to shifts in the scoreline and the flow. The World Cup also had that pattern. Maybe this is what football is now.

Mainly there was a striking level of targeted physicality, rehearsed blitz-transitions, groups of players running suddenly forward quickly in formation at certain triggering events. Anthony Elanga’s opener for Newcastle captured this best: 12 seconds, two passes, 70 metres covered in a single perfectly straight line, no off‑the‑cuff inventions or what you might call conventional “creativity”, but a perfect moment of planned collective intelligence and breathtaking athleticism.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

This was the pattern elsewhere too, games defined by rapid breaks, by powerful players sourced for their ability to win duels and to carry the ball, and a weekend that felt like another ratcheting up in the Premier League’s journey into hyper‑physicality.

Isn’t it a trend? Is this the next stage in the league’s narrow but furiously intense evolution? There are several managers in new jobs who have reputations for the game of sprints, blitz‑ball: most notably Matthias Jaissle at Newcastle and Roberto De Zerbi at what was, on Saturday, the least De Zerbi‑ish of Spurs, a Spurs that seemed to have absorbed only the mouse part – play dead, hide, roll over – of that fast‑breaking cat‑and‑mouse football.

There are two things worth saying about this. This is not a rejection of Guardiolaism and positional play. Keeping the ball was always about preparing for the moments when you don’t have it. Guardiola’s later Manchester City team would often win by direct means.

But pure possession can also be boringly risk-averse, a kind of footballing atrophy where everyone just sits quivering on the touchline like a swarm of beached jellyfish at dusk. The spectacle is more gripping when the emphasis is on those transitions either side of the passing patterns.

More specifically, it is also an interesting development for Pep’s successor at City, Enzo Maresca, Coolio to his Tupac, whose methods are still very much pure Pep origins, based in control of the ball and rigid positionism, like the last soldier still fighting the second world war from inside a bush on Iwo Jima in 1976.

Is Maresca ready for this? Is he even ahead of it? He gave a televised interview at the weekend where he spoke about the tension between control and risk, possession and creativity, and where he defined players being encouraged to run into unexpected positions as “chaos”. On Monday morning there were headlines describing the Premier League weekend in those terms. But this isn’t chaos. We’ve seen chaos. We’ve seen attack ships on fire off the shoulder of Orion, jinking wingers, dogs of war, hitting the space, Lee Chapman, Rod Wallace and Eric Cantona making heavy metal music with two bass guitars and an antique viola. You want chaos. We can give you chaos.

What the Premier League brought at the weekend, the quick breaks, the freedom to attack at selected moments, was more a kind of hyper-managed shock and awe, targeted speed and physicality born out of calculated risk, numbers, data, heavy briefings.

It was also exciting to watch, which is no bad thing in the world’s most tightly contested, space‑averse league. No doubt there will be tightening, a reaction to the reaction, instant counter‑moves and contingency planning. August can also be odd and silly season-ish, the dog days of a World Cup summer. But it did at times feel as if we were in a post‑something moment. If not quite post‑Pep, whose influence will continue to loom, a tactical Machiavelli with plenty of tapes still left in the vault.

Emergency services described extinguishing the blaze as a “significant and complex” operation, with eight fire engines and water carriers deployed to bring it under control.

UK Power Networks, which operates the electricity network across south-east England, had to isolate an overhead power cable while crews worked below.

A spokesperson for West Sussex fire and rescue service said: “Approximately 140 vehicles were damaged, and a number of the vehicles involved in this fire were parked at a site used for holiday parking. Any affected consumers are advised to contact their operator directly.”

There were no casualties, it said.

The fire also caused significant damage to two breakdown and recovery businesses and a banger racing team.

The Bears banger racing team said in a fundraiser that they had lost everything.

Autocovery and K&L Automotive had also previously donated abandoned vehicles to fire stations across West Sussex for training purposes, according to local reports.

Sussex police said a 67-year-old man arrested on suspicion of arson had been bailed pending further inquiries.

“Power was shut off to the immediate area, affecting a number of businesses and homes, and nearby roads were closed as a precaution,” a spokesperson said.

“Emergency services remain on scene at this time and the public are advised to avoid the area.”

“We are advising any passengers who are concerned that their vehicle might have been affected to contact their parking operator directly.

‘Project Magic’: RFL in talks with NRL over radical changes to investment deal

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 18:59:39 GMT

Super League clubs rejected £35m deal last week

The 14 owners due to discuss plans at meeting

The Rugby Football League is exploring radically different terms to the funding deal initially offered by Australia’s National Rugby League with talks under way over seeking a £50m loan package to replace the guaranteed investment of £35m that was rejected last week.

The Guardian has seen details of an alternative vision produced by Rugby League Commercial in a document entitled Project Magic, which the 14 Super League clubs owners will discuss at a meeting on Tuesday .

Nigel Wood, the RFL chief executive, is understood to have circulated the document to the Super League owners last Wednesday, the day before they voted to reject the NRL’s offer. Discussions between the two competitions over investment from Australia have been ongoing since meetings in Las Vegas in January, with the NRL chief executive, Peter V’Landys, due to visit the UK next week in the hope of finalising the deal.

The NRL offer would have seen it invest £7m a year for five years in return for a 10% stake in Super League, with the money to be distributed to the clubs. Instead of selling a stake in Super League, the Project Magic document details the RFL’s desire to seek from the NRL a £50m payment-in-kind loan, which it would use “to fund central growth initiatives and accelerate global expansion”.

In another significant departure, the £50m would be retained centrally by the RFL rather than distributed to the clubs, which may prove a sticking point for many. The Project Magic document details what the RFL describes as a 10-year plan to grow the sport, and includes ambitious targets such as expanding Super League to 18 or 20 clubs, launching a joint direct‑to-consumer streaming platform with the NRL for non-domestic markets and creating a fully professional women’s competition.

The RFL’s plans for investing the £50m are also outlined in detail, with £13.5m to be spent on improving the clubs’ commercial capabilities, £10m on the player pathway and £5m on broadcasting services.

An RFL source said that the loan proposal is no longer its preferred option, but it is being considered significant enough for the clubs to discuss on Tuesday.

While the Super League clubs were broadly united in rejecting the NRL’s initial offer, agreeing on a way forward may prove more difficult.

Many of the competition’s bigger clubs such as Wigan, Warrington and the champions Hull KR are strongly in favour of partnering with the NRL, whereas smaller clubs like Wakefield are more sceptical amid concerns they could be left behind.

Although the RFL appears to be advocating demanding an increase of almost 50% in funding from the NRL, it is unclear whether the Super League clubs will support the proposal, with many preferring a smaller cash injection to a centrally managed loan.

One source with knowledge of the discussions described Project Magic as an attempt by Wood to retain control and influence at the RFL if the NRL deal closes.

NRL sources have described its position as a “take it or leave it” however, and it is far from certain it would be willing to offer a £50m loan.

Moreover, there are further significant obstacles to the deal being completed, as the NRL is demanding significant governance reforms, including the creation of an independent commission to run the sport in the UK, which would further reduce the influence of the RFL.

The US has threatened to impose severe sanctions against any country or entity maintaining economic ties with Iran, hoping to achieve with economic measures what military means have so far failed to do.

Iran, meanwhile, vowed retaliation against any country that took part in the US-led isolation campaign.

Launching what he called Operation Economic Outcast, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, called it an unprecedented campaign and compared it with the D-day Normandy landings, a turning point in the second world war.

“Today, in that same spirit, we are launching an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe,” Bessent said on Monday. “Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone.”

Asked whether sanctions would be applied to China, which bought an estimated 80% of Iran’s shipped oil last year, he replied: “We want to make clear here today that no one is above the reach of US sanctions. That if they facilitate transactions and are part of the ecosystem that turns Iranian oil into money, into repression, they will be targeted.”

Bessent said the US had identified those that continued to deal with Iran and each violator would be given a deadline to cut ties or face US sanctions. He said the deadlines imposed would depend on individual circumstances.

“Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system,” he said. “The clock just started ticking.”

Bessent said Donald Trump was “making phone calls to world leaders with specific requests to cease their interactions with the regime”, but he did not specify whether the US president would talk to his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping.

China’s embassy in Washington told reporters: “Regarding the ​Iran issue, sanctions and pressure do not help resolve the problem. China calls on the relevant parties to take responsible actions and resolve the issue through political and diplomatic means.”

Tehran said it would retaliate against the sanctions using a range of measures. Maj Gen Ali Abdollahi, the armed forces’ chief of staff, said the retaliation could take the form of land, sea or air operations or cyber-attacks.

The announcement of secondary sanctions against Iran comes nearly six months after the the US and Israel launched an attack on Iran that killed its supreme leader Ali Khamenei. Early expectations that the regime in Tehran would collapse or agree to Washington’s demands to give up uranium enrichment and other key elements of its nuclear programme were dashed.

Hardliners appeared to strengthen their grip on government in Tehran and responded by declaring the closure of the strait of Hormuz, attacking ships that ignored its declaration. Trump imposed a counter-blockage on Iranian oil exports through the strait, leading to an impasse that has had profound effects on the global economy.

Sina Toossi, a senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy, said: “After nearly six months without a military or diplomatic victory, Washington appears to be trying to accomplish through intensified economic strangulation what military force has so far failed to achieve. But Tehran is answering that zero-sum approach with one of its own.”

The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, however, said further military action was not off the table. “By no means are we foreclosing using ‌kinetic strikes anywhere in the ​strait of Hormuz or around Iran,” Hegseth ⁠told reporters on Monday.

In apparent anticipation of the US measures, the United Arab Emirates, a close US and Israeli ally, announced it was suspending trade ties with Iran. Turkey, another trading partner with Iran, which has been critical of the US-led campaign against the Islamic Republic, has yet to respond to the US threat of sanctions.

Andrew Miller, a senior fellow at the Center for American Progress, said: “The announcement of new economic sanctions on Iran and those countries trading with it signals what is plain to all: this war has brought the United States no closer to eliminating Iran’s nuclear programme or crippling the Iranian regime. The prime minister’s remarks came hours after the US president, Donald Trump, showed little interest in retreating from the spat, posting on social media that Canada had been “ripping off the United States of America for years” and threatening a swath of new, economically devastating tariffs on cars and trucks.

Carney instructed his negotiators to walk away from trade talks last week. Tariffs on an array of Canadian products took effect over the weekend, affecting around 5% of Canada’s exports to the US, and Canada said it will retaliate in early September.

On Monday, Carney toured a shipyard with Quebec’s premier, telling attendees Canada “could not accept” a proposed trade deal that would have weakened French language protections after trade talks collapsed between the two countries last week, adding that his government “will not give what they have asked”.

The prime minister’s decision to abandon trade talks with the US spurred declarations from political leaders and pundits in Canada that the country is now fully locked into an economic war with its longtime ally.

Quebec, Canada’s predominantly French-speaking province, has long sought to protect its distinct identity, at times with laws that clashed with the federal government and the Canadian charter of rights and freedoms.

In recent years those rules have also frustrated US negotiators, who have framed them as trade irritants. Bill 96, for example, requires products sold in Quebec to have a French description and for trademarks using generic terms to be translated into French, while Bill 109 compels media services such as Netflix, Spotify and Apple to promote and prioritize French content for Quebec users.

Quebec’s premier, Christine Fréchette, said Carney had made the right decision in walking away from talks that looked to cross a “red line” for Francophones.

“Our culture, our language is central to our identity and it is important to exclude that from the negotiation table,” she told reporters over the weekend. “It’s something that is crucial for us and it won’t change, even though we are threatened with different tariffs, it won’t change. Polling from earlier in the month shows that dislike for Trump is highest in Quebec. Separatists in the province have seen a sharp decline in support amid the economic wounds inflicted by the US.

Last week, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, the sovereigntist politician most likely to emerge victorious in upcoming provincial elections, said his party would delay a possible referendum into seceding from Canada until Trump is out of office. On Monday, Trump’s top trade representative, Jamieson Greer, called reports that French language protections were up for debate a “a funny fake story”.

The Guardian view on Britain helping Ukraine: build the weapons independence Kyiv needs

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 17:53:47 GMT

Moscow hopes western politics will weaken support for Kyiv. The UK and Europe’s answer should be to make Ukraine increasingly capable of defending itself alone

The events of the past few days on Europe’s borders may mark a turning point in Russia’s war on Ukraine. While the political skies in Kyiv have darkened for Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the military picture looks brighter. Ukraine can already send swarms of drones against Russian oil facilities, e-commerce warehouses and airfields. Andy Burnham’s arrival in Kyiv marks a step forward. Britain is releasing classified information on its components of Scalp, the French version of the Anglo-French Storm Shadow cruise missile, enabling its assembly in Ukraine. This is more than another weapon for Kyiv. Britain is helping Ukraine become less dependent on the western armoury.

Moscow sabre-rattles, but Britain should hold its nerve. Kyiv has been at the mercy of its allies, waiting to replenish weapons stockpiles and release sophisticated arms. Producing its own hi-tech armoury gives Ukraine greater freedom of action because western governments have let go. Two years ago it was different. Joe Biden waited until November 2024 before letting Ukraine strike deep into Russia with US weapons. Yet thresholds once deemed dangerously escalatory have since been crossed without provoking a Russia-Nato war. Kyiv is now being trusted with something more consequential: a measure of weapons independence.

It needs this. Ukraine cannot overcome its manpower disadvantage by fighting Russia soldier for soldier for every kilometre of its vital eastern fortress belt, where Kyiv is losing ground. If Moscow can freely push ammunition, drones and equipment towards Donetsk, eventually something will give. Cruise missiles offer another strategy, making it harder and costlier for Russian forces to reach the front. Europe is thinking defensively too. Ukraine relies heavily on the US-made Patriots to down ballistic missiles, but global shortages of interceptors, a situation made worse by the US war with Iran, have left it exposed. With European help, Ukraine’s defence industry is developing an anti-ballistic system intended to reduce that dependence. Kyiv is ramping up its own ballistic missiles. If both are successful, Ukraine would be better able both to strike and defend itself without first appealing to Washington.

War is a terrible thing, but what is the alternative? Moscow offers little evidence that territorial success would satisfy it. Despite enormous casualties and painfully slow advances, Vladimir Putin rejects proposals that fail to meet Russia’s broader conditions while expanding military power rather than preparing his people for compromise. Then there is the rise of the far right in Europe, large parts of which are pro-Russia. If Mr Putin thinks that the outlook for Russia’s position will improve politically over the next two or three years, he will bargain harder. Why accept merely the Donbas today if the coalition supporting Ukraine might be weaker tomorrow? That option disappears if either Russia’s war burden becomes intolerable or the west convincingly insulates its material help from political change.

History offers lessons. In Vladislav M Zubok’s Collapse: The Fall of the Soviet Union, Boris Yeltsin is startled to hear that Ukrainians, including millions of Russian speakers, want independence in 1991. Once convinced this is their democratic will, however, he accepts it. Russia, he says, will “recognise this new political reality”. Mr Putin starts from the same sense of historical intimacy and reaches the opposite conclusion: that Ukraine’s democratic choices cannot override Russia’s claim to a privileged role in its future. That is a revanchist error he ought to regret.

Along with Macau, it was the only place in China where the anniversary could be publicly marked and the truth preserved.

But the crackdown on the 2019 uprising in Hong Kong has crushed the freedoms that the region once enjoyed. That year’s vigil was the last. On Friday, two leaders of the Hong Kong Alliance, which organised the commemoration, were convicted of incitement to subversion under the draconian national security law. Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, and Chow Hang-tung, 41, face up to 10 years in jail.

A third defendant, the 74-year-old former legislator Albert Ho, pleaded guilty in January. All three have been imprisoned since their arrests in 2021. The court ruled that the alliance’s stated aim to “end one-party dictatorship” in itself constituted using unlawful means to overthrow the Chinese government – despite acknowledging that the group never used or advocated violence, or even set out a path to its goal.

The convictions are shameful, but not surprising. They follow the jailing of the prominent pro-democracy activists known as the “Hong Kong 47” in late 2024 and the 20-year sentence handed to the media tycoon and activist Jimmy Lai in February. Yet while this trial shows the authorities’ determination to eradicate Hong Kong’s previous freedoms, it also reflects the Communist party’s determination to control and rewrite history across China.

Hundreds, perhaps thousands, of people were killed in the 1989 massacre. Xi Jinping made a rare reference to the events last week, reaffirming the party’s “correct” response, in a speech paying tribute to the former leader Jiang Zemin. But the subject remains one of the most taboo in a country long adept at erasing uncomfortable truths – so sensitive that even words such as “remember” and “today” are censored on social media on the anniversary. This June, the Tiananmen Mothers group of bereaved relatives, who have long mourned under heavy police escort, were barred from visiting their loved ones’ graves on the date of the killings.

Against such brutal edicts, memory appears fragile. Most younger people on the mainland have no idea of what happened. Yet late last year, previously unseen footage suddenly emerged of the court martial of a general who defied the order to use force against demonstrators. The video was posted on YouTube – which is blocked in China – and sheds new light on events. General Xu Qinxian, who was jailed and lived under heavy restrictions until his death in 2021, said that a commander imposing the order might become “a sinner in history”. Whoever leaked the footage, and whatever their reasons for doing so, it is clear that some still resist the national amnesia.

Remembrance and mourning are not crimes. In a message to Andy Burnham, Ms Chow, a barrister who studied law in the UK, warned that Britain had a “non-delegable duty to adopt a more robust stance” to China. She was right. The UK was the other signatory of the treaty that supposedly preserved Hong Kong’s relative autonomy until 2047. For years in the annual vigils, Ms Chow, Mr Lee and other courageous Hong Kong people stood up for those on the mainland who had been silenced. Others should now stand up and speak for them as they pay the price for that solidarity.

Twelve people arrested after A66 crash that killed seven including two police officers

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 17:51:54 GMT

Nine men and three women aged between 19 and 61 arrested as part of investigation into events leading to deadly collision

Twelve people have been arrested on suspicion of offences including being involved with organised crime as part of the investigation into events leading to a crash on the A66 that killed two police officers and five others.

Cleveland police confirmed that nine men and three women were detained by officers investigating the events that led up to PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough dying when a Volkswagen Passat travelling the wrong way on the A66 near Middlesbrough collided with their marked armed response vehicle. All five men who were in the second car, aged between 17 and 23, were pronounced dead at the scene.

Police said some of those arrested as part of the A66 investigation, whose ages range from 19 to 61, were suspected of various offences.

Four people were arrested on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group and four on suspicion of possessing a firearm, while four of the suspects were also accused of possessing class A and B drugs with intent to supply.

Police have said the five men killed in the crash may have had links to “serious and organised criminal activity”, adding that four of those killed in the car that hit the police vehicle had previous convictions.

The fatal crash sparked a wave of concern about a social media trend for posting videos of dangerous, high-speed driving, which the prime minister, Andy Burnham, on Monday called “truly reprehensible”.

Cleveland police said there was currently “no evidence that filming of the activities on Friday night and Saturday morning was for the purposes of TikTok”, but Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, wants assurances from the tech companies and from the online communications regulator Ofcom “that this content is being proactively sought and removed”.

At least one of those killed in Saturday’s crash had previously posted reckless driving footage online.

The Guardian on Monday found a video on YouTube seen 2.5m times showing a Honda being driven at breakneck speed through a council estate and then down a narrow country road. Google, which owns YouTube, terminated the account after being asked for comment.

The arrests have come as part of a “wide-scale investigation into the criminality which took place” in the hours leading up to the crash, which has involved the help of officers and staff from Durham, Northumbria and North Yorkshire police forces.

As part of the investigation a Volvo XC60, believed to be associated with the activities of the passengers of the Volkswagen Passat, had been identified and recovered, police said.

Assistant chief constable Wayne Fox said his force had engaged in “a fast-moving and complex investigation, with significant links to serious and organised criminal activity” and claimed the “events of that tragic night will have a lasting and profound impact on the Cleveland area and the communities we seek to protect”.

He said: “We have a duty to respond to, and thoroughly investigate, the serious criminal activity that resulted in this fatal incident, and to bring all those responsible to justice. Our robust response will continue in the weeks and months to come, as we continue to tackle those that seek to cause harm to our communities and tackle serious and organised crime.

“Officers and staff across Cleveland have shown incredible resilience in continuing their work in the face of tragedy. Two of their colleagues lost their lives while serving the people of Cleveland and, while the impact will be felt by our people for a long time to come, they have continued to act with the utmost professionalism.

“I am also extremely grateful for the support we have received, and continue to receive, from the public of Cleveland and our wider police family.”

Earlier on BBC Radio 5 Live, defence minister, Luke Pollard said he wanted to see social media companies “step up”.

“I think we all need to give the police time,” he said. “But there’s also things we can be doing in the meantime to make sure that the internet is a safer place for everyone, that doesn’t celebrate and load views and therefore financial incentives on people to generate such awful content.”

Earlier this month, five young men were killed in Ireland and four other people injured after the car the men were travelling in was driven the wrong way down the M50 motorway.

More than £500,000 has been raised for the families of the two officers who died, while floral tributes have also been left beside the A66 close to the site of Saturday’s crash.

One said: “Behind every uniform is a person with a life, family, friends and people whose lives they have touched along the way.”

The Duke of Sussex has stepped down from the board of a major African wildlife charity that had been at the centre of a human rights controversy.

The charity’s admission followed an independent review into allegations made by members of the Baka community.

In a 2024 report published by the Mail on Sunday newspaper, community members accused African Parks rangers of beating, waterboarding and raping locals to stop them from accessing their ancestral forests, which are now in a conservation area.

After the review, African Parks published a statement acknowledging that human rights abuses occurred in the Odzala-Kokoua national park, which it manages. It said that it had improved its safeguarding processes both at the park and institutionally.

A spokesperson for Harry said the duke, who was president of the charity for six years before he became a member of its board of directors in 2023, remained an active and avid supporter of African Parks.

“The duke is proud of his 10 years with African Parks and fully supports the ongoing strengthening of its board,” the spokesperson said.

“His commitment to conservation in Africa continues, and he remains a supporter of African Parks’ mission.”

Survival International, a global human rights charity that campaigns for the rights of Indigenous people, had called on Harry to step down as a member of the board.

Caroline Pearce, the executive director of Survival International, said it was “outrageous that for 10 years Prince Harry has served African Parks” while people working for it had “been responsible for abuse and violence against Indigenous people. His departure doesn’t undo that record — African Parks itself must now be held accountable, and must abandon this model of fortress conservation for good.”

Founded 26 years ago, African Parks manages more than 20m hectares (50m acres) in partnership with 13 African governments and hundreds of local communities.

African Parks expressed “deep gratitude” to the duke on concluding his tenure after his 10-year commitment to the organisation.

“His relationship with the organisation dates back to Malawi in July 2016, when he supported one of the largest elephant translocations in history. He served as president for six years before being appointed a member of the board of directors,” it said.

“Over the years, the duke has brought global attention to the urgent need for biodiversity protection for the benefit of people and wildlife, and has contributed greatly to promoting philanthropy for the cause of conservation in Africa. The duke remains deeply committed to this cause, and remains a strong supporter of African Parks’ work.”

The announcement comes as the Duke and Duchess of Sussex are due to relocate to the UK from California with their children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five.

What comes in the wake of Woke 1.0?

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 17:33:03 GMT

Readers respond to Nesrine Malik’s article about the shift away from US society’s progressive and inclusive zeitgeist

Regarding Nesrine Malik’s article (Here is the news from the US: Woke 1.0 is over. But what did progressives do wrong?, 18 August), the mistake of Woke 1.0 was to believe that a self-evident truth was, well, a self-evident truth. I grew up in a divided society in which it was crystal clear, at least to my community, that we were second-class citizens. Nothing ever seemed to change and in the end we fought a war over it. Today attitudes are a lot different, but new truths are universally embedded.

What we learned was that the self-evident truth of “first-class” citizens was that their position was one established long ago by right and might. Against that sense of rightness, you cannot appeal to another truth that is diametrically opposed. I raised boys and girls in a progressive, liberal home. It was some surprise to me that my boys were not onboard with Woke 1.0. Their truth was Jordan Peterson’s “equality of access, not equality of outcome”, and a belief that their own privilege as middle-class, intelligent white males was good luck to be defended.

Phrases such as “toxic masculinity” and “check your privilege” were heard as an attack, and qualifiers like “not all men” and “I don’t mean you” as insincere.

It is not all doom and gloom. We chip away, parents and siblings, and even in the pushback in defence of Woke 1.0 at home, we feel the softening. I think that is where the hope lies in the next phase of progressiveness – the changing of minds in the home and among friends, one self-evident truth at a time. That is not to deny the need for the public political 2.0 movement that will inevitably arise, but to acknowledge that its roots will be in smaller truths and smaller conversations. So you can start now, and with hope. Name and address supplied

“Defund the police” is one of the most tone-deaf expressions I’ve ever heard. Safety is high on the human hierarchy of needs. Most Americans associate policing with safety. Something like “community policing” would resonate with most Americans and pique curiosity in how police and citizens can work together.

This is only one example of how liberals snatch defeat from the jaws of victory. We need to forget ideological purity and instead formulate simple, easily understood positions that point towards positive solutions to real problems. We have to be more than “not them”. Bert LoveShrub Oak, New York state, US

Nesrine Malik asks what harm progressives did. I think CS Lewis summed it up nicely: “Of all tyrannies, a tyranny sincerely exercised for the good of its victims may be the most oppressive. It would be better to live under robber barons than under omnipotent moral busybodies. The robber baron’s cruelty may sometimes sleep, his cupidity may at some point be satiated; but those who torment us for our own good will torment us without end for they do so with the approval of their own conscience.”David ForsterPenzance, Cornwall

As a retired special school headteacher, I warmly welcome Alan Milburn’s proposal to expand supported internships for young people with special educational needs and disabilities (Turbocharge special needs internships to help tackle UK youth jobs crisis, says Milburn, 16 August). For too long society has concentrated on what these young people cannot do rather than what they can, with the right support and opportunity.

I often meet former students who, once established in a workplace, have not only held down jobs but progressed to positions of greater responsibility.

Alan Milburn should pay more attention to the £2.5bn of national insurance contribution (NIC) exemptions for employers taking on young workers under 21 and apprentices under 25. Only the second is mentioned in passing in his interim report. Neither is included in its total spending on employment for young people. Adding these to the Department for Work and Pensions employment service costs would have very significantly reduced the 25 to 1 ratio of benefits to employment that has been so much publicised in the media.

Take-up rates for these reliefs introduced in 2015 do not appear to exist. HMRC-commissioned surveys revealed that over half the 340,000 employers claiming young workers NIC exemptions were not aware that they were.

Milburn could switch the resources to specific funding of jobs and apprenticeships to provide better, more visible incentives. This could lead to more than the “modest impact” of the only partly known funding at present. Adrian SinfieldEdinburgh

If my experience of just one young person with special needs being employed by a major hotel group is anything to go by, we should be emphasising the value that these young people bring to the workplace and what an incredible asset they can be. A young woman was waitressing at breakfast in a high-end hotel recently. She was very good at her job, really efficient with such a smile and great spirit. She clearly loved her job. None of the surly service you sometimes get from someone who feels the job is “below” them.

We had a chat and she told me that she was neurodiverse and all about the project that supported her into this job. Chatting with her made me feel that employers were missing out on employing some of their best staff if they don’t get involved with projects providing supported internships. As these young people are so highly motivated, they return the investment in bucket loads. Joy McLaughlanLondon

We need public records on the delivery of social housing

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 17:32:53 GMT

Marco Scalvini on why it’s necessary to know what was promised by developers and local authorities, what arrived and what it costs to live in social housing

Your editorial on London’s social housing (16 August) makes a persuasive case for treating social housing as economic infrastructure. However, infrastructure is normally monitored and social housing is not, either when it is delivered or across the years in which it is meant to remain affordable. A home is counted as affordable on the day that planning permission is granted and is rarely examined again, through completion, tenure change and the service charges that can make it unaffordable within months of occupation, as your reporting on shared ownership has shown.

Southwark, like almost every local authority, publishes every pound of the financial contributions developers pay, yet offers no scheme-level account of whether the promised social rented homes were built. The consequences showed at Elephant and Castle, where residents needed three years of freedom of information battles to force out the viability evidence behind an affordable housing commitment that ended at 82 social rented homes in place of more than a thousand. By the time it came out, the estate was gone, and a record that arrives after demolition can only count the losses. On the Old Kent Road, where the council plans around 20,000 new homes and only a few thousand are yet built or under way, the record could still be kept in time to shape what is delivered.

You close with Nye Bevan’s idea of housing as an essential service like the NHS, and the comparison is instructive. The NHS publishes waiting lists and inspection results, and is held to them, whereas housing has no equivalent, whoever the landlord is. If social homes are economic infrastructure, they deserve public, dated records of what was promised, what arrived and what it costs to live in them. Marco ScalviniLondon

Problems brewing for the proper pint as Camra membership falls

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 17:01:13 GMT

Cost of living has hit campaign group while multinationals are threatening to squeeze out independent breweries

For centuries, the wooden real ale pump has been the hallmark of a good British boozer. But now problems are brewing for the proper pint, as the Campaign for Real Ale has seen its membership sink to an eight-year low and its accounts show it is firmly in the red, making an £800,000 loss last year.

Real ale is a traditional draught cask beer, a “living” product that is produced and stored in its cask. It differs from a cold, fizzy lager, in which the yeast is killed and carbon dioxide is added. Real ale contains live yeast so it continues fermenting until it is served.

Outside the Devonshire pub in Soho, central London, there is an ever-present horde of drinkers downing pints of Guinness, a stout made by the multinational company Diageo. But the landlord and co-owner Oisín Rogers says: “Real ale is all I drink.”

He says: “It is a properly handmade British product produced in exactly the same way it has been for centuries. It has never been industrialised like some of the other drinks that are for sale in bars in London.” His favourite tipple, is, appropriately, a pint of Landlord, made by the family-owned Timothy Taylor brewery in Keighley, West Yorkshire.

Tom Stainer, Camra’s chief executive, says independent breweries are facing unfair competition from multinationals. If you walk into a pub on the high street, you are often confronted with the same few beers, most of which are made by the same large companies, Stainer says.

“Our recent beer report highlighted that the beers people want aren’t available in bars because of the ways the huge international brewers operate – they have a stranglehold on the industry,” he says. “We call it an illusion of choice – a lot of people walk into bars and don’t realise everything in front of them is owned by the same big company.”

He says these “big global brewers who have deep pockets and huge influence” make it “hard for small brewers to get to market”. The incentives offered to large pub companies include cheap packages for beers, wine and soft drinks, with a multi-year tie-in, and minimum purchase orders where “pubs are forced to sell a certain amount of this product”.

Stainer adds: “We have heard of pubs taking off independent beers because they are too popular and stop people buying that product they have a minimum purchase order for.”

Camra is calling for the Competition and Markets Authority to investigate the big beer companies’ stranglehold on the market.

There are no such problems at the King Charles I pub in King’s Cross. As an independent, community-owned venue, the team can choose what’s on tap. They have a healthy range of cask beers, swapped out every five weeks.

Matt Roberts, the manager, says: “I like to choose local beers – today we have one from Southwark, some from Kent and one from the West Midlands. Cask ale is still very popular, it makes up around 30% of our sales. We are lucky we don’t have a big pub company telling us what to sell.”

Despite the delicious range of cask ale on offer, including the very drinkable Bankside Blonde by Southwark Brewing Company, Guinness still appears to be the order of the day among the customers.

Camra is facing a nadir: last September it announced it had been forced to cancel its pivotal Great British Beer festival, formerly the largest of its kind in the UK, for the foreseeable future due to financial pressures. Writing in the accounts, the chair, Ash Corbett-Collins, said it had been “one of the most challenging years Camra has faced”, pointing to a restructuring in which “a number of roles were sadly made redundant”.

The cost of living crisis is making it more difficult to run a membership organisation, Stainer says. “When you look at your bank balance each month, membership might be something you might economise to offset your huge energy bill or the rise in food prices.” A Camra membership is £35 a year.

Andrew Balding making serious tilt at prestigious British Flat trainers’ crown

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 17:00:17 GMT

Balding says victory is ‘very unlikely’ but there is a good chance he will improve on second-place finishes achieved in 2021 and 2024

The British Flat trainers’ championship winners’ club is among the most exclusive in the sport, with just a dozen new members through its doors in the past 50 years. Aidan O’Brien, John Gosden, Richard Hannon Jr and Charlie Appleby, meanwhile, are the only trainers to win a first title outright this century.

Becoming the fifth seems to be the last thing on Andrew Balding’s mind, however, despite an exceptional week at York’s Ebor festival that took his prize-money total for the season past £7m, his domestic Group One tally since 10 July to four and left him just under £700,000 behind O’Brien in the title race.

“Our luck will run out at some stage,” Balding said on Racing TV’s Luck On Sunday over the weekend, “but we are enjoying it while we can. The trainers’ championship is the least important thing in my opinion, if the right races are abroad then that’s where they should go.

“It’s a big climb anyway and Aidan will win £2m more before the end of the year, so it’s very unlikely anyway.”

It is true that a good deal would need to fall into place for Balding to improve on his second-place finishes in 2024 and 2021, behind O’Brien and Charlie Appleby respectively. “It’s a big climb anyway,” though, is hardly the language of an ambitious and ultra-competitive player in any sport – and you do not build and maintain a 250-horse stable in the results-driven world of Flat racing if you are anything but.

Balding, as he is the first to admit, enjoyed a huge slice of racing luck when he inherited the trainer’s licence at one of the sport’s finest and most historic yards from his father, Ian, in 2003.

Park House Stables, near Watership Down in Hampshire, was founded by John Porter, the most successful trainer of the Victorian era, in the 1860s, and was home to 23 Classic winners – including three Triple Crown winners – between 1868 and 1900.

Porter was champion trainer in 1899, while Ian Balding, who died on 2 January this year, was a second champion at the yard in 1971 when he prepared the brilliant Mill Reef to win the Derby, the King George and the Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe.

A rich inheritance in any walk of life can be easily squandered, but Andrew Balding has instead built the operation to an entirely new level over the past 23 years. As a result, he not only has the proven Group One quality required to mount a serious challenge for the title – he has the numbers, too.

John Gosden, in 2023, was the last title-winning trainer based in Britain. He saddled 130 winners from 600 runners for a total of £7.21m in prize money, including seven Group One winners, beating O’Brien’s total of £6.46m – from just 21 winners in all, eight in Group Ones – by £750,000.

Mostahdaf’s wins in the Prince of Wales’s Stakes and International Stakes made him the stable’s biggest individual winner by far, with £1.13m all by himself. But the top 10 earners combined picked up a total of £4.05m, and Gosden ran no fewer than 210 individual horses over the year. It was sheer force of numbers that ultimately got him over the line.

Balding, with £7.06m this season, is already within sight of Gosden’s winning total three years ago. O’Brien, though, has already banked £7.77m and is on course to eclipse his personal record of £8.12m in the 2025 championship.

But whether he will add “another £2m” is debatable. O’Brien has won the St Leger for the past three seasons and has the top two – Christmas Day and Pierre Bonnard – in the ante-post betting for the Doncaster Classic next month, so we can probably give him that. He is also likely to field the favourite in most – or perhaps all – of Britain’s five Group Ones for juveniles.

But O’Brien is not omnipotent (though admittedly there are times when it can feel that way). He has never won all five of the juvenile Group Ones in a single season (and while he was a nose away from doing so in 2017, when Laurens pipped September in the Fillies’ Mile, that remains the only time he has landed four).

Among the remaining all-aged Group One prizes, Balding’s Falmouth Stakes winner, Blue Bolt, is favourite for the Sun Chariot Stakes and third-favourite for the QEII on Champions Day. And both John Gosden’s Ombudsman and the winner last year, Calandagan, are in front of O’Brien’s Constitution River in the betting for the Champion Stakes, the biggest prize left on the schedule and a race where Balding’s Kalpana, the King George winner, could yet emerge as a contender.

But it was quantity, rather than Group Ones, that made the difference for Gosden three years ago and Balding has already sent out 218 individual horses this year.

Musselburgh: 2.15 Vegasmile 2.45 Aodhan 3.15 Only Dream Big 3.45 Furhaan (nb) 4.15 Coconut Bay 4.45 Jojo Rabbit

Lingfield: 2.30 Havana Touch 3.00 Thai Baht 3.30 Let’s Go Hugo 4.00 Musical Soldier (nap) 4.30 Dialstone 5.02 Sovereign Bright

Stratford-upon-Avon: 5.10 Diamond Grace 5.40 French Diablo 6.15 Beorma 6.45 Getmyfriend 7.15 Youdecide 7.45 Roccana Rose

Fifteen of those have already contributed at least £50,000 to the total and there will be useful prizes for horses of that calibre all over the country as the turf campaign concludes. Balding’s three handicap winners at York last week picked up nearly £200,000, and there is even a sprinkling of £40,000 and £30,000 races on the all-weather in November and December to consider too if the race were to get really tight.

Balding is still a long-shot for a first trainers’ title, but nothing like as big an outsider as he was this time last week. While the right races for a horse such as Item, the International Stakes winner, might well be elsewhere, there are hordes of talented horses in the stable, with plenty of targets to choose from in the months ahead.

Balding played an impressively straight bat to the championship talk on Sunday but having worked so hard, this year and since 2003, to get to this point, is a title tilt truly “the least important thing” on his mind? “I’ve lost count of how many messages I’ve received over the years about my appearance,” the 48-year-old wrote. “Especially that I have ugly teeth and thin hair. That I have an ugly ‘wart’ on my nose and well-meaning advice to get some Botox.”

Frederiksen’s global profile has grown this year as she stood up to US president’s repeated claims on Greenland, a semi-autonomous Danish territory. She is also a staunch supporter of Ukraine against the Russian onslaught.

In a moment of striking candour, Frederiksen admitted annoyance with pushy beauty advice while offering her own guidance how to deal with it.

She said she did not volunteer opinions about other people’s looks and said that “I’m perfectly fine with my body – as it is when you’re a woman approaching 50.”

Frederiksen said she was fine to stay in conversation with the public on a range of topics but encouraged Danes to set the bar higher with their chosen subject matter.

“If you’re going to write to me (and you’re more than welcome to), I hope you’ll use your time to talk about something more meaningful,” she said. “Not my nose.”

Although the mean-spirited suggestions made her feel “indignant”, she said, “today, I’m sending an extra loving thought to all of you who have to put up with the ‘perfect imperfections’ we all walk around with every day.”

Rupert Lowe, the leader of Restore Britain, is on course to earn as much from the social media platform X as he does from his salary as an MP, after surging income from posts that include demands for mass deportations.

Lowe has earned £932 an hour for his posts on X, formerly Twitter, since the start of the year, according to his own declarations in the register of MPs’ financial interests, which detail how many hours he has spent on X for each payment he received from the platform.

The figure is more than twice the £377 an hour on average he earned last year. His hourly rate rose steeply again this summer, reaching £1,476 since the start of June.

X critics claim it is further evidence that X is favouring and incentivising divisive political content, pulling the UK’s political discourse to the right. Elon Musk, the site’s owner, has repeatedly amplified Lowe’s posts.

Under X’s revenue-sharing scheme, premium subscribers such as Lowe are paid based on the performance of their posts. The scheme resulted in record payouts last year. The platform recently announced forthcoming changes, designed to reward original content and commentary.

Lowe’s total income from X since the 2024 general election has now surpassed £105,000. He earned more than half of that in the first eight months of 2026.

Should his average earnings for 2026 so far continue throughout the year, he would earn just over £93,000 – close to the current MPs’ £98,599 annual salary. He could easily exceed that figure should the higher rate of earnings of recent months persist.

Lowe has previously said he donates his net MP’s salary to charities and worthy causes in his constituency of Great Yarmouth.

The politician’s extraordinary success on X has led to concerns among some campaigners, who fear it is a sign that Musk’s site is effectively funding an MP that reflects the hard-right views of the billionaire.

“We tend to treat a politician’s online reach and their income as two separate stories, but for Rupert Lowe they’re part of the same mechanism,” said Ambrose Pym, a researcher covering the far right and technology who analysed Lowe’s rising X earnings. “The more his content is seen, the more X pays him for it.

“Scrutiny is rightly falling on other sources of foreign money in British politics. However, a US-based billionaire simultaneously paying and boosting an ideologically aligned British politician through his own platform is going strikingly under-reported. X’s financial and reach incentive structure rewards division and is shaping British politics with almost none of the scrutiny it deserves.”

Lowe, who founded Restore Britain after leaving Nigel Farage’s Reform UK, describes his party’s most significant achievement as “dragging mass deportations [of migrants] into mainstream politics”.

Asked about his accelerating X earnings, Lowe told the Guardian: “If I wanted to make money, I would not be in politics. I donate my entire net MP salary to local charities in my constituency – being a politician is the most expensive job I’ve ever had.”

His recent posts on X show the extraordinary amount of engagement the Restore leader secures on the platform. Over the weekend, one of his posts stated: “An illegal migrant could read ten thousand Home Office pamphlets in some woeful attempt to ‘integrate’, I’d still want him deported.

“They broke into our country – they are not welcome here, and they all need to be removed. This is not complicated.” It received 1.3m views, 25,000 likes and 3,000 reposts.

Last week, a post about how the UK should replicate Portugal’s ban on the burqa in many public spaces received almost a million views.

Lowe’s previous posts have included describing diversity policies as a “wicked, malicious, viperous cancer” and have criticised illegal migrants as “unvetted foreign males” loitering “where your daughter walks home”.

The Guardian has contacted X with a request for comment.

Burnham’s visit to Kyiv marks a renewal of badly needed support for Ukraine

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 16:33:22 GMT

As well as pledging military help and diplomatic backing, the prime minister could be useful in dealing with the US

Since moving into Downing Street in July, Andy Burnham – a foreign policy neophyte – has expressed strong support for Ukraine. But on Monday he saw the bitter human cost of the war up close for the first time, visiting Kyiv during his first international trip as prime minister.

The occasion was the 35th anniversary of Ukraine’s independence. Volodymyr Zelenskyy gave awards to the families of fallen soldiers. Relatives wept, hugging Ukraine’s president. Photos of young men in their prime were shown on a giant screen.

The setting was St Sophia cathedral in the old heart of the Ukrainian capital. Built in the 11th century, the building predates Moscow and is a symbol of Ukraine’s ancient statehood. Next to it were modern weapons used by Kyiv in its struggle against Russia, including quadcopter drones and unmanned land robots.

In a speech in front of other western leaders, Burnham compared Ukraine’s fight to that waged by Britain during the darkest days of the second world war. “My nation kept the flame of European freedom alive in the 20th century, you hold that flame in the 21st,” he declared.

Like other high-profile visitors, Burnham arrived with a gift. Since 2023 the UK and France has been providing Kyiv with long-range Storm Shadow or Scalp (as the French version is known) cruise missiles, used to knock out Russian naval ships and command centres.

It was now handing over British blueprints for key components, Burnham said, so Ukraine could eventually make its own version with France.

More Storm Shadows could go some way to dealing with Ukraine’s biggest problem – the wave of ballistic missiles fired by Russia that rain down on Kyiv and other cities most nights. As of now, Ukraine has run out of US-made Patriotic interceptors capable of shooting them down. The Trump administration is disinclined to provide more.

The British cruise missiles carry a larger payload than the long-range drones favoured by Kyiv. They could be used to destroy enemy ballistic missile launch systems, which can be quickly moved, and are dotted around sites in western Russia. Depending on their range, they could also disable military runways and aerodromes.

But nobody expects production to start soon. In the meantime, the Kremlin has responded with characteristic belligerence. Vladimir Putin’s press spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said Moscow would destroy any Ukrainian Storm Shadow factories, and accused London of taking part in the war and adding “fuel to the fire” though it is France that is helping with building them.

Last week Russia threatened “consequences” over the supply of British drones to Kyiv and withdrew its ambassador from London. It is unclear how Putin might escalate further. He has already sent assassins to poison Russian dissidents on UK territory including the murder in 2006 of Alexander Litvinenko, killed with radioactive tea.

Burnham appears unmoved by what he dubbed “outrageous” Russian threats, an encouraging sign for Kyiv. On Monday he pointed out that it was Putin who “started the fire” with his illegal and unprovoked invasion, and assured Zelenskyy of his “personal commitment” to Kyiv’s existential cause.

Ukraine has warmly welcomed the Storm Shadow initiative. Oleksandr Merezhko, head of the Ukrainian parliament’s foreign affairs committee, told the Guardian he hoped manufacturing could begin in “months, not years”. “We have proved many times we can do impossible things in producing weaponry,” he said, adding that the missile strengthened Kyiv’s position in negotiations with Moscow.

Of Burnham’s visit, he added: “For us, it’s hugely symbolic and important. It illustrates that for the UK Ukraine remains a top priority. You are an important bridge and have rectified the situation whenever we have a crisis in our relations with the US. Your king is a valuable diplomatic tool and puts in a good word for us with Trump.”

The trip also signalled to allies that the UK will continue to play a leading role in the coalition of the willing after the departure of Keir Starmer. Co-hosting a coalition meeting for the first time, Burnham said Europe would do everything it could to source more Patriotic interceptors for Ukraine. Zelenskyy has asked for 300 to help the country survive the coming winter.

Burnham’s speech made clear that he regards Ukraine’s struggle as Britain’s too – at a time when the US has in effect given up on its attempts to broker a peace deal, and has halted direct military aid. “Ukraine has been Europe’s protector, not a drain on our security but the frontline in keeping Europe safe,” he said. “The Ukrainian people deserve not just our continued support but our gratitude and respect.”

Ukrainian leaders and soldiers are grateful for British diplomatic and moral support, though they know that London’s military power is limited. Storm Shadow is deemed to have been one of the UK’s most useful contributions but stockpiles were modest.

Ukraine’s focus has been on developing its own long-range drones and cruise missiles, such as Fire Point’s Flamingo, which have been used to strike refineries and warehouses deep inside Russia. The goal is to attack Russia with 1,000 drones and some missiles a day this year, not when Storm Shadow production lines are ready.

But the deal that Burnham has agreed with Zelenskyy is an important renewal of goodwill. At some point Zelenskyy will probably need the help of European allies whenever the White House re-engages with the peace process. Burnham may become an important interlocutor with Trump, and today’s trip is from Ukraine’s perspective an encouraging start.

Green Man review – Wolf Alice, Shame and secret sets keep the Welsh festival’s flame burning

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 16:22:02 GMT

Bannau Brycheiniog, WalesThe traditional fire might be banned this year, but festivalgoers are treated by energetic performances by Four Tet, Tamikrest and Westside Cowboy

Driving towards the bucolic Welsh valley that’s home to the Green Man festival feels a little apocalyptic this year. Charred peat and grassland smoulder on the hillsides, the remnants of one of the 20 wildfires that blazed through south and west Wales the previous week. The dangerously dry conditions pose a problem for the festival organisers: the traditional closing ceremony, during which a towering effigy of the titular Green Man adorned with punters’ handwritten wishes is set alight, has been cancelled. A sensible decision, but one that left longtime festival-goers with a serious question: where would all those wishes go?

Then, the heavens open. Manchester quartet Westside Cowboy pack out the main stage arena on Friday afternoon, thousands of soggy cagoules bobbing along to the band’s charmingly ramshackle blend of British indie and amiable Americana. “We were over there last year,” grins vocalist and guitarist Jimmy Bradbury, gesturing towards the significantly smaller Rising stage. They’re clearly over the moon – and it’s infectious. To close the set, the band down instruments – save a guitar and a handheld drum – and gather round one mic for a rallying performance of In the Morning. The recorded version sounds like a lullaby, but here they transform it into a euphoric boot-stomping finale.

That energy charges through the rest of the day, even as the rain clears up. With his exhilarating blend of highlife, funk and electro, Ghanaian singer Ata Kak bounds across the stage with enough zeal to fuel a small army. London post-punks Shame incite endless moshpits with their rowdy, self-deprecating swagger and calls to “free Palestine”. Dry Cleaning’s Florence Shaw delivers a typically off-kilter performance of her jaded, spoken-word indie, bringing out Jeff Tweedy – of headliners Wilco – for the first ever duo performance of My Soul/Half Pint. Over in the Far Out tent, Karla Chubb of Sprints plucks a teenager out of the crowd to take over her guitar during their final song, Little Fix, freeing her up to crowd surf on one condition: “You have to promise to not touch my bum,” she tells the audience.

Malian rock band Tamikrest supply the psychedelic desert blues, and Gambian party-starter Suntou Susso orchestrates a giant conga line through the crowd. Cult producer Daniel Avery maintains the intensity, but in a surprising way:: all headbanging metal guitars and ferocious live drum’n’bass beats, only briefly punctuated by the pulsating techno he’s better known for. Anyone left slightly disappointed gets their fill at Four Tet’s headline slot, which crescendoes from ambient techno into body-rattling bass.

Green Man’s lineup is hardly built around old-school star power. Still, both buzzy New York electro duo Fcukers and Wolf Alice make a convincing case for energetic performers, the latter in particular during the weekend’s final headline set. Clad head-to-toe in leather, Wolf Alice’s Ellie Rowsell commands the stage with powerhouse vocals that oscillate between indie crooning, near-operatic belting and snarling, punky screams, and leads the crowd in a collective howl at the moon. After a performance of that wattage, the replacement for the burning ceremony can’t help but feel a bit anticlimactic: Scotland’s Pictish Trail lead an acoustic performance of the Waterboys’ The Whole of the Moon, accompanied by aerial acrobats in glittering costumes, but the restless crowd never really get going.

Thankfully, a secret closing set brings together Fcukers, Hot Chip’s Alexis Taylor, Way Dynamic, the Itch, Another Country $$$$ and SNL UK comedian Jack Shep for rounds of back-to-back DJ sets with crowd-pleasing Madonna remixes and a Don’t You Want Me singalong. It makes for a euphoric finale, and wish fulfilment of the highest order.

KRON4 News in San Francisco reported that York was initially arrested on suspicion of engaging in prostitution but that count was amended to a charge of disorderly conduct. He was also charged with possessing criminal tools.

A no contest plea is not an admission of guilt but the defendant in question does accept the punishment for the alleged crimes in question. The East Palestine Police Department and the Mahoning Valley Human Trafficking Task Force were involved in the arrest. York, 46, was born and raised in Youngstown, a 30-minute drive from East Palestine and still has a home in the area.

York is the nephew of former 49ers majority owner Edward J DeBartolo Jr. York took day to day control of the 49ers in 2008 when he became the team’s CEO. After acquiring his mother’s shares, he became the team’s principal owner in 2024.

“As this is a legal matter, which has been resolved, we will not be providing any further comment at this time,” the 49ers said in a statement. The NFL said in a statement that it is “aware of the matter which will be reviewed under the personal conduct policy.”

Since York took over as CEO, the 49ers have reached three Super Bowls but lost each time.

Frankie Thompson: Horrible Things review – a show to make you shudder with laughter

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 15:41:12 GMT

Pleasance Courtyard, EdinburghFrom Jacob Rees-Mogg as a child to Frank Sinatra’s ego in space, this is a wild collage of clowning and performance art

There are plenty of works-in-progress on the fringe. Frankie Thompson insists (or has the voice of Peppa Pig do so) that her show is a work-in-regress, an expunging of Horrible Things from the deepest recesses of her, and our, recollection. Thompson, whose brand of clowning-meets-performance art more or less guarantees something interesting will happen on stage, parades these Things as lip-synced audio and audience-terrorising stunts, all marshalled by our brisk and wild-eyed host, brooking no nonsense in a polka-dot dress.

Women in the crowd can relax: Thompson’s Horrible Things are usually male, her victims in the crowd likewise. The first sketch sound clips an interview with 12-year-old Jacob Rees-Mogg, and if you ever doubted lip-sync as an art form, I offer you Thompson’s performance here as the very junior minister. As his every word damns the way this country’s ruling classes are raised, her hyper-expressive face and nanosecond-precise timing pass sharper commentary than a thousand satirical words ever could.

There’s more where this came from: a collage of interviews laying bare the tawdry machismo of the whips’ office; a skit questioning the wholesomeness of Cliff Richard and his Summer Holiday. Occasionally, the theme is diluted, with a song about paint sample names, say. But there’s always another shudder of horrible around the corner, as when Thompson recruits a mime orchestra from the audience to accompany a recording of Frank Sinatra’s bizarre 1980 release Trilogy: Past Present Future, the final album of which is a sci-fi fantasia of the male ego unleashed, in which Ol’ Blue Eyes disappears entirely up his own Uranus.

Revenge is then wreaked on the men present in several interactive interludes, in which chaps are dragooned on stage to dance, be babies, be stabbed, be expelled from the room. I will never love members of the public looking ill-at-ease on stage, but if it must happen, let it happen in the hands of a comic as adroit as Thompson – who backs herself into uncomfortable corners too, now licking the floor, now lathering herself in shaving cream. By doing so, in this airing of some dank corners of our cultural memory, she posits laughter not as the best medicine, but the best exorcism.

At Pleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 August. Then at Soho theatre, London, 9-21 November.

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 15:40:33 GMT

After higher prices for winter kick in, energy debt unpaid for more than 30 days likely to rise, says Energy UK

Households in Great Britain could owe their energy suppliers as much as £7bn by the end of the year after higher gas and electricity prices forecast for the winter kick in, an industry group is warning.

Domestic energy debt and arrears climbed by about £500m over the past year to a record £6bn at the end of June as the Middle East conflict continued to stoke rising gas market prices.

The amount of energy debt left unpaid for longer than 30 days is likely to accelerate to £7bn by the end of the year, according to the trade association Energy UK, as the government’s cap on gas and electricity prices is expected to climb to a three-year high.

The regulator is expected to confirm later this week a 4% increase on the energy price cap for millions of households from October as “too many households continue to feel the strain of high energy bills”, the group’s chief executive, Dhara Vyas, said.

She urged Andy Burnham’s government last week to consider a “targeted and more permanent” solution to the rise in energy bills – including a social discount tariff – rather than rely on “stopgap, ad hoc or emergency measures”.

The increase will more than wipe out the impact of the new prime minister’s promise to cut VAT from household electricity bills from October, which aimed to give voters “some breathing space” by shrinking bills by an average of about £45 a year.

“The current arrangements fail to provide the help needed and work out more costly,” Vyas said. “A social discount will address the fuel poverty gap and provide the right amount of support to the right households at the right time – reflecting that needs vary across different customers.” The forecast energy price cap rise means that over the final three months of 2026 the typical household faces a gas and electricity bill equivalent to £1,729 a year, forecasters at Cornwall Insight predict.

The consultancy expects electricity rates to rise from 26.11p a kilowatt hour to 26.57p, and gas charges will rise from 7.33p to 7.90p for households that pay via direct debit. However, the actual bill for a household will depend on how much each consumes.

The average bill under the price cap was calculated assuming lower annual energy use than in previous years, because the high cost of energy has forced many households to use less gas and electricity as debt levels rise. Using the previous methodology, the price cap would be forecast to rise to £1,940.69 from October – the highest level since the summer of 2023.
