How can we stop destroying the prospects of a generation? Scrapping compulsory GCSE resits will be a start

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 15:31:56 GMT

Michael Gove calls the axing of his Tory strategy ‘bringing back stupid’. He doesn’t seem to care that it did more harm than good

GCSE results day was marked with the usual front pages filled with pictures of beaming students. What you didn’t see was the invisible third of 16-year-olds in England who failed their maths and English GCSEs, the obstacle to their future.

That’s 360,000 failed in a system designed by Michael Gove as education minister to mark out winners from losers. It’s a cast of mind shared by many in his party who still yearn for the 11-plus, which consigned a random number of children to failure before they’d hardly begun. A few councils still do it.

Once failed, this one-third must resit English and maths to do any other course: colleges cannot provide them with a blessed start from failed schooling, as they are refused funds for any student not taking repeated resits. Only about 17% of the wretched resitters ever pass. Quite apart from the despair, David Hughes, head of the Association of Colleges, points to the waste: of the far-too-few 16 teaching hours a week for students on post-16 study courses, resitters must be taught seven hours of hated English and maths that most of them will fail. That leaves just nine hours for the vocational courses they choose. No wonder UCL research shows the damage done: self-confidence is lost, many drop out altogether. That doesn’t happen in Wales and Northern Ireland, where resits are not mandatory for continuing study.

Labour gets it. Both the previous education secretary, Bridget Phillipson, and the current, Lucy Powell, well understand the damage done by this Gove-devised torment: finally compulsory resits will end in 2028. Instead, those who fail can take a new “stepping stone” qualification in functional maths and English, proving adequate literacy and numeracy skills.

But an ideological dispute remains among Powell’s advisers. They will still make every 16-year-old take English and maths GCSE in the first place, even if they will probably fail. Many only need the stepping-stone qualification anyway. This doesn’t sit well with Andy Burnham spreading his successful Greater Manchester baccalaureate (MBacc) nationally, a scheme that offers vocational courses suited to local employers alongside academic subjects from age 14, to keep them engaged and avoiding Neet status: not in education, employment or training.

But ideological purists think dividing them early between GCSE groups and stepping-stone groups sets up a two-tier discrimination, downgrading some who might have passed a full GCSE. But with a million Neets, the key priority must be making school encouraging, not rejecting.

Gove sticks to his Gradgrind resits. He calls Burnham’s approach “bring back stupid”, anti-intellectual and hostile to ambition. But had he invested in nursery education, where destinies are most surely set, there might be fewer 16-year-olds with failing grades to bully now. New research reported by the Institute for Fiscal Studies shows how entering childcare one year earlier gives an average 10% improved maths score by age 14 to 15, and a 28% higher score for those with a mother without qualifications.

The good news is that Labour’s emphasis on skills has been infectious, with a surge in applications to technical courses, well beyond the current demographic bulge, while university applications still rise by 3%. Alan Milburn’s commission to solve the crisis of 1 million Neets has real policy steam behind it to urge more skills training.

But further education (FE) has a lot of catching up to do. There are many ways England has not just neglected but discriminated against non-academic education. Despite recent extra funding for colleges, this still doesn’t cover the entire cost of any extra student accepted, an additional 25,000 are expected to enrol this autumn, and colleges lack space and staff after colossal cuts in the Tory years: over-19s adult education fell from £5bn in 2002 to £1.5bn in 2025.

Recent extra money for pay “only stopped the gap getting wider”, Hughes says, when FE staff are paid £10,500 less than school teachers, and are in short supply when construction and engineering jobs pay so much more. Why, he asks, do colleges pay VAT costing £200m, while schools are reimbursed?

The spur of Labour’s new growth and skills levy is incentivising employers to take on beginners with short courses. But as applications quadrupled for degree apprenticeships, more sought-after than Oxbridge places for earning while learning, places have halved.

Why do university students get maintenance loans, but FE students can’t? “Because too many will never earn enough to pay them back,” says Hughes bluntly. Worse still, Neets on benefits are barred from full-time courses, which is perverse.

Needless barriers need fixing. Neets who need driving licences for jobs and apprenticeships, essential from care to plumbing, find the waiting time for a driving test is 21 weeks or more.

Burnham’s eloquence on valuing “the hard hat as much as the academic cap” earns Gove’s contempt, but it has raised FE spirits. Talking to college heads, they see that Labour knows what to do. As ever, the problem is overcoming Britain’s forever low esteem for technical education. It will take heavy lifting to shift mentalities towards encouraging that third of 16-year-olds instead of tormenting them.

Our climate is changing rapidly – and our politicians sound increasingly surreal

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 15:17:07 GMT

On a panel show last week, everyone in the audience wanted to talk about the climate emergency, but the lines rolled out by a Tory MP simply dissolved on contact with reality

As it is August, and everyone with stronger opinions is currently on holiday, last week I went on Any Questions?, the BBC Radio 4 panel show. I had prepared beforehand with a friend whose life’s work it is to make sure people don’t say anything stupid on the radio (or TV), and we’d talked about everything – the strait of Hormuz and energy prices; bus fare caps and the relative price of eggs; racism in the press and in public life; the AI bubble and the next financial crash; how many bathrooms Harry and Meghan currently have in the US, and whether a property even exists in the UK with that amount of toileting hardware.

Predictably, perhaps, the audience’s questions did not spread themselves neatly across the full suite of current affairs, though Harry and Meghan’s return did come up – it was more a matter of which question about the climate crisis best represented the fact that everyone wanted to talk about the climate crisis. The news had just dropped that El Niño would deliver us an unprecedentedly wet autumn, but that was unlikely to soothe the parched earth of the record-breakingly hot, dry summer. Crops are failing, the land is on fire and nobody has not noticed.

The question that best caught the mood was: “Have we left it too late to avert the crisis?” I said there was no such thing as too late, channelling the economist Ann Pettifor, one of the architects of the original Green New Deal, back in the 00s, when it looked as if some politicians, at least, were in the market for ideas. She argued that we had to proceed as though there was still hope, because the alternative – grim nihilism – was no basis for a cooperative, generative body politic, and however many degrees of warming we were facing, we’d need one of those. Isabel Hardman from the Spectator said that it was already too late for some things, and not for others. Things weren’t looking good for birch trees in the south and east of England, for instance. It was a sombre but not bitter point of difference.

Then the Conservative MP, Nigel Huddleston, came in. When detached from the phrase “net zero”, he seems like a reasonable, personable guy. But they’re not allowed to detach. Conservatives are tribally required to say that transforming to a carbon-neutral future is too expensive at this time. Even while they can see the impact of fossil fuels all around them, even when sitting in front of 200 people who palpably believe that there is no such thing as too expensive, when the prize is a beautiful planet that you can live on, Tories have to hold the line.

The purge of the net zero believers from the Conservative party has a brute logic; Kemi Badenoch has chosen this as a red line, the signal difference between herself and the government. She can’t very well hold together a loose coalition between those who cleave to this pillar of new Conservatism and those who don’t. But when you take that position, which must have sounded solid in a strategy meeting, and perform it in front of normal people, who wake up every day to a rapidly changing climate, it sounds unhinged. All the standard lines, about how the UK accounts for only 1% of emissions globally, and that we should leave all the transformation and future-proofing to China, dissolve on contact with reality.

Someone in the audience gave the only sensible response, which was to make a timeless and highly legible gesture involving his hand and his head (I call it legible, there is some contention about whether it means “wanker” or “dickhead”). Obviously I started laughing because I’m only human, but he got told off by a member of the production team and I got a bit of a glare as well. It’s one thing to understand the exigencies of classic Westminster politics, it’s another to watch these rhetorical manoeuvres in real life, where they are too ridiculous to take seriously, but too serious to laugh off. For the climate, it may be too late and not too late; but we definitely don’t have time to carry on indulging this surrealism.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

‘Parisians out!’ Why the French have had enough of French tourists

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 15:16:53 GMT

As holidaymakers descend on Brittany this summer, trebling the population of some villages and towns, local people are unimpressed

Name: “Parisians out!”

Age: It officially commenced at the start of August.

Appearance: Scratched into cars and painted on walls, mainly.

Where? In southern Finistère, specifically in the Bigouden area.

In France, you mean? Yes, the western edge of Brittany.

Why wouldn’t Parisians be allowed in Brittany? They are, but they’re not wholly welcome. Many residents want Parisian tourists to go home.

Why? Because they’re sick of them.

When did this start? It’s said to have originated from a sharp rise in second homeowners from the French capital dating back to the pandemic, but this summer it began with a “Parisians Out!” sign being displayed in the town of Plogoff.

That’s not very nice. The mayor of Plogoff agreed. “We can defend our peace and quiet, our environment and our quality of life without rejecting or stigmatising those who come to our area,” he wrote.

Did that put a lid on things? It did not. Some days later in the town of Plobannalec-Lesconil, a car was scratched with the words “No to Parisians”. Two more cars were similarly vandalised.

How did the vandals know the cars belonged to Parisians? Cars registered in Paris have “75” in their number plates.

That sounds like a bad idea. Ironically, the vandalised cars were all owned by local people who had moved to Paris. Later, graffiti saying “Refugees welcome, tourists go home!” was found on a wall in the area.

Aren’t these places sort of dependent on tourism, from Paris and elsewhere? Yes, but the pressure on local infrastructure is apparently overwhelming. The population of some villages and towns in Finistère trebles in July and August.

I can see how that would be maddening. Also, the heatwaves and wildfires led people to change their plans and take “coolcations” on the northerly Brittany coast, adding extra pressure.

So the anger is confined to Brittany? Not at all. People are handing out “Parisians go home” leaflets on the Île de Ré, and threatening second homeowners in Corsica.

Threatening? A dormant Corsican independence movement has been revived this summer, with second homeowners told: “Do not consider yourselves safe on our national territory.”

That sort of language is totalement inacceptable. Agreed.

Do say: “Between the excesses of tourism and the rights of local people, a difficult balance must be struck.”

Don’t say: “Welcome to Bognor Regis, Parisians!”

Brydon Carse dropped by England as investigation begins into handcuffs incident

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 14:31:00 GMT

Bowler spoken to by police outside bar in Derby

Carse replaced in squad for second Test by Sonny Baker

Brydon Carse has been stood down from England’s squad for the second Test against Pakistan this week while the footage of him in police handcuffs outside a bar in Derby city centre is investigated by the sport’s disciplinary body.

Carse was filmed by a member of the public while he was detained briefly on suspicion of “being drunk and disorderly” outside Molly Malone’s Irish Tavern in the early hours of Sunday morning. The 31-year-old fast bowler had been celebrating victory against Derbyshire in the County Championship with his Durham teammates.

The former England captain Ben Stokes and the fast bowler Matthew Potts were also present at the scene, with Carse said to have been in handcuffs for “a few minutes” before he agreed to move on and was let go without charge.

Though not officially on England duty at the time – he was in the squad for the first Test in Leeds last week but was then sent to play for Durham – Carse is centrally contracted. The matter is now being looked into by the Cricket Regulator – the sport’s disciplinary body – regarding a possible disrepute charge.

In the meantime, and in light of a string of drink-related incidents that have plagued the England men’s team over the past nine months, Carse has been dropped from the Test squad. While he was not expected to play unless there was an injury, Carse has been replaced by Hampshire’s Sonny Baker.

A statement from the England and Wales Cricket Board on Monday read: “Following a referral from the ECB, the Cricket Regulator have confirmed that they will investigate events on Saturday night in Derby.

“Brydon Carse will no longer be available for selection for the second Test while this investigation is ongoing and the full facts are obtained. Brydon will be replaced in the squad for this match by Sonny Baker.”

According to sources, the footage of Carse came after he had been denied re‑entry to the bar shortly before closing time. He had left the building following “an exchange of words” with another member of the public who spilled a drink on him. Durham, though not his direct employers, are not said to be pursuing the matter, nor are Potts or Stokes considered to have done anything wrong.

Carse had been due to travel to London on Monday, with England’s 16‑man squad reconvening after the three-day innings victory secured at Headingley last Friday. They go into two training days at Lord’s before the match starts on Thursday.

The issue presents Joe Root with an early off-field headache at the start of his second spell as Test captain, having made one of his first acts the removal of the team’s midnight curfew. Root has now brought forward by a day his pre-match press conference to meet the issue head on.

Questions about the team’s relationship with alcohol are inevitable, likewise those about his authority. The Carse situation came in the same week that Root backed his players to be “grown up” and “good role models and good human beings”.

The decision to drop Carse while an investigation takes place follows a precedent set this summer. Stokes and Gus Atkinson both missed the second Test against New Zealand at the Oval in June when the Cricket Regulator looked into a late‑night incident in a bar in Chelsea after victory in the series opener at Lord’s.

The midnight curfew was in place on that occasion, even if it was later argued the precise details of it had not been well communicated. Atkinson had been involved in a physical altercation with a Saracens rugby player – he was not the aggressor, as per the ECB – while Stokes was simply present at the same venue.

The ECB chose a different path on the eve of the Australia tour last winter, however, when Harry Brook was punched by a nightclub bouncer the night before the Yorkshireman captained a one-day international in Wellington, New Zealand. Brook was given a clandestine fine at the time, something which came to light only at the end of the Ashes.

In between Brook’s altercation and the story being broken by the Daily Telegraph came the team’s notorious mid-Ashes break in Noosa, when opener Ben Duckett was filmed inebriated outside a backpackers bar and the footage emerged on social media before the Boxing Day Test. Duckett was cleared to play.

Carse was backed heavily by Stokes during that 4-1 defeat, playing all five Tests and finishing as England’s leading wicket-taker, albeit conceding runs with it. A hand injury delayed his start to the English summer – and scuppered an intended spell at the Indian Premier League – but he had returned to fitness during the Hundred.

While England were intending to stick with Atkinson, Jofra Archer, Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue this week as they target a first Test series win in 18 months, Carse was deemed first reserve. The retirement of Stokes in June and the new four‑pronged pace strategy should, in theory, mean opportunities down the line, unless this latest late‑night incident has affected his place in the pecking order.

Cycling chiefs criticised for response to Fin Tarling’s death: ‘This simply cannot happen’

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 14:17:21 GMT

Richard Plugge criticises UCI for its lack of action

‘Riders must be certain they can race on a safe course’

Richard Plugge, the manager of the two-time Tour de France winner, Jonas Vingegaard, has criticised cycling’s governing body, the UCI, for a lack of action following the death of the teenage rider Fin Tarling 10 days ago and said cycling’s leading teams should take responsibility for ensuring safety in races.

“Neither UCI president David Lappartient, nor anyone else, stands up and says: ‘Wait a minute, we really need to think about how we are going to prevent this from happening in the future,’” Plugge, the manager of the Vingegaard-led Visma-Lease a bike team, told the cycling website WielerFlits.

“Maybe we as teams need to take responsibility for safety in races ourselves again. The lack of anger about what has happened is very disappointing to me.”

The 19-year-old Tarling was killed during the Volta a Portugal when he was descending mid-race in pursuit of the peloton and collided with a non-race vehicle that was coming towards him on the race route, despite the road closure.

“This boy encounters a car on a descent,” Plugge said of Tarling. “Can you imagine this happening during Formula One? That a car is suddenly driving on the track in the opposite direction? This actually does happen in a cycling race.

“We are just carrying on. What disappoints me is that everyone says it is terrible, but then immediately a ‘but’ follows. We need to skip everything after the ‘but’. This simply cannot happen.”

Jonathan Vaughters, the manager of the EF Education-EasyPost team, has called for a reduction in the number of races on the professional racing calendar.

“The problem is lack of standards and oversight and the need to keep too many races that do not meet professional standards on the calendar,” he said.

“There are many races running on too small a budget to be hosting a professional-level race. We don’t need 600 days of racing. How about 100 days of racing, all of which are safe?”

While a formal investigation into Tarling’s death is now under way, neither the UCI nor the Portuguese Cycling Federation (FPC) have been willing to comment any further, particularly on media statements made by the Portuguese police (GNR) which confirmed that Tarling had been isolated and racing without a police escort.

The FPC said: “As the organiser of the Volta a Portugal, we believe it would be neither appropriate nor responsible for us to speculate on matters that are currently being investigated by the competent authorities.”

The UCI said: “As the circumstances surrounding the incident are still being established, we will not be commenting further at this stage.”

Unlike Europe’s three Grand Tours, in France, Italy and Spain, the Portuguese race, like many other smaller events, operates a rolling road closure, which relies on secure policing at the front and back of the race convoy.

Rolling road closures were highlighted again last week when the Australian rider Maeve Plouffe said that she had nearly been hit by a car while racing in the Tour of Britain Women.

“There is a hole in the system of rolling road closures,” the Association of Professional Cyclists president and former professional Adam Hansen told the Guardian. “We have to fix this.”

Hansen added: “The most dangerous moments I had in a race did not result in a major incident. It was pure luck that I did not die sometimes. The organisers just think if nothing happened, it was fine.”

Plugge argued that the serial failures to prioritise athlete safety meant that changes to the structure of many races had now become inevitable.

“If cycling from A to B on public roads over 200km is no longer feasible, then we must ride laps of 15, 20, or 25km, provided those routes can be 100% secured. The riders must be certain that they can race on a safe course.”

Why does the New York Times keep calling the left ‘divisive’?

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 14:00:36 GMT

The newspaper often uses the word to describe elections with progressive contenders, implying a previous whole destroyed by the left

“El-Sayed and Stevens Project Party Unity After Divisive Race,” announced the New York Times on 5 August, the day the progressive Abdul El-Sayed beat out his centrist Democratic rival, Haley Stevens, in the Michigan senatorial primary. “Divisive” is now the Times’s favorite attack word, deployed repeatedly to disparage and try to undermine the astonishing recent advances by progressive candidates.

Four days after that first story, the Times again landed “divisive” under “Obama and El-Sayed Discuss Unity After Ugly Michigan Primary.” El-Sayed, it asserted, had “narrowly prevailed in a divisive primary after campaigning on a progressive and anti-establishment platform”.

On 12 August, the Times reported that David Crowley, who narrowly beat out Democratic socialist Francesca Hong in the Wisconsin gubernatorial primary, “promised to leave behind the divisive Democratic primary and focus on Mr. Tiffany”, his Republican opponent. Other stories slip it in more subtly. That same day, in a piece about representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez allegedly distancing herself from “Woke 1.0”, the Times cited Middlebury College professor Erik Bleich, who “pointed to the calls to defund the police as a divisive goal”.

“Polarizing”, a close cousin to “divisive”, appears regularly, too. The Times especially likes to apply it to New York mayor Zohran Mamdani. A reporter insisted in October 2025, for example: “As Mamdani’s campaign upends New York politics, no single stance has polarized New Yorkers as passionately as his pro-Palestinian activism and caustic criticism of Israel.”

Perhaps most outrageous was the Times’s choice of headline for a recent review of David Zirin’s new book about Howard Zinn: “America’s Most Divisive Historian Gets a New Biography.” How, exactly, was Zinn “divisive”? And who are those other historians who are also divisive, just not as bad? Neither Adam Hochschild, in his review, nor Zirin, in his biography, nor any discussion of I’ve ever seen in 40 years as a practicing US historian (and co-author, along with Robin DG Kelley, of a book with Zinn), talk about Zinn that way.

The Times’s choice to cast Zinn as divisive out of the blue, on top of its repeated usage of the word since the midwest primaries, suggests there’s a conscious campaign underway to utilize the concept however it can.

Overall, the Times’ repeated charge of “divisive”, along with “polarizing”, implies a previous and virtuous whole that is currently being destroyed by the left. It assumes voters agree that in the face of deep fear of Trump and his allies, we have to stick together, and that progressive candidates can’t beat Republicans in the midterms.

But the Times’s mythical unified country never existed. The United States has always been riven by race, class, gender, religion, immigration status and much more. And vigorous debate has always been at the core of truly democratic politics.

For the Times, “unity” is a stand-in for the powers-that-be in the Democratic party and “their preferred strategy of running moderate campaigns that won’t offend aging incumbents, never-Trump Republicans, and the multimillionaire-and-up donor class,” as the editors of Hammer & Hope Magazine recently put it.

The mealy-mouthed, centrist candidates the party’s leadership has chosen in the name of unity have repeatedly alienated or failed to energize voters, especially African Americans.

The Times does on occasion employ “divisive” to describe far-right Republicans, such as with Florida governor Ron DeSantis. But that, in turn, colors its usage against the left, which, implicitly, is behaving fanatically and dangerously, too. As the paper claimed on 16 August, after the midwest primaries, “Democrats Face a Potential Tea Party Moment.”

Note, moreover, the recent actions by “moderate” Democrats the New York Times has apparently not deemed divisive: James Carville, the political consultant, who called Democratic socialists “a pack of fools” on Fox News, or Abigail Spanberger, the governor of Virginia, who in May vetoed a bill granting collective bargaining rights to public workers, betraying the union base that had elected her.

In Michigan, it’s Islamophobia that’s in fact “divisive”, not the Muslim candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who, along with many of the other candidates the Times calls divisive, is not coincidentally a person of color.

By charging progressives – and especially democratic socialists – with divisiveness, the New York Times is doing everything it can to shore up a fantasized unity in which corporate powers, Wall Street, and billionaires control the Democratic party, and the rest of us fall into line to vote however they like.

But it’s the Times that’s trying to divide us, as we form ever broader, ever more dynamic and ever more effective coalitions to challenge the masters it serves.

Dana Frank is professor of history emerita at the University of California, Santa Cruz. Her newest book, Balancing Acts: How a Japanese Immigrant Built a Life in the Face of Racial Danger – Until Federal Agents Arrived, will be out from Beacon Press in April 2027

‘A rock star on her own terms’: why we’re still so fascinated by Meg White

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 14:00:35 GMT

Recent incorrect attempts to reveal the White Stripes star’s whereabouts reflect how much we’re still obsessed with the one-of-a-kind drummer

In February 2011, the White Stripes announced they were no longer going to tour or release new music. The decision wasn’t based on “artistic differences” or “health issues”; instead, the decision was “mostly to preserve what is beautiful and special about the band and have it stay that way”.

In the ensuing years, vocalist-guitarist Jack White cultivated a wildly successful solo career and continued working sporadically with his other bands, the Raconteurs and the Dead Weather. Drummer Meg White, meanwhile, retreated from music, preferring instead to be a private citizen. In recent years, she politely declined to speak for a 2023 Elle story and didn’t attend the White Stripes’ 2025 Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction.

As a culture, we’re fascinated by musicians who stay out of the spotlight. Over the years, journalists have tried to track down elusive artists such as Cleveland singer-songwriter Bill Fox (who actually gave several interviews last year) or Suburban Lawns’ Su Tissue. We’re not entitled to know details of their personal lives, of course, which is why this fascination occasionally slides into pernicious territory – like the now-deleted Daily Mail article that recently attempted to find Meg but instead stalked the wrong person.

Meg had an uneasy relationship with being a public figure during the White Stripes’ active existence. She was notoriously shy, once telling NPR about the advice a teacher gave her: “She wrote in my yearbook to speak softly and carry a big stick, you know? And I took to that heart.” The White Stripes also canceled tour dates in 2007 due to Meg’s “acute anxiety”, something Jack spoke about candidly and empathetically later. “To go full-speed from a dead-halt is overwhelming, and we had to take a break.”

Such vulnerability made Meg enormously relatable, someone you wanted to root for to succeed. But people also feel protective of her because she was often treated so poorly when the White Stripes were an active band. Meg started playing drums in 1997 at Jack’s behest – the first song the duo played together was David Bowie’s Moonage Daydream – skipping formal music lessons in favor of more unvarnished creativity.

This irked people who expected virtuosity. A now-archived 2016 article – Why We Can’t Forget Meg White – And the Sexist Way We Talked About Her – outlined the sexism in exhaustive detail, from Pitchfork calling her drumming “pancake-handed” to a 2007 Pearl Jam message board thread titled “Official Meg White can’t play thread.” (Both jabs are still online.) Long after the White Stripes ceased recording, the negativity persisted. In 2023, a journalist apologized after intense outcry to his offhand comment that “the tragedy of the White Stripes is how great they would’ve been with a half-decent drummer.”

The observation is especially absurd because the White Stripes were great precisely because of her approach to drumming. She and Jack complemented each other perfectly; her combination of steely focus and serene nonchalance balanced his more outgoing presence. “Meg is the best part of this band,” Jack told Rolling Stone in 2005, adding: “When she started to play drums with me, just on a lark, it felt liberating and refreshing.”

Indeed, Meg was a powerful player who propelled the White Stripes’ blues/punk/garage rock hybrids with a steady hand. Her thumping kickdrum propels The Hardest Button to Button like a thundering metronome; the garage-rock classics Fell In Love With a Girl and Hotel Yorba lift off due to her buoyant, ramshackle playing. Later-era singles like Icky Thump and Blue Orchid boast a heavier edge thanks in no small part to Meg’s seething, sizzling grooves.

And, unlike other duos, the White Stripes didn’t hire additional musicians to flesh out their live sound. It was always Meg and Jack against the world – her forceful rhythmic backbone anchoring his wild-hair extroversion, whether a grimy guitar line, a soulful organ, antique piano part or even a lively marimba. Criticized at the time, the White Stripes’ Glastonbury 2005 performance looks like a revelation through a modern lens; Meg looks unflappable, even ecstatic, as she mouths along with the words and steers the set. On the pair’s ominous cover of Dolly Parton’s Jolene, her light-touch cymbal hits generate tension for much of the song – until it explodes as she ferociously attacks her entire drumkit, mirroring the moment when the narrator collapses in anguish.

“It will always be us two,” Jack told Rolling Stone in 2005. “I will never do the White Stripes with another drummer. She’ll never do it with another guitarist.”

He’s kept his word: when the duo was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, Jack didn’t perform in Meg’s absence. Instead, Twenty One Pilots whacked through Seven Nation Army, while Olivia Rodrigo and Feist picked through a delicate We’re Going To Be Friends. However, Meg sent a note of gratitude that Jack read; he also noted she helped write and shape the speech he gave. “A lot of punctuation corrections too,” he quipped. “She’s pretty good at that.”

With this honor, Meg became just the third female drummer inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, after Gina Schock of the Go-Go’s and Velvet Underground’s Moe Tucker. Like those two artists, Meg reinforced the idea that you could be in a band, create your own style and carve out your own destiny. She didn’t wait around for permission to be an artist.

Meg’s iconoclastic music career and drumming skills are finally receiving their due, in no small part because younger fans and musicians aren’t saddled by the same sexist cultural baggage. Speaking to Elle in 2023, Rodrigo noted Meg’s playing and the White Stripes themselves taught her “the value of simplicity in music … that a truly great song doesn’t need to have crazy production or layers of sound. It just needs to move you. You can sense her passion in every song she plays.” But in the end, Meg proved you could be a rock star on your own terms – both during and after your music career.

This article was amended on 24 August 2026. The article titled Why We Can’t Forget Meg White – And the Sexist Way We Talked About Her was published in 2016, not 2006 as an earlier version stated.

Which eco-friendly laundry detergents actually clean your clothes? I put 11 to the test

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 14:00:35 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Our writer spent weeks putting capsules, sheets and liquid detergent through their paces to find the best for your clothes and the planet

Sustainable cleaning subscriptions that make life easier

Nothing makes falling into bed more enjoyable than freshly laundered sheets, especially if they’ve just been dried in the sunshine. It’s a definite bonus, though, to know your clean bedding won’t bring you out in a rash or pollute your local river.

Laundry detergent can be a troublesome product. A few years ago, I suffered a full-body rash after using pound-shop detergent on my sheets. I switched to a big-brand product and never had a reaction again, but there’s still the question of whether its ingredients may be causing environmental harm after they’ve gone down the drain.

The sulphates, phosphonates and bleaches that many detergents use to remove stains and brighten fabric can cause lasting environmental damage, especially to aquatic life. I’m lucky enough to live next to the sea, and the output of my washing machine is unlikely to be doing it much good.

Brands such as Smol, Ecover and Bio-D claim to be eco-friendly alternatives, but can they tackle dirty laundry as well as standard detergents – and are they as green as they say? To find out, I challenged 11 of them to clean my clothes, soften my sheets and remove stains, including makeup, raspberry juice and ground-in mud. Here are the ones that rose to the challenge, and those that were no more effective than using nice-smelling water.

Best laundry detergent overallSmol Bio capsules, 24

Best budget laundry detergentEcoegg Laundry egg, 70 washes

Best-smelling laundry detergentEcover Non-bio laundry liquid, 1.43l

Best laundry detergent for sensitive skinBio-D Fragrance-free laundry liquid, 1l

I’ve spent decades writing about products, from smartphones to hay fever remedies, so I’m professionally sceptical of manufacturers’ claims to magically improve our lives by buying their stuff. Given how long I’ve been testing duvets, blankets, mattresses and their toppers and other washable homewares for the Filter, it’s about time I found the best way to launder them.

Inevitably, there was a lot of washing. To fairly compare all these detergents on key variables, including stain removal, fabric softness and lasting fragrance, I spent three weeks running my washing machine twice a day. At about 5kg per load and 22 loads, that’s more than 100kg of soggy laundry in the name of Filter research.

Before any socks could get washed, though, I had to choose and source my test detergents. I scoured ingredients lists and company information for evidence of ethical and environmental kudos, including certifications from bodies such as B Corp, Allergy UK and the Vegan Society. I also looked for sustainable packaging, innovative ways to reduce weight and waste, and bottles that could be refilled without buying more plastic.

My house is no science lab, but I did what I could to ensure that my testing was fair and thorough. I devoted one day each to 11 detergents across three weeks. Each time, I used the detergent to wash two sets of laundry in my standard front-loading Beko washing machine. One load was 2kg of clothes that included sweaty running kit, underwear and coloured T-shirts, washed at 20C. The larger 4kg load was washed at 40C and contained white items, including a duvet cover and a large white towel that was my stain-test guinea pig.

Each morning, I daubed the poor towel with mucky substances, including liquid foundation, tomato ketchup, cat food, garden mud and a juicy squashed raspberry. I photographed the blotches before and after washing, then used them to compare how the detergents removed dirt.

Other factors were more subjective. I’m not a perfume-wearer, but I love a gently fresh fragrance from my laundry, as long as its source doesn’t bother my skin. I buried my nose in every load of laundry when it was fresh from the machine, and then again when it was dry. I put a couple of freshly laundered socks aside each time, then sniffed them again after a few days to see how well the scent had lingered.

Price was important, too. Laundry detergent can get expensive, especially for families. I calculated the price per wash for a small (2kg) load, but also awarded value-for-money kudos to detergents that never needed a double dose.

I was left with a little spare after testing, so I was able to donate the detergents to Yellow Door, my local domestic abuse refuge.

All I really want from a detergent is clean laundry and good eco credentials. Smol triumphs on the first of these key factors and does well on the second. With B Corp certification, it’s a solid eco choice. It doesn’t quite score five stars, though: Smol isn’t entirely free of hazardous ingredients, and you can only get it on subscription.

Why we love itSmol’s subscription isn’t a contract, so you’re not tied into a payment trap, and you can order a one-off box (you just pay postage for the “free” nine-capsule introductory offer; mine was £1.99). Regular deliveries mean you won’t run out of detergent or ever need to lug it back from the shops, and you can skip or pause whenever you want.

The detergent was my favourite by far. Smol’s capsules contain chemicals, including some derived from fossil fuels, which is probably why Smol can say it uses “less chemicals” than big brands. It works, too: in the 40C stain test, Smol was the only detergent to remove any trace of the mud I’d ground into my towel. With my 20C load, my clothes emerged outstandingly bright and clean.

Everything smelled delightful, and that was important for me. Smol doesn’t give its detergent’s fragrance a name, but says it’s “unique to Smol” and created using what the brand claims are ethically sourced essential oils, including orange, pine, elemi, lavender and patchouli. If you’re a fan of punchy fragrances, you may want to add fabric softener for extra scent, but I loved the gentle, soothing aroma that lasted for days.

It’s a shame that … Smol’s concentrated formula is slightly lower on harmful chemicals rather than free of them, like a natural or plant-based detergent would be. The company is transparent about its ingredients, though (here’s the full list), and there are no parabens, phosphates or phthalates. It’s also a shame that you can’t buy Smol at the shops.

Type: bio, non-bio or fragrance-free capsules (I tested non-bio) Size: 24 capsulesMaximum loads: 24Price per load: 25pScent tested: standard Smol fragrance using orange, pine and other essential oilsSustainability: B Corp certified, concentrated formula, certified free of microplastics, 100% plastic-free packaging (sustainable FSC-approved cardboard)Certified cruelty-free? YesVegan? Yes

This refillable egg-shaped plastic cage looks like it should come filled with Maltesers for Easter. Instead, you fill it with the supplied “mineral pellets”, a mixture of tourmaline and detergent pellets, snap it shut and plonk it in with your laundry for up to 70 washes, all for less than a tenner. A full 70-wash refill costs an even more impressive £6.65.

Why we love itThe 70-wash lifespan of each Ecoegg mineral pack is more than double that of most products in this test. If you live on your own and don’t roll around in mud too often, one Ecoegg could last all year. It’s also the most convenient detergent in my whole test: no liquid mess, no plasticky pods.

There’s a sustainability claim baked into Ecoegg’s name, which is surprising for a product made from plastic and containing cleaning agents. The name is more than justified, though, not least because the egg itself is refillable and can be used for years. The mineral pellets are free of phosphonates, sulphates and parabens, and I didn’t suffer any skin trouble with the “fresh linen” fragrance pellets I tested, but if you’re particularly sensitive, there is a fragrance-free edition too, which is approved by Allergy UK.

My Ecoegg did a fine job of cleaning underwear, de-stinking running kit and leaving my bedsheets feeling soft and smelling fresh, which is impressive for a detergent that works out at 14p a wash for a small load.

It’s a shame that … the detergent wasn’t powerful or sudsy enough to remove stains in one wash in my hard-water area. The makeup, mud and raspberry marks on my white towel remained noticeable.

Type: non-bio mineral pelletsSize: 1 eggMaximum loads: 70 before it needs refillingPrice per load: 14pScent tested: fresh linenSustainability: no phosphates or parabens, refill pellets available, FSC-certified cardboard packaging, Allergy UK-approved fragrance-free range Certified cruelty-free? No, but claims to be cruelty-freeVegan? Yes

As well as ticking all the right aroma boxes, Ecover is also one of the best-value products I tested, especially as it’s so often available for less than its £10 RRP. Its cleaning performance is excellent, too, and its formula is lower in hazardous chemicals than its big-name rivals.

Why we love it Ecover’s 1.43l bottle is not bad value even at its full price, and in my washing test I found that a little goes a long way. Not only did one capful of this detergent create the most impressive suds of all the detergents in my test, despite me living in a hard water area, but it also rinsed away completely to leave my fabrics looking bright and smelling unbelievably good. Stain removal was well above average, with mud, cat food and ketchup all washing away – although raspberry and the makeup left shadowy marks.

Ecover achieved these impressive results with a formula that uses rapidly biodegradable ingredients, excludes phosphates and optical brighteners, and largely avoids petrochemical ingredients derived from fossil fuels. Its fragrances, too, are 50% naturally derived – and the lavender and sandalwood variety was my favourite in the whole test. It’s not overpowering (some may find it too subtle, in fact), and it lifted my mood and lingered for days.

It’s a shame that … Ecover contains sodium lauryl sulphate and laureth-7, which may trigger reactions in sensitive skin (I didn’t suffer any). Some organisations, including the UK-based Naturewatch Foundation, have urged stockists and consumers to boycott Ecover after it was bought by SC Johnson, which tests on animals, but Ecover itself is still certified cruelty-free.

Type: non-bio liquidSize: 1.43lMaximum loads: 40Price per load: from about 18pScent tested: lavender and sandalwoodSustainability: factory certified platinum zero waste by True, bottles are made from 100% post-consumer recycled plastic (caps 50%), refills availableCertified cruelty-free? YesVegan? Yes

Bio-D’s fragrance-free liquid is the only other detergent in my test to be accredited by Allergy UK. Despite being fragrance-free, it left my clothes and sheets smelling fresh. Its biodegradable formula is great for delicates, not least because it’s designed to be used at low temperatures, but like Ecoegg, it struggled to shift my stubborn stains.

Why we love itI confess I was surprised by how well Bio-D’s naturally derived formula cleaned my laundry. The gentle liquid left my stinky running kit smelling and feeling wonderfully clean even at 20C, and it generated enough suds to be effective for hand-washing, too. My fabrics looked bright but didn’t feel as soft as with some of the other detergents. If you’re after softness and fragrance, Bio-D’s lavender fabric conditioner is worth adding.

It’s a shame that … my ground-in mud, makeup and raspberry stains sailed through almost untouched, so this may not be your first choice of detergent if you have to deal with lots of mucky school shirts.

Type: non-bio liquidSize: 1lMaximum loads: 25 Price per load: from about 20pScent tested: fragrance-freeSustainability: B Corp certified, bottles made from 100% post-consumer recycled plastic (except caps), solar-powered manufacture, fully traceable ingredients, refills available, Allergy UK-approved fragrance-free range Certified cruelty-free? YesVegan? Yes

Best for: families who need reliable cleaning without a big price tag

Ineos is well priced for a detergent that beat most others in fading my dreaded raspberry stain. It also left my sweaty running kit smelling gorgeous after a mere 20C wash.

Ineos is not quite what I’d call an eco detergent, but it does take a few steps in the right direction. Ineos contains some plant-based ingredients (just enough to warrant its claim of being “plant powered”) and omits phosphonates and optical brighteners, but the formula still contains synthetic ingredients, including one that’s harmful to aquatic life.

It didn’t make the final cut because … I would have liked the lovely fragrance to last longer than a day.

Type: non-bio liquid; size: 1l; maximum loads: 33; price per load: from about 21p; scent tested: rhubarb and pomegranate; sustainability: some plant-based cleansing ingredients, bulk sizes available; certified cruelty-free? Yes; vegan? Yes

Best for: anyone who wants their detergent to act like a second perfume

Method is Ecover’s sister product, and its eco credentials include recycled bottles, cruelty-free testing and a formula designed to work at lower temperatures. However, it contains many of the standard synthetic detergent ingredients.

On the upside, it’s a capable cleaner with a strong, lasting floral scent that many will love. The bottle’s a bit dribbly, but once I managed to get the liquid into my washing machine, it made an excellent attempt at removing the raspberry stain in a single 40C cycle.

It didn’t make the final cut because … owned by US conglomerate SC Johnson, Method is not a particularly eco-friendly choice thanks to ingredients including laureth-7, sulphates and optical brighteners.

Type: bio liquid; size: 990ml; maximum loads: up to 33; price per load: 20p; scent tested: peony blush; sustainability: 100% recycled plastic bottle (except cap); certified cruelty-free? Yes; vegan? Yes

Best for: families, and children sensitive to cleaning chemicals

Miniml’s biodegradable formula contains almost entirely (99%+) plant-based ingredients – for example, a coconut-derived surfactant – and felt gentle on my skin and fabrics. It did a fine job of freshening up and softening my clothes and sheets, although it couldn’t rescue my longsuffering stained towel. I expect it would take a few more washes before the slightly faded marks stop being noticeable.

It didn’t make the final cut because … the gentleness of Miniml makes it a great family choice, and it can even be used for hand-washing, but it may admit defeat against a muddy school kit.

Yes; vegan? Yes

Best for: eco-conscious householders who want a full range of green cleaning products

Faith in Nature, which has B Corp certification, makes all sorts of plant-derived household cleaning products that can be refilled. As with Ecover, it contains laureth-7, which may trigger sensitive skin, but I didn’t suffer any reactions. It smelled delicious, felt soft and looked bright.

As with many of the detergents made largely from plant-derived ingredients, though, Faith in Nature couldn’t remove my makeup and raspberry stains. I faded them slightly by spot-cleaning with a little of the detergent, but that still didn’t shift the marks completely. I think the lesson here is that if you want to wash with truly green detergent, don’t get makeup on your clothes.

It didn’t make the final cut because … I just couldn’t work out how to squirt the liquid into my machine’s drawer without dribbling it all over my hands.

Type: non-bio liquid; size: 1l; maximum loads: 30; price per load: about 33p; scent: aloe vera and rosemary; sustainability: B Corp certified, recycled plastic bottle, larger 5l and 20l bottles can be returned for free, refills available; certified cruelty-free? Yes; vegan? Yes

Best for: anyone who’d like to display their detergent as well as use it

Newcomer Eat Dirt is one of the most beautifully packaged products I’ve seen. Its one-litre tin is much easier to recycle than a plastic bottle, but I’d rather hang it on the wall or use it as a vase. It’s a glorious piece of visual design, although I did find it a pain to open.

Once I managed to get a capful of liquid into my machine’s drawer, I was struck by its delicious smell. Its cleaning agents are reassuringly green too, although there are a few standard detergent ingredients, such as the preservative phenoxyethanol. It left my clothes looking clean and bright and feeling soft, and although it couldn’t shift the makeup and raspberry stains, it left my towel smelling sensational.

It didn’t make the final cut because … Eat Dirt is expensive, especially if you only want a one-off rather than a monthly subscription. It’s aiming to be available in stores soon, though, and I’m hoping that will bring the price down.

Type: non-bio liquid; size: 1l; maximum loads: 50; price per load: 50p; scent tested: bitter orange; sustainability: mostly naturally sourced ingredients, recyclable tin, often delivered in secondhand boxes; certified cruelty-free? No, but claims to be cruelty-free; vegan? Yes

Best for: saving space and spills in your cleaning cupboard

Laundry sheets are like slightly spongy pieces of A5 paper infused with detergent and designed to dissolve in your washing. They’re easy to use, and they’re much lighter than liquid or pods, so they score sustainability points for being less carbon-intensive to transport (although they are being shipped from China).

I loved the lightweight logistics of Nimble Cares’ sheets, but I was slightly disappointed by their cleaning power. I used a whole sheet on my large load (half a sheet is recommended for small loads), and it still couldn’t shift the mud, makeup or raspberry. My fabrics did feel soft, though, and the use of allergen-free perfume is helpful if you have sensitive skin.

It didn’t make the final cut because … even if you stick with the half-sheet recommendation for smaller loads, this is a pricey detergent. Nimble’s failure to publish information about its use of toxic chemicals falls short of the Good Shopping Guide’s ethical benchmark.

Type: non-bio detergent sheets; size: 30 sheets; maximum loads: 60; price per load: from about 26p; scent tested: spring blossom; sustainability: mainly plant-based ingredients, no plastic in product or packaging, light weight reduces carbon footprint; certified cruelty-free? No, but claims to be cruelty-free; vegan? Yes

Best for: families regularly dealing with muddy school uniforms

Dr Beckmann describes its new sheets as “a great eco choice” because they have less packaging than powder or liquids, but their ingredients are pretty standard detergent fare, including sulphates, perfumes and chemicals that are “harmful to aquatic life with long lasting effects”.

On cleaning power, though, Magic Leaves do well. The dissolved sheet fought a particularly winning battle with my ground-in mud – a weak spot for the eco-liquids – and left my whites looking bright. Its results didn’t outclass Smol’s, though, and Smol ticks far more sustainability and ethical boxes with B Corp and Leaping Bunny certifications and plastic-free packaging.

It didn’t make the final cut because … despite the green claims, its ingredients are pretty standard laundry detergent fare. You’re hit by the familiar old laundry detergent smell the moment you open the packet.

Type: non-bio sheets; size: 25 sheets; maximum loads: up to 50; price per load: from about 7p; scent tested: fresh breeze; sustainability: biodegradable, lightweight packaging reduces transport emissions; certified cruelty-free? No; vegan? Yes

Limit your sustainability expectations if you want clean laundry. “I don’t think any detergent can ever be completely sustainable, because there will always be an environmental impact somewhere along the line,” says Ross Osborne, sustainability director at cleaning supplies company Jangro. “The more honest question is whether one detergent is more sustainable than another.

“You have to look at the whole picture. That includes the ingredients, how biodegradable they are, their potential effect on aquatic life, how much product is needed, the packaging, where it has been manufactured, how far it has travelled and whether it actually works.”

In my testing, I was impressed to discover how well many of the detergents cleaned my laundry using non-synthetic and biodegradable cleaning agents. These include naturally derived surfactants (as used by Bio-D, Miniml and others) and the mineral tourmaline (as used by Ecoegg), plus essential oils for fragrance (as used by Smol).

A vital factor is a detergent’s ability to clean at cool settings, says Lauren Hill, product manager at appliance manufacturer Haier. “Detergents designed for lower temperatures reduce the energy used during the washing cycle. Also consider concentrated formulas that contain less water and require smaller packaging, which reduces transport emissions.”

Other steps in the right direction include plastic-free and refillable containers, recycled bottles (not just “recyclable”), and innovations such as lightweight laundry sheets, which can help reduce transport emissions. One of the most original sustainability measures I encountered during this test was Eat Dirt’s decision to often deliver its products in used boxes, eBay-style. That shows an imagination and lack of brand vanity I wish others would follow.

Bio (biological) detergents may sound more environmentally treacherous than non-bio, but that’s not necessarily the case. It just means they contain enzymes (usually protease, amylase and lipase) that help break down common stains such as food, sweat and blood. Enzyme-based products can be an effective bleach-free way to clean around the house. As a cat owner, I swear by the Naturally Gone enzyme spray for getting rid of the dreaded “cat wee” whiffs.

“Enzymes are a good example of a biodegradable cleaning agent that actually works,” says Osborne. “Different enzymes deal with different types of soiling. Proteases help break down protein-based stains, amylases work on starch and lipases tackle fats and oils. This helps a detergent clean effectively at a lower temperature rather than relying on hotter water or larger quantities of conventional chemistry.”

Repeated studies have found that enzymes can trigger reactions in people with eczema or sensitive skin, though, so if that applies to you or your kids, you may be better off sticking with non-bio detergents. Non-bio formulas can still rely on potentially hazardous surfactants such as sodium laureth sulphate, so look for naturally derived surfactants – such as the coconut-based ingredients cocamidopropyl betaine, lauramine oxide and cocos nucifera oil in Miniml – if your skin can’t tolerate bio formulas and you’re trying to shop sustainably.

For more, read our easy plastic-free kitchen swaps and the best refillable beauty products

Jane Hoskyn is a features journalist with three decades of experience rearranging bookshelves and “testing” gadgets while deadlines loom. She would always rather be running in the woods, which is probably why she needs to wash her clothes so often

‘Better than The Godfather’: how we made brutal Yorkshire crime classic Red Riding

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 13:34:33 GMT

‘The show’s hardly an advert for Yorkshire. Sets would have a burnt-out car and maybe an upturned shopping trolley. Locals would say, “Can’t you put a nice floral arrangement there instead?”’

I’d been writing screenplays with Michael Winterbottom and in 2006, his producer Andrew Eaton said: “There’s this quartet of novels by David Peace. Are you interested in adapting them?” I read the first, 1974, and was drawn to it and repelled at the same time. It was strong meat, full of anger and injustice. It’s anchored in reality, especially the Peter Sutcliffe and Stefan Kiszko cases, but heightened and stylised. “Fiction torn from the facts,” David called it.

I was scared stiff because the novels were so experimental but I desperately wanted to do it – even if adapting all four would mean waving goodbye to several years of my life. The books span a decade with a huge cast of characters, so I condensed a lot.

Eaton was keen on a different director and format for each film. It meant each had its own reference points. I thought about Chinatown a lot with 1974. The design and costumes were all smoky and brown, like the 70s. The cast went for the material big time. David Morrissey really did his research and Sean Harris is nothing if not method. It’s a very masculine story but we wanted strong female characters too – we had Maxine Peake and Rebecca Hall. I kept the most horrendous violence off-screen. Violence you imagine is much worse than anything you’ll see. Your mind does the work.

The police interrogation scenes, where they torture suspects, are terrifying and deliberately so. Stefan Kiszko, on whom Daniel Mays’s character is based, was released in 1992 and died 18 months later, having been wrongly imprisoned for 16 years. A man with a mind of a 12-year-old who just wanted his mum. The corruption and brutality in Red Riding are bleak, but so is the real world. While I was writing, the headlines were full of cases like Stephen Lawrence, Madeleine McCann, Natascha Kampusch, Shannon Matthews, Josef Fritzl …

I was warned that Sutcliffe was litigious, so I should use what he actually said in his police interview. That was fine. I couldn’t have made it up anyway. Red Riding was compared to James Ellroy and described as Yorkshire noir, which is spot-on, although David said it was a pity they used a French word. He preferred Yorkshire dark. I added some redemption at the end because I needed to save somebody and finish on a note of love.

This article includes content provided by dailymotion. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

We made 1974, 1980 and 1983 but, for budgetary reasons, not 1977, which broke my heart. It was always intended as a quartet, so it felt like vandalism. I hold out hope that somehow we’ll get to do the missing fourth. The films got a theatrical release in the US, screened back-to-back, which is full-on, but a cult audience went for it. Critic David Thomson called it “better than The Godfather”. Nic Pizzolatto said it influenced True Detective. People are still discovering it. They tend to say: “But you seem like quite a nice guy!”

My agent sent me the scripts but said: “Just to warn you, there’s no money in this.” I got halfway through the first episode, phoned her back and asked: “Who else is attached?” She said: “Sean Bean, David Morrissey, Paddy Considine, Peter Mullan and Maxine Peake.” I said: “Put my name on the list please.” The scripts were so well-written, it was a no-brainer.

Everyone was on Equity minimum, there were no trailers, not even a green room area. It was a tremendous experience to have a cast of that calibre, throwing their all into something that wasn’t going to buy them more than a pair of shoes.

David Peace’s books put you inside the mind of each character and are dense with detail. They were a major resource for building my character, washed-up solicitor John Piggott. In one scene, he flashes back to finding his father’s body. They literally strapped a camera rig on to me, so viewers see it through Piggott’s eyes. He becomes the unlikely hero, despite being a dope-smoking, heavy-drinking loser. He takes on the might of the crooked West Yorkshire police and partly succeeds. Amid the darkness, he’s a bit of light at the end of the tunnel.

Piggott’s a shoddy, unkempt idiot – he sleeps in his suit and at one point, he eats a raw Findus Crispy Pancake – but he saves the girl at the end. He carries her out of a mineshaft in his arms, like a Bruce Willis action hero. Shooting scenes in the underground paedophile’s lair was grim. There was a room with the dentist’s chair in it, mattresses on the floor, a child’s shoe. It brought home the horrors of what these monsters were doing. You needed a shower at the end of the day.

I grew up in York during the 1970s and vividly remember the Ripper era. I used to cycle back from my then-girlfriend’s house in the pitch black. Tension on the streets was palpable – you’d pedal home as quickly as you could. Everyone felt Sutcliffe’s elusiveness and how the police were overwhelmed. The show’s hardly a tourist advert for Yorkshire. On location, set dressing would be a burnt-out car on the grass verge, maybe an upturned shopping trolley. Locals were like: “Can’t you put a nice floral arrangement there instead?”

Red Riding is an extraordinary achievement. Three different directors and formats. It’s hard for me to fault it. It had ripple effects on my career. Ridley Scott had just started work on Robin Hood with Russell Crowe. The casting director gave him a Red Riding DVD because it had so many British actors. He watched it one weekend and, on Monday morning, phoned up to acquire the US rights, then cast me as Friar Tuck. He must’ve seen me eat the frozen Crispy Pancake and thought: “That’s my man!”

The Red Riding Trilogy is available to stream on Amazon’s Studiocanal Presents channel

Burnham accuses Russia of ‘outrageous threats’ against UK as he visits Kyiv

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 12:07:59 GMT

Moscow warns of increased tensions with Britain as PM offers Ukraine declassified details of missile components

Europe live – latest updates

Andy Burnham has accused the Kremlin of “outrageous threats” against the UK as Russia warned of an escalation in tensions after the UK’s decision to present Ukraine with newly declassified blueprints to allow Kyiv to improve its production of long-range missiles.

Speaking in Kyiv, Burnham compared Ukraine’s struggle to Britain’s fight against Nazi Germany. “My nation kept the flame of European freedom alive in the 20th century, you hold that flame in the 21st,” Burnham said in a speech in front of St Sophia cathedral to mark the 35th anniversary of Ukraine’s independence.

“Despite Russia’s outrageous threats to my country, we will continue our support for Ukraine.”

In his first trip abroad as the prime minister, Burnham will give Ukraine previously classified information on the British manufactured components for long-range cruise missiles. The prime minister is also set to ink a new deal to share Ukrainian battlefield data with the UK’s Ministry of Defence and some private companies to train AI models.

Vladimir Putin’s spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said the exchange would add “fuel to the fire” and scupper any moves towards a peace deal.

Burnham hit back in an interview shortly after his speech. He said: “Who started the fire? That’s the question, isn’t it?”

During a conference call while in Kyiv with 34 leaders in the coalition of the willing, countries that have promised to help keep Ukraine secure in the event of a truce with Russia, Burnham also urged other nations to help Kyiv secure more US-made Patriot missiles.

He said the coalition was “doing everything we can all do and working with our allies outside of this coalition to dig into our own stocks and help others dig into their stocks”.

Moscow said it would identify and destroy the locations of missile production sites. “Britain is involved in this war on the side of the Kyiv regime,” Peskov told reporters. “Britain methodically and regularly adds fuel ‌to the fire, and methodically and regularly hatches schemes to prevent even the slightest progress in the peaceful settlement process.”

Kyiv was braced for another wave of Russian missile attacks as it marked Independence Day on Monday, attended by other European leaders alongside Burnham.

The prime minister’s decision to declassify the information about the UK-made components of the Storm Shadow/Scalp missiles will enable Ukraine to eventually build its own version, though this may take years.

In his speech, Burnham said Ukraine had “endured 12 years of naked aggression, the occupation of Crimea, and now four and a half years of Russia’s full-scale invasion, all aimed at crushing the independence that we are here to celebrate.”

He said: “Russia’s actions have not changed the path this nation is on. It’s confirmed it. You have stood tall and defiant in the face of everything Russia has thrown at you. And you have taken your place as a proud, sovereign European nation, a vibrant democracy with a bright future ahead.”

He said Europe owed a debt of gratitude to Ukraine for its fight. “I want to tell you something you probably don’t hear enough: thank you. Thank you all. Thank you. Thank you for the incredible stand you have taken because we are all stronger for it.”

The prime minister visited Ukrainian soldiers while in Kyiv, including joining them in playing a Smiths song on the electric guitar.

Speaking to reporters afterwards, he denied he was deliberately ramping up the rhetoric and said the decision to provide the new blueprints was a continuation of the longstanding UK policy to back Ukraine.

Asked by ITV News if he was “poking the Russian bear,” Burnham said: “Obviously with a change of prime minister people think there has been a change in policy. Well I’m here to say there isn’t. I’m going to do what our predecessors have done.

“If we don’t take a firm stand, who would be next? It’s right to do this. It’s in Britain’s interest to stand firm.”

Kyiv has said Russia is amassing more ballistic missiles and considering whether to mobilise an extra 300,000 soldiers. The missiles have been used to bomb Ukrainian infrastructure and warehouses, and to attack the capital, causing increased civilian casualties. There is a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors, the only weapon that can effectively counter them.

Burnham swerved putting pressure directly on countries including Spain and Greece to hand over their own stockpiles of the weapons. He said the UK did not “have those systems to be able to hand over but we will certainly use whatever influence we have got. Obviously there are other threats that people are facing. It’s a complicated world right now.”

The UK has also announced it will help France set up assembly lines in Ukraine for long-range missiles, which the French president, Emmanuel Macron, promised last month. It has also previously announced that it will allow Ukraine to launch attacks with British-made drones, prompting warnings from Moscow that the UK will pay a “high price”.

Russia has withdrawn its ambassador to the UK, with no replacement in sight. The long-serving ambassador, Andrey Kelin, left last month after seven years in post, according to the Russian embassy in London. A spokesperson said that relations had “deteriorated to an unprecedentedly low level entirely on London’s initiative”. A UK government spokesperson said the UK’s ambassador would continue in post in Moscow.

Details of the Independence Day commemorations have not been made public amid fears of a Russian attack.

Macron and the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, will attend the coalition of the willing meeting by video link. Burnham travelled to Kyiv with the president of the European Council, António Costa, and the prime minister of Luxembourg, Luc Frieden.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy is facing his biggest internal challenge after his former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov called for the country to hold elections for the first time since the war began. The Ukrainian president has said any poll risks splitting the country and would be “a tsunami for the state”.

How growing up in ‘Chemical Valley’ inspired lawyer to sue industry she used to work for

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 12:00:32 GMT

Hélène Duguy is taking on companies accused of failing to stop Pfas pollution in the area of France she calls home

The factories were just part of the landscape for Hélène Duguy growing up in the heart of an area known as France’s “Chemical Valley”.

“Those factories are visible from my mother’s apartment,” says Duguy, 34, whose mother still lives in St-Genis-Laval, south of Lyon.

Until recently, her mother did not accept that there might be any danger associated with living in close proximity to chemical factories. “She just trusted the municipalities to do their job,” Duguy says. “I think it remained something quite remote for her – she understood there was a problem, but Pfas is invisible, so it’s very hard to understand the reality of it and what it could mean for you.”

It was only after a warning was issued about the safety of homegrown food and locally produced eggs that the scale of the contamination became more tangible. “She’s now even considering selling her flat,” Duguy says. “I was with her last weekend and I told her that for me, the contamination she is exposed to continuously is extremely worrying […] Here I feel very close to people who I was raised with, so this makes the issue very relatable, very tangible, and also it makes the fight more concrete.”

Today, as an ambitious young lawyer, Duguy is part of a team taking the companies running the factories to court.

“I have a very deep sense of justice and law has really become the way for me to express that,” says Duguy, who joined the ClientEarth legal team six years ago.

The NGO, which describes itself as “one of the world’s most ambitious environmental organisations”, has brought legal action against some of the biggest and most polluting companies in the world, from the fossil fuel firm Shell to the agricultural company Cargill.

Now it has set its sights on the chemical industry, and Duguy has been appointed to lead the charge. ClientEarth is challenging the EU’s reapproval of one of the most controversial pesticides – glyphosate. It also recently filed a complaint to the European Committee of Social Rights arguing the Belgian government has violated its residents’ rights to protection and health by failing to prevent widespread Pfas pollution.

Pfas are a class of thousands of chemicals used in a wide range of household products. They have been linked to cancer, birth defects, decreased immunity and other serious health problems. They are often described as “forever chemicals” because they do not break down in the environment.

Their use and production are associated with widespread environmental contamination, with pollution recorded at an estimated 17,000 sites across the UK and Europe. “We’re creating sacrifice zones for the sake of a toxic industry that has no place in a European society,” says Duguy. “Our goal is not just to get compensation, but to force regulators to act, and that’s why this litigation path is very strategic.”

As well as working on these cases, Duguy advises and supports lawyers across Europe. She advised lawyers on the Miteni case in Italy, in which 11 former executives from the chemical company received jail sentences of up to 17 years after they were found guilty of polluting the water and soil in a 100 sq km area with Pfas.

She is also supporting lawyers in France who are taking the chemical companies Arkema France and Daikin Chemical France to court for allegedly causing widespread pollution in St-Genis-Laval, at the heart of “Chemical Valley”.

The scale of the pollution in the valley has unravelled over several years after journalistic investigations revealed the extent of the problem. Investigations have found Pfas in the air, soil and water, and in the blood of local people.

Sign up to Down to Earth

The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential

after newsletter promotion

Residents in towns around these factories, including in St-Genis-Laval, have been advised not to consume locally produced eggs or poultry meat. And yet despite these risks, locally led environmental campaigns have faced barriers over concerns the cost of the cleanup could affect jobs. This is a narrative Duguy believes has been “built by the industry”.

“When you think about creating a toxic-free environment or a toxic-free society, you need to look at everything holistically. If you have less jobs in those toxic industries, you could create new jobs in safe industries. While we keep providing opportunities for those toxic industries to thrive, we prevent other safe industries from really becoming important for the economy,” she says.

Still, Duguy acknowledges the argument can be hard to make when jobs are on the line. “I think NGOs often don’t really understand what’s happening at the local level,” she says, remembering the pride she herself felt at coming from somewhere that felt like a “hub of innovation”.

It is not just her personal background that Duguy believes makes her well placed to work on these cases. Before she joined ClientEarth, she worked at the law firm Squire Patton Boggs, providing advice to the very companies she is now seeking to hold to account.

In this role, Duguy was part of the firm’s public policy division, where she advised the industry on chemical and environmental law and how they could “limit the impact of those requirements on their businesses”.

While clearly conflicted by the time she spent doing this work, Duguy says the experience gave her an insight into why corporate actors think the way they do.

After one year in the role, she moved to ClientEarth and has set up a network of some of Europe’s best environmental lawyers. “We support each other, find synergies and collaborate,” she says. “It’s incredibly rich and also shows how much people are looking to access justice and to change things at all levels.”

For Duguy, the goal is simple: turn complex legal battles into real-world accountability before the damage becomes irreversible. “The problem with Pfas is that it’s something that you cannot grasp, but hopefully those actions that we’re launching will trigger some kind of emotion that can lead to action,” she says. “If not, we will just continue to face really awful consequences and then try to think of solutions when it’s too late.”
