After 100 days of the deadliest Ebola outbreak, it can be stopped. Here’s how

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 11:54:08 GMT

Ebola is a disease that spreads through communities, so we need to listen to communities if we want to halt its spread

Each time we travel to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), we go first to listen. In Bunia, we have met dozens of community representatives: survivors, women, young people, local organisations, health workers and leaders from affected areas.

Their message was direct: involve us. We know our communities. We know where families seek care, how information moves and why trust is breaking down. Give us the means to help drive the response. They were right.

Ebola spreads through communities – and communities hold the knowledge required to stop it.

They can identify illness early, alert health teams, help trace contacts, challenge dangerous rumours and support families through treatment and safe, dignified burials. The response will move faster when communities lead alongside national authorities and health workers.

The government of the DRC declared its 17th Ebola outbreak 100 days ago after confirmation of the Bundibugyo virus.

The outbreak has since become the deadliest ever recorded, with about 2,500 deaths.

Behind this unprecedented toll are families grieving and communities confronting Ebola alongside conflict, displacement and fragile access to care.

At the centre of it all are the people who show up every day. Health workers care for patients. Laboratory teams identify the virus. Contact tracers follow its path. Community health workers build trust where fear and misinformation have taken hold. Burial teams help families honour their loved ones safely and with dignity.

They are working under extraordinary pressure, often in insecure areas.

Some have contracted Ebola in the line of duty; some have paid with their lives.

Their service must be met with action: protection, training, reliable equipment, timely payment, psychosocial support and access to vaccination, testing and treatment. Their safety is central to stopping transmission.

The response has made progress. Under the leadership of national authorities, Congolese responders, WHO, the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) and partners have expanded surveillance, deployed laboratories, supported treatment centres, reinforced infection prevention and delivered essential supplies.

Uganda has interrupted transmission and declared the end of its outbreak, proving the Bundibugyo Ebola virus can be stopped. Decisive national leadership and close cooperation with communities broke the chains of transmission.

The emergency continues in the DRC. Cases are still being detected outside known contact lists. Each one points to a chain that has not yet been found. Every delay gives the virus another opportunity to spread.

The next phase must reach the village.

The DRC’s village-centred strategy takes the response to the places where transmission occurs. Surveillance, testing, treatment, vaccination, infection prevention and community engagement must operate together, close to affected families. Teams need the authority and resources to act quickly.

This is how we stop Ebola at its source: identify infection early, isolate and care for patients safely, follow every contact and prevent the next transmission.

Community leadership will determine whether this works. Women’s groups, young people, religious leaders, traditional healers, survivors and community health workers know where families seek care, how information moves and where trust is weakening. They can identify concerns early, challenge dangerous rumours and help response teams reach people who may otherwise remain invisible.

Their knowledge must shape the response. When they raise concerns, they must see action.

Trust is earned through delivery. A family that reports a suspected case needs safe transport and immediate care. A community that supports vaccination needs clear information about what the vaccine can do. Families who lose loved ones need dignity, compassion and support through safe burial procedures.

Health facilities also require urgent protection. As of 18 August, 163 health workers have been infected and 47 have died in the DRC, while Uganda has recorded four health worker infections. Every facility needs trained staff, protective equipment, clean water and sanitation.

An infection in a health facility places workers, patients and families at risk. A protected health facility becomes a centre for early detection, safe care and public confidence.

Financing remains a decisive test. Governments and partners have made commitments that must now reach the response.

National and local teams need predictable funding for surveillance, laboratories, treatment, vaccination, logistics, infection prevention and community engagement. Frontline workers must be paid on time. Supplies must arrive before stocks run out.

Delayed financing costs lives; fragmented financing leaves gaps. Ebola exploits both.

Cross-border coordination must remain strong. People move to trade, work, study, seek care and support families. Countries need rapid information-sharing, aligned surveillance and prepared health facilities along major routes.

The first 100 days have made the priorities clear: find every case; follow every contact; protect every frontline worker; bring testing, treatment and vaccination closer to every affected community. Turn every pledge into action.

Africa CDC will continue working with the DRC, alongside neighbouring countries, communities and partners, to bring the full strength of international and continental cooperation behind the nationally led response.

This outbreak can be ended. Uganda has shown what focused leadership and community action can achieve. The DRC can do the same.

Dr Jean Kaseya is director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention. Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus is director general of the World Health Organization

McLaren’s Lando Norris and Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton are genuine contenders for the Formula One world championship, according to the Mercedes team principal, Toto Wolff, who watched Norris take a decisive win at the Dutch Grand Prix.

With Mercedes’s early-season dominance looking to have been all but erased, Wolff noted that there would be no quick fix for the team who could not develop at the same rate as their rivals because they had opted to use their budget differently.

Norris won the race at Zandvoort for McLaren with the team having brought several car upgrades to the meeting, beating the Mercedes of the championship leader Kimi Antonelli and George Russell into second and third respectively. Ferrari have also moved closer to Mercedes, who won eight of the opening 12 meetings including all of the first six.

Antonelli leads Hamilton, who was fourth in Zandvoort, and Russell by 59 points in the championship and Norris by 83. However, Wolff expected the fight to become tougher in the title run‑in, with 11 races remaining.

Wolff said that he and Mercedes are “absolutely conscious of the threat” adding: “It’s not only Norris, it’s also Ferrari, even if you have a gap of 50 points to lose, that’s something you need to be worried about. This is going to be tough. It could become tighter, we need to do the optimal job every single weekend, every single session, every single weekend.”

Norris’s win at Zandvoort was his second in a row this season, while Ferrari have also taken two, one apiece for Hamilton and his teammate Charles Leclerc. Both teams have deployed an extensive series of upgrades, while Mercedes have brought only one major development thus far, at the Canadian GP.

The teams all operate under the same budget cap and, as it stands, Mercedes are opting not to use their allocation in the same way as their rivals, who have front-loaded their upgrades early in the season.

“We haven’t got the money to put developments on account,” Wolff said. “We are trying to evenly split that through the season based on our calculations of when we can bring the biggest updates and optimising the championship points. We just can do what we can do. That’s why it is a development race. So the ride has been a bit tougher than at the beginning of the year.”

Mercedes are not expected to bring another major upgrade until the grand prix in Malaysia, branded as the Bahrain GP, in October with three races still to come before then. Ferrari are understood to be bringing their extensive engine upgrade to the next round in two weekends’ time at Monza, where the Scuderia hope to make a major step forward. Wolff confirmed that Antonelli will take a new engine at his home race in Italy and with it the attendant grid penalties.

Why is the John Lewis ‘uni essentials’ list so strange?

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 10:00:31 GMT

It used to be that dorm rooms were chaotically messy. Does this new generation really need an £80 spice rack and velvet clothes hangers?

Of all the questions this year’s freshers may be nervously asking themselves as they prepare for this next phase – did I pick the right course? Will I make friends? Is uni worth 30 grand when my future job prospects may be limited to dusting a datacentre? – one is particularly pressing: “How many clothes hangers do I need to bring?”

Fret no longer, enquiring young minds: John Lewis has the answer on its packing checklist for students. Thirty to 40, it claims, wildly, “consisting mostly of standard velvet or plastic hangers”. “Standard” velvet? I missed this memo.

I found the list via the student news site the Tab, which posted a TikTok mocking J-Lew’s notions of what constitute “essentials”: a £495 Marc Jacobs bag, a £399 desk and an £80 spice rack carousel (I also spotted a £185 Ralph Lauren quarter-zip for those must-attend “man in finance” costume parties).

In fairness, most of the stuff on there is fine, but the Stanley cups and shower squeegees conjure a slightly dispiriting picture of wellness-focused, sensible, hygienic youth. I know that’s their generation’s reputation, but it would be nice if parents could be persuaded not to stock up, instead letting them go rogue and fill their kitchens, bathrooms and bedrooms with chaotically impractical stuff they choose themselves. Isn’t that what early adulthood is all about?

I’m optimistic, based on my own experiences: you needed a hazmat suit, not a shower squeegee, for my elder son’s student bathroom; the main feature of the younger’s kitchen was the Death-Star-sized air fryer he and his flatmates won at bingo.

He’s back home, post-graduation, and the surviving uni purchases are all over the house: deflated duvets, half-melted spatulas, singed tea towels. I WhatsApped to ask if there was anything particularly good or bad. It was mostly fine, he replied (from his bedroom), although the colourful multipurpose pan I was influenced into buying in a moment of emotional weakness proved underwhelming. The real “door-opener”, apparently, was a kilo bag of Belgian chocolate chips I got him, so that is my freshers “essential” tip: social currency (and a delicious snack) for £18.99.

Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist

The men claiming to defend women’s sports are throwing sex toys at female athletes

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 09:00:30 GMT

The WNBA has attracted grifters who care little for basketball – and whose latest stunt exposes the hollowness of their supposed concern

I regret to inform you that yet another dildo has hit a WNBA court. The Chicago Sky v Golden State Valkyries game was sullied by sex toys being chucked on to the playing surface on Friday. Aren’t we tired of all this yet? To paraphrase the Sky’s Natasha Cloud, it takes a lot of effort to bother with such a juvenile act.

This is yet another controversy for the WNBA, a league that up until a few years ago, most media observers ignored. The WNBA is full of incredibly talented players and has a rich history, but most sports fans treated all but ignored it for the majority of its 30-year existence. But when Caitlin Clark went pro, the league surged. Ratings, attendance, and interest exploded. But not all attention is good attention.

Clark has been polarizing from the start, owing to the fact that she’s a white superstar in a league that has historically been dominated by Black players. That alone makes her a prime candidate for culture warriors to weigh in. But now, the level of debate around the league has somehow become worse. Clark’s teammate, Sophie Cunningham, chose this fraught moment to declare she’s against trans women playing in girls’ and women’s sports. Never mind that the league has never had a trans player assigned male at birth and this is all just a hypothetical scenario she’s concerned about. Cunningham is better at getting attention than scoring points. Protests outside Fever games are often covered on the news more than the games inside the arena, which is hardly the kind of attention the WNBA has been looking for. A league that has long prided itself on its LGBTQ fans and players is now at the center of transphobic controversy. And then, it started raining dildos.

The Sky-Valkyries game is not the first time sex toys have been thrown on to the court at a WNBA game – the dismal incidents started last season. It’s not even the only league where this has happened. Regardless, the timing is pointed. The WNBA is not just a sports league – it’s also a furious petri dish for the opinions of people who often don’t even like women’s basketball. A group of crypto traders took responsibility for previous incidents and the most recent one in Chicago, declaring their support for Cunningham’s stance against trans women playing in the WNBA (which again, has not happened). You’d think they’d have come up with a new stunt, but apparently, good ideas are in short supply these days (they tried the same stunt last season to promote a meme coin, and there appears to be plenty of self-promotion behind these recent ones too). And if the group – and many of the anti-trans brigade who have descended on the WNBA – truly cared about women’s sports, perhaps funding scholarships and teams for young female athletes would be a more constructive way of going about it.

With outlets like Fox News forced to cover the league and hucksters like ex-NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom coming out to glom onto the controversy, the WNBA seems to be drowning in the kind of press no one wants. There’s a long history of athletes speaking up about their political and cultural opinions, but this seems especially dire when a women’s basketball player is actively speaking out against a community that has historically supported the sport. The WNBA finds itself in a culture war ignited by one of its own players, and the absurd spectacle of young men throwing sex toys at female athletes in the name of protecting women’s sports is just another front in that conflict. The “stick to sports” mantra that was so popular during the first Trump administration has become a punchline every time a dildo gets thrown on a basketball court.

The sex toy incidents are just the physical manifestation of what Cunningham has done to her league – a needless plea for attention that serves no one but the person making the fuss. This was not a subject the WNBA was dealing with until she said something. It’s now something the WNBA can’t get away from. If women’s basketball is to maintain its recent growth it needs to continue producing stars like Clark, four-time MVP A’ja Wilson and the ridiculously talented Olivia Miles. What it doesn’t need is players who court controversy for their own personal gain. Cunningham was barely on most fans’ radars until she became a meme, an honor usually reserved for such cultural luminaries as The Rizzler and the Real Housewives of Beverly Hills. Good for her, I guess. No doubt her post-career podcast will be thrilling. But where does she leave the WNBA? Drowning in the aftermath of childish pranks, it seems.

after newsletter promotion

No doubt there will be further moronic stunts this season, especially during the high visibility period of the WNBA playoffs and finals. The league can’t stipulate the terms of players’ speech. It can only ban those young men who disrupt games (and it is only young men who have been apprehended for the stunts so far), although there seems to be an endless supply of them. If the WNBA is going to sustain itself and bring in more genuine fans (as opposed to people solely interested in the league because they want to make a political point), it will need to address all of this in some meaningful way. The bond it has built with many of the LGBTQ fans who have helped sustain and build the league is being torched, with the help of one of its own players. And now outside agitators have joined the party.

Can Burnham justify giving the go ahead to oil drilling? Yes, but these must be the conditions

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 09:00:29 GMT

Carbon capture and storage could make the Rosebank site compatible with UK net zero commitments – if its owners are willing to pay the price

The British government must soon decide whether it should give consent to two oil and gasfields, Rosebank in the North Atlantic and Jackdaw in the North Sea. Amid both insecurity of energy supplies and deadly evidence of the climate crisis, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, is facing pressure from the oil and gas industry and unions on one side, and environmentalists on the other.

Labour’s manifesto commitment not to approve new drilling licences offers little help, because the fields already have licences, granted by the previous Conservative government in 2022 and 2023. But last year, Edinburgh’s court of session ruled that the environmental impact assessments on which this decision relied were unlawful. The Conservative government had, the court ruled, failed to include the emissions generated when the oil and gas from the fields is burned. The court allowed work to continue on the fields, but a new assessment had to be done and approval sought again.

The issue facing the new energy and climate secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is whether the additional information on the fields’ global emissions alters the grounds for consent.

Although invariably discussed together, the two fields are very different. Jackdaw is a small gasfield, with a production life of only 11 years. Its total carbon emissions will be only around 24m tonnes. Annually this would equate to around 0.8% of the UK’s total emissions. The gas would be piped into the UK, so would be consumed domestically. As this would probably displace dirtier liquified natural gas (LNG) imported from the US, it would make a small contribution to the UK’s energy security and emissions reduction.

By contrast, Rosebank is a large oilfield, with a 25-year life. During that time it would generate around 250m tonnes of carbon emissions. The oil would be sent to the Netherlands for refining, since the UK no longer has the appropriate capacity – and very little, if any, is likely to be used in the UK. So it would not contribute to our energy security.

There are good reasons, therefore, for the government to make different decisions on the two fields. Jackdaw can be justified (just) on energy security grounds. The UK needs gas over the coming decade, and there is a benefit to a little more of it being domestic. Jackdaw will stop generating emissions in 2037-2038, when the UK, and the world, will still be well above net zero.

Rosebank, by contrast, will still be producing oil in 2050, when the UK is legally obliged under the Climate Change Act to achieve net zero emissions. Indeed, by 2050, the Paris agreement (which forms the bedrock of the UK’s international commitments) expects the entire world to be just a decade or so off achieving net zero emissions. For that reason, the International Energy Agency expects global oil demand by that date to be lower than today and falling, if governments around the world follow their own stated climate policies.

Jackdaw is frankly too small to have any meaningful impact on global supply and demand in the decade it will be producing. But because of its size and longevity, the same cannot be said of Rosebank, which between 2040 and 2050 will be making a material contribution to global oil supply just when the market should be starting to decline. The greater the supply, the lower the price, and the higher the demand. So Rosebank has implications for both global emissions and international climate change policy.

Rosebank could be given consent while avoiding these consequences if the government required it to pay for some or all of its emissions to be captured and stored in disused oilfields or saline aquifers. Most of Rosebank’s emissions will occur when its oil is burned. So, making carbon capture and storage (CCS) a condition of its licence would effectively mean requiring it to pay to capture and store the equivalent volume of other producers’ emissions.

Though controversial, CCS is a proven technology: one of Rosebank’s owners, Equinor, has been using CCS in its Norwegian Sleipner field since 1996, is reported to have stored over 20m tonnes of CO2 without leakage. The UK government’s own CCS programme, operated by the North Sea Transition Authority, has now licensed 21 CCS projects at different stages of development. But Rosebank is not one of them.

The oil and gas industry has yet to acknowledge that its production can ultimately only be consistent with net zero emissions if it uses CCS. Giving consent to the Rosebank field on condition that it pays for its emissions to be captured and stored – say, from 2035 onwards – is the only way to make it compatible with the UK government’s domestic and international climate change commitments. By joining the UK CCS programme, Rosebank would probably be eligible for government support.

The additional costs of CCS might mean that Rosebank’s owners would decide not to go ahead with it. But this would merely demonstrate that the project cannot in practice be undertaken in a way that is consistent with the UK’s net zero commitments.

It is also critical that for both Jackdaw and Rosebank the government insists on strict methane limits. Methane is a more potent greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide and both fields will have significant emissions.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The government should make two other announcements at the same time. The first is to secure thousands of jobs by accelerating the labour-intensive decommissioning of oil and gasfields in the North Sea. At the same time, the government should publish a net zero transition roadmap, explaining how the UK will “defossilise” its economy over the next 25 years.

Rosebank’s and Jackdaw’s operators say they will create around 3,500 jobs in development and around 880 in operation. These are not negligible, but they will not save the oil and gas industry or the wider economy of north-east Scotland. Between 2013 and 2023, jobs in the sector fell by more than half, from 441,000 to 213,000. This has nothing to do with UK climate change policy, but is simply the inevitable consequence of the exhaustion of the British North Sea basin (around 90% of the UK’s oil and gas has now been extracted).

With around 1,700 wells due to be plugged and abandoned in the next six years and 500 already overdue for removal, decommissioning is a huge task. It will create many more jobs than drilling would (it is estimated that decommissioning will generate up to 25,000 UK jobs over the next decade and deliver about £6.8bn in economic benefit).

A net zero transition roadmap would cover both the anticipated technological pathways in energy, transport, industry and agriculture, and the implications for businesses and households. Such a roadmap would reassure firms, unions and consumers concerned about what the net zero goal really means, and deprive the media and opposition parties of the chance to speculate wildly about its costs.

It would give investors much-needed certainty. France has already produced such a roadmap, and other countries are also committed to doing so. Britain should join them.

Michael Jacobs is professor of political economy at the University of Sheffield and a former energy and climate change adviser to Gordon Brown when he was prime minister

‘It’s absolutely criminal’: US tipping culture has reached the UK – and is causing chaos

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 09:00:29 GMT

Service charges used to be a matter of choice, but now consumers feel obliged to pay them for even a cup of coffee. How do we navigate this minefield and who is really profiting?

In a London pub, Greg Double was brutally confronted with the reality of Britain’s evolving tipping culture. “I was annoyed about the pint being eight quid, but then when you put service on top, it’s absolutely criminal,” he says. In the past, you might have told the bar staff to keep the change or have a “drink” on you, but since when did we routinely tip in pubs? Or coffee shops? Or, worst of all, at self-service machines? Tip creep is happening.

Tipping was awkward enough in the UK when the general rule was 10% at a restaurant, plus anxiety about whether you should tip the hairdresser, babysitter or food-delivery driver. Now, with tipping suggested ever more frequently, US-style, it has become a minefield to Britons. The amounts edge higher – in fancier London restaurants, a 15% service charge is relatively commonplace. And it’s often asked for – in coffee shops for example, when you pay – before any service is delivered.

Tipping may be a social behaviour, but politics and economics also inform it. Since October 2024, all service charges and tips in Great Britain must go to staff, which boosts low salaries. Hospitality businesses, struggling with the rises in minimum wage and national insurance, are surely happy that it’s tipping customers who are supplementing wages, rather than themselves. As the news site London Centric pointed out recently in an article headlined “How American tipping culture came to London”, adding an “optional” service charge avoids tax, puts more money in the pockets of staff and means businesses don’t have to raise prices, which puts off customers.

But how “optional” is a service charge when the person serving us is looking expectantly as they hand over the card machine? Now, the variables around tipping seem endless and changeable, with each of us having to create our own rules.

Double, a creative director for a PR company, says that in a coffee shop without table service, he wouldn’t tip – but he might if he were sitting there, working, “to take into account that I’m going to make this coffee last”. He wouldn’t tip if he’d walked up to a bar and bought a drink for himself, but he might acquiesce if he bought a round. Since drinking Guinness became fashionable, it almost calls out for a tip. “Because you’re like: well, you’ve had to wait around for five minutes for every pint being poured,” says Double. “If you order four pints of Guinness, you immediately see the bar staff think: ‘Oh, for god’s sake.’”

Double also highlights a new tipping anxiety. Sometimes a bar worker will press zero on the tip screen before handing you the payment machine, “if they don’t think they’re worthy. There’s even that Britishness of the bar staff.” But what if they don’t? “It almost makes me think that if they’ve not pressed ‘no’ to the tip, that means they think they deserve one.”

Many of those I speak to think tech has pushed this change forward – and rapidly. The shift away from cash towards card and digital payments is usually framed as removing “friction”, says Prof John Vines, the chair of design informatics at the University of Edinburgh’s School of Informatics. “It’s about being more convenient. This is all a trend towards making it easier for us to spend our money.” The software in point-of-sale terminals prompts the customer for a tip. “These systems are presented as a way of making giving a tip easier. We don’t have to think about it too much, we don’t have to fiddle with coins and notes. But, really, it’s about encouraging us to spend more.”

Faced with three options on a screen, with the third perhaps an outrageous 35% tip, I often panic and go for the middle box. I wouldn’t want to seem cheap by going for the first option, but I end up feeling bullied into giving a generous 20% or more.

“Again, that’s presenting those options to you partly to reduce that friction – it’s taking away the need for you to mathematically calculate things. But, of course, it’s a way of controlling the options as well,” says Vines. “While we have the ability to press zero, the act of getting asked at the point of sale likely increases the chances of someone giving something, especially in situations where, at least in the UK, we culturally don’t expect a tip to be given in the first place.”

Is it too cynical to suggest that tech companies who run the software, and who take a cut of every transaction, are making more money from pushing tips? “That probably is a bit cynical, but also probably true,” says Vines, with a laugh.

It goes deeper than tech companies skimming a percentage. “A lot of our technological infrastructure is dependent on platforms and systems that come from the US and, in particular, California,” says Vines. “We tend to import a lot of the values and customs that are embedded with them. Even if it’s not intended, they get inscribed into these systems and flatten out the diversity of other cultures, the things that would be acceptable or normal elsewhere.” The example of tipping, while small, he says, “actually is an example of how [US tech companies] that get imported actually have quite significant long-term consequences, because it rewrites social expectations.”

It’s embarrassing, says Peter, who works in a pub in Lincolnshire, to ask customers for tips. A few months ago, they got new card machines that automatically suggest adding one. Peter always presses no before he hands it over to customers. “It can rub people up the wrong way,” he says. The pub’s manager occasionally asks people if they want to add a gratuity, “but even he doesn’t do it very often. It just feels pointless to us. You only tip someone if they’ve looked after you, you’ve been sat down and it’s been good service. You don’t tip someone for just pouring you a pint.”

Tipping culture was also changed by the pandemic, even in the tip-heavy US. “During Covid, we started tipping people that we didn’t traditionally tip,” says Michael Lynn, an emeritus professor of consumer behaviour and marketing at Cornell University and the author of The Psychology of Tipping. It was akin to “hazard pay”, he says, plus there was a perception that some people were more likely to be struggling financially. “People started being willing to tip and businesses took that as a message that consumers will bear it.”

The accepted level has always increased over time, says Lynn. This could be due to any number of factors. “The population of the US is more urban than it used to be and urban people tend to tip more than rural people,” he says. Then there’s the move away from cash. “People who pay with a card or digitally tend to tip more than people who pay with cash.” And big tippers – who do it for reasons of status, or to ensure good future service – ruin it for the rest of us. “It creates this upward pressure,” says Lynn. “It’s got to stop somewhere, right? We’re at close to 20% today [in US restaurants].”

Several times a year, I have a gnawing anxiety about whether or not to tip my hairdresser. It’s not that I don’t think he deserves it, but would it be condescending? “One of the impediments to tipping is concern about status and power implications,” says Lynn. “Money commodifies the relationship. If you view it as a social relationship, you don’t want to contaminate it with tips. It’s very hard to tip people that you have a long-term relationship with.”

Why do I tip my hairdresser (I’m too embarrassed to press “no”), but not the plumber or the dentist? It’s usually because with the latter two – or an accountant, a lawyer or a doctor – “I’m worse off than they are”, says Lynn. “Not only financially, probably, but also they’re helping solve a problem for me. When I go to something in a hospitality context, or even for a haircut, it’s generally something positive. I’m enjoying myself and that worker is doing not such pleasant work.”

The late anthropologist George M Foster, says Lynn, “argued that tipping began as an attempt by patrons to say: ‘Don’t envy me because I’m having fun and you’re working.’ The primary evidence he had for this was that the word for tip in many languages is ‘drink money’.”

Social expectation is the main reason people leave a tip. The second, he says, is “social connection and rapport. If a server is attractive, if a server is the opposite sex, if the server smiles, calls you by name, squats down, there are so many variables that impact the social connection, but they all have a pretty substantial impact on tipping.”

This, of course, is affected by blatant bias, sometimes unconscious, in the person leaving a tip. Some research shows that Black waiters and cab drivers receive lower tips, says Lynn. “Having said that, there are also a number of studies not finding this. There’s enough data on both sides that my conclusion is clearly there is racial discrimination, but it’s not universal and we don’t fully understand when it occurs and when it doesn’t.”

You get more tips from the opposite sex, says Lynn, so “waitresses tend to get slightly better tips. And attractive waitresses get better tips than less-attractive waitresses.”

When British football fans went to the US earlier in the summer for the World Cup, many were baffled and frustrated by the tipping culture. One fan told the BBC it was “weird” to be asked for a tip when buying a bottle of water. Ollie Thomas, a football content creator, says he went “with the expectation of [tipping] being very much in your face and quite intrusive. But I live in London and I didn’t think [restaurant tipping] was any different, really.

“The main difference I found in the US was that the service was a lot better. I guess the backdrop of the US tipping culture is that there is a massive weight of expectation on the customer’s shoulders to tip because the waiters don’t earn much money. Whereas it feels like there’s not that level of pressure on the customer in London because the general living wage is a bit higher here.”

But even in the US, says Lynn, tip fatigue is real. “In surveys, I was asking people: ‘Would you rather tipping be eliminated?’ In 2016, about 32% of people said yes. By 2018 it was 42% and by 2022 it was 52%. I haven’t repeated that since, but other surveys have asked similar questions. It seems to have gone back down to about 40%. But, absolutely, people say they’re being asked to tip for more services than ever before and, even for traditionally tipped services, they’re being asked to tip larger amounts. It negatively impacts consumer sentiment.”

So, how do we deal with this emerging tipping nightmare? We could do with some guidelines that everyone can agree on, perhaps beginning with a national discussion on how much we really want US tech companies to influence our proud British cheapskate culture. As for current good practice, Jo Bryant, an etiquette coach and training director at The English Manner, says we should continue to tip in restaurants, but watch out for the service charge. “People shouldn’t feel pressure to double tip. For restaurants, generally, it’s around 12%.”

However, there’s no reason to tip at the bar in pubs or coffee shops “apart from for food or table service”, says Bryant. But if it’s somewhere you go regularly, you may want to consider tipping: you don’t want to become known as the non-tipper. It’s completely acceptable to press the “no” button to a tip request in a place we wouldn’t usually tip, even with the person serving you in front of you, but do it briskly and confidently. “As soon as you start apologising and making a thing that you’re not tipping, then it becomes awkward.”

What about in more grey areas? If in situations that feel more condescending or uncomfortable – tipping someone who cleans your house or looks after your children, say – Bryant suggests just giving a generous tip at Christmas. “If you wrap it up into the Christmas cheer, it can feel less awkward.”

It’s very British, says Bryant, to view tipping through a lens of anxious social appropriateness and class. “Americans don’t have that feeling at all. I’ve provided etiquette classes to Americans and get tipped. It’s a great novelty. They’ll say goodbye to you and put a note in your hand. I think it stems from the Brits not talking about money. We’ve always been awkward about wealth and class and status.”

It’s why, she says, we never developed a tipping culture – and why it feels unsettling. “We all just find it so brazen to be getting out your wallet and handing money to people … we’ve been left in this slightly muddy zone.” We could fight it – and I’m open to fighting the influence of US tech – but faced with an expectant barista offering me the choice of three buttons, I’m more likely to panic-hit the middle one and hope it wasn’t 25%.

Leeds deliver timely Super League showcase while NRL investment hangs in balance

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 07:00:55 GMT

Wigan and Leeds tussle at the top but can all clubs come to an agreement over the investment the sport needs?

Three rounds to go until the Super League playoffs begin, and it is difficult to know whether to keep your eyes fixed on the pitch or off it. Leeds sit top after their impressive win at York on Sunday afternoon ended Wigan’s 48-hour stay at the summit, but the Rhinos are embroiled in a two- or perhaps even three-way battle for the League Leaders’ Shield in 2026.

The Rhinos and Wigan are level on points and have intriguing games against St Helens and Hull KR respectively this week. Should either or both slip up, Warrington could yet come into the picture for a top-two finish but you would be forgiven for your eyes already veering past this coming weekend’s fixtures and to the penultimate round on two fronts.

September arrives and with it the business end of the season, with Leeds and Wigan squaring off in a blockbuster showdown at Headingley that will, in all probability, decide top spot. The playoffs feel like they begin early this year with games of such magnitude – and by the time they meet in West Yorkshire on 5 September, Super League may also be transformed.

The possibility of the NRL investing in the top flight has proven to be the sporting summer’s longest-running saga: but we are now entering the championship rounds. Clubs decided to reject an initial offer from the NRL on Thursday, which would have brought in £7m for each of the next five years in return for equity in Super League.

The feeling is clear: Super League is worth more – but how much more? This is where things get interesting. Some clubs are far more keen to do a deal and land the NRL’s expertise, as well as their money, for not much more. The feeling among the most pro-NRL camps is that without the NRL, Super League will struggle to have a prosperous medium to long-term future. But others are not so downbeat, and insist that Super League should hold out for a lot more money; transformative sums, in fact. The right answer is probably somewhere in the middle, with the reported £7m per year unlikely to change anything other than buffer the losses of club owners somewhat. Super League needs real sea change, not pocket-money level handouts.

We are now also into the final months of Super League being exclusively shown on Sky Sports, with the league’s long-standing broadcaster opting to take only three games per round next year. The location of the other four depends on the NRL deal; if it falls through then Premier Sports – which will show the World Cup this autumn – are interested.

But with the NRL’s backing, a deal with Dazn becomes the favourite – which would yield little in terms of income in the immediate term, but perhaps more further down the track. Clubs will meet again this week and the NRL’s supremo, Peter V’Landys, is heading for the UK in the next fortnight to thrash out a deal. It is now or never; if the NRL walk away this time, they will not return.

However, there is clearly a product worth investing in – as Sunday’s match in York proved. The 66-16 scoreline looks ugly but it is important to remember York were only promoted this season at short notice and given half the central funding – £650,000 – of the other sides due to Super League expanding to 14 teams. That is something whoever is in charge next year must correct.

But York’s first season as a top-flight club has shown there is potential for elite rugby league in North Yorkshire. A full house was present here, a great occasion in the summer sunshine, but the game itself was firmly in favour of the league leaders.

Their attacking triumvirate of Lachie Miller, Brodie Croft and Jake Connor dismantled York to such an extent that at one stage, all plethora of Super League records looked to be in doubt when Leeds led 30-0 after 25 minutes.

With Wigan still to play, points difference may yet likely be immaterial: but the Rhinos showed little regard for that when picking the Knights apart.

“We didn’t come here expecting to score 66 points so I’m happy with that,” Leeds’ coach, Brad Arthur, said. “I think the mentality of the team drifted a bit in the second half but it does become hard when you’re ahead by so many points. But the spine players like Jake and Lachie did a great job.”

Riley Lumb scored a wonderful hat-trick and the Rhinos looked in impressive form as the serious challenges loom on the horizon. But by the time those challenges do arrive next month, starting with Wigan, Super League’s future looks likely to have changed for ever.

Do the NRL deal, and there is a new journey ahead. Walk away? That in itself prompts a fascinating discussion about where the game goes next.

The hill I will die on: A music festival isn’t a music festival without children

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 06:00:54 GMT

Ignore the party poopers who say toddlers spoil the fun. I’ve braved the raves with my twins – and I’ve seen how families add to the magic of events

The woman I used to be died the day I gave birth to twins. That life – full of spontaneous travel, impulsive decisions and a decorated social calendar – evaporated, giving way to a blank canvas of motherhood and two glorious little human beings. While I was inside that summer, many of my friends continued on their child-free paths. They posted pictures of themselves enjoying festivals, sleeping in tents with pop-up communities that I used to be a part of.

So when the twins turned one last summer and we’d found our rhythm, I decided to take on the challenge of sharing the magic of live music with them. It went better than I expected. Before their second birthday, we had danced at day festivals such as Situation Dance, put on by Femi Koleoso from Ezra Collective, camped out overnight in the Brecon Beacons for Green Man and been to the child-focused TOTFest.

Some people think it’s wild, bordering on neglectful, to take children to festivals that also cater to adult punters. They tend to think that children and families need to be separated entirely from spaces where there is any drinking or adult fun happening. Mothers, especially, are used to being told that everything we could possibly enjoy ourselves is going to damage our children. Thankfully, wise women around me whose kids are now grown up have reminded me to ignore these pressures, and go with my maternal instincts.

Taking young children to festivals does require another level of research and responsibility. Ear defenders are packed; festivals more aligned with drugs and debauchery are avoided. But different worlds can coexist. Selecting the family camping area when you book is game-changing. The adult audiences get their late-night raving in, and the early risers include not just families, but the wellbeing crowd heading to yoga or for a swim.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Having families around often has a positive effect on an event. People operate more within the realm of moderation when there are kids present, and you have to be a real Scrooge to get upset at barefoot children with glitter on their faces having fun alongside their parents.

I, for one, don’t want to spend the rest of my life solely listening to the Wiggles, and made the tactical decision early on to expose my babies to a wide range of sounds. We’ve got instruments at home and they’re fascinated by how it all works. They’ve taken to live music so easily, it’s a joy to watch them engage with something so human and far away from any screens.

People often say that other countries in Europe are ahead of us in terms of being inclusive of families and children, but I’d say the UK really shines during its festival season. My favourite ones are a microcosm of what coexisting can look like in the real world. I’ve found my village in the fields and car parks that host these events. My motherhood canvas is filling up with music, and I’ve found festivals are places where we can all get a bit of something that we want.

Iman Amrani is a freelance writer and producer

Marine Le Pen’s career has been resurrected – and she is a bigger threat than ever

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 04:00:52 GMT

No longer banned from next year’s presidential election, Le Pen is a far more formidable force than her understudy, Jordan Bardella

France loves a battle-scarred survivor. Charles de Gaulle, François Mitterrand and Jacques Chirac clawed their way back from political failure to become presidents of the republic. There is a significant chance that Marine Le Pen will be next.

Now that the Paris appeal court has unshackled her from an electoral ban for fraud, the far-right veteran has double appeal in the race for the French presidency next year. She will run, as always, as an outsider and a scourge of the political elites – despite continuously holding electoral office since 1998. She can also now pose as a “miraculous survivor”, a “mother courage” and “a battling granny”, as senior French political figures, including former ministers, described her to me during recent conversations in Paris.

Le Pen will be a much more formidable candidate than her young understudy Jordan Bardella might have been. The other candidates were wary of Bardella, but they did not fear him. They do fear a resurrected Le Pen.

Her party, the National Rally (RN), has a new campaign slogan: “Renaissance”. The rebirth of Le Pen’s political career, the party says, foretells the rebirth of France.

One might almost think Le Pen had been acquitted of fraud on 7 July. She was not. The judges essentially ruled that voters, not the courts, should decide who is president. They reduced Le Pen’s five-year ban from electoral politics, imposed by the Paris criminal court last year, to time already served.

She is now a twice-convicted embezzler of more than €4m in EU funds. If her final appeal to France’s highest court is heard rapidly and rejected, she might have to campaign next spring wearing an electronic tag on her ankle.

And yet. Two opinion polls since her reprieve suggest that she could defeat all imaginable opponents in the two-candidate second round next year.

Previous polls were almost as good for Bardella, but there were reasons to believe that he would not stay the course. The two-week-long second-round campaign traditionally stress-tests the capacity of the candidates not just to govern France but to represent it. Voters will wonder: do they have a stature présidentielle? Bardella will be 31 in September. He has been an RN party apparatchik since he dropped out of college at the age of 19. Would voters have been able to imagine this talented but glib young man toe-to-toe with a Vladimir Putin or a Donald Trump?

That question – presidential weight – is especially important for older voters. Of the 50 million registered French voters, 28% are over 65. Unlike younger people, they turn out in huge numbers.

A recent Ifop poll showed Le Pen beating the former prime minister Édouard Philippe, the strongest of the many candidates looking to carry Emmanuel Macron’s centrist torch, by 54% to 46% in the second round. She had almost exactly the same lead among the over-65s. It is the first time any poll in any national election put the RN ahead with the “grey vote”.

Bardella was also popular with older voters but his appeal to young and old was starting to fade. He comes from a working-class, Italian migrant family but had begun to show a Nicolas Sarkozy-like attraction to the high life, including, reportedly, a romance with an heiress from Italy’s remnant nobility.

Le Pen was born into a wealthy family and political business but cultivates an image as a gruff-voiced people’s champion, a single grandmother living with her best friend, a breeder of cats and, above all, a survivor.

There is, however, another issue that is crucial for older voters: economic stability. Le Pen’s feeble TV debate performances on the economy in 2017 and 2022 helped Macron to defeat her.

The RN’s economic policies remain an incoherent jumble of high social spending and low taxes, free markets and state interference. Bardella tried to shift the party towards a more traditional rightwing, low-tax policy and a more reformist approach to the EU, taking inspiration from Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

But Le Pen’s return means a return to “Marinomics” and a policy of wrecking the EU from the inside. With France €3.5tn in debt and permanently teetering on the brink of fiscal crisis, the prospect of a far-right government may disturb older and better-off voters.

Le Pen will have an obvious riposte. Macron bamboozled you all twice with his clever people’s talk, she will say. Look where that got you: another €1tn in debt. Time to give a down-to-earth woman a chance. I could hardly do worse.

But she could. Much, much worse.

A President Le Pen or a President Bardella would take France and the EU into dangerous new territory. Bardella, at least, appeared aware of the difficulty of being so outlandishly anti-EU, and of trying to govern with slogans. Le Pen does not.

A Le Pen presidency from next May is not a certainty. But it is, for the first time in seven decades of the family’s involvement in politics, a strong possibility. The comfort blanket for mainstream parties of right, left and centre – the implausibility of a 31-year-old slightly more pragmatic President Bardella – has been snatched away.

Mujtaba Rahman is the managing director for Europe at Eurasia Group, a political risk research and consulting firm

Scrapping of Berlin swimming day for Black children becomes latest in long list of race-linked pool rows

The Guardian Mon, 24 Aug 2026 04:00:52 GMT

Rightwing voices seize on plans to offer Black children an exclusive afternoon at an outdoor pool in the German capital

It was meant to be an outing for Black children in Berlin and their families, offering them an exclusive afternoon at an outdoor pool set up by a local theatre.

But the plans, slated for earlier this month, had to be scrapped after they were seized on by rightwing and conservative voices to whip up outrage, leaving organisers fending off racist emails and threats.

Berlin’s Volksbühne theatre said it had extended the invitation in hopes of dismantling some of the barriers that would normally keep these children away from the pool. While other groups had similarly been invited to use pool exclusively without incident, the idea of Black children enjoying a private afternoon at a public pool proved to be controversial among some.

“Berlin is a livable, diverse, colourful and free city. So why do we need safe spaces?” a local Christian Democrat politician, Aileen Weibeler, said on social media, while the far-right Alternative für Deutschland co-leader Alice Weidel described it as “an apartheid” in which “white people are temporarily denied access”.

It was the latest in a long list of incidents linking swimming pools to racism. Across North America and Europe swimming pools have often acted as a flashpoint for wider racial tensions and exclusions.

Earlier this summer, an open-air swimming lake in the eastern German city of Halle made headlines after it refused entry to bathers who did not speak German. In the Netherlands, the Institute for Human Rights recently ruled against a pool after it was found to have singled out a Black child for an identity check.

The list of incidents spans decades. In 2013, the Swiss town of Bremgarten moved to restrict asylum seekers’ access to swimming pools. In Bulgaria, Roma have sounded the alarm about being discriminated against at public pools, while in 2022, a swimming pool in Romania was fined just over €2,000 (£1,716) for barring entry to Romani children.

Some of the association between racism and pools most likely comes down to the intimacy of these spaces, said Jeff Wiltse, the author of Contested Waters: A Social History of Swimming Pools in America. “They’re visually, physically, and socially intimate spaces, and I think that continues to pique people’s social anxieties,” he said.

Wiltse has long studied pools in the US, recasting them as sites that reflect the wider tensions in society at any given time, from James Brock in 1964 pouring hydrochloric acid into a whites-only pool where Black men were swimming, to the Texas police officer who in 2015 pinned an unarmed Black teenager to the ground and drew his gun as he sought to break up a pool party.

In the US, “throughout much of the 20th century, swimming pools were homogenous spaces”, he said. “There was explicit racial segregation of public pools.”

In the late 1940s, as public swimming pools in the US began to be racially desegregated, private pools began to spring up, particularly in suburbs that were almost exclusively white. Many people came to see swimming pools as “a certain type of social space in which the people there are all socially similar”, said Wiltse, who advocates tackling the issue by increasing public investment in community pools that could bring together people from different ethnic and racial backgrounds.

The racialised history of pools – and its continued legacy today – has helped to give rise to a stark racial divide when it comes to swimming ability, one that has had deadly consequences. In the US, the fatal-drowning rate of Black and African American children is three times higher than that of white children.

The statistics are even worse in England, where recent data found that children from Black, Asian and minority ethnic communities are 3.5 times more likely to drown than their white counterparts. Recent figures from Sport England suggest that 95% of Black adults and 80% of Black children do not swim at all.

In 2022, Katrice Rodrigues set out to change this with the launch of Unity Swimming, a community organisation that runs weekly classes aimed at Black and Asian communities.

“People get angry at that, saying: ‘How can it be inclusive if it’s just for Black and Asian communities?’” said Rodrigues, who is also a keynote speaker on diversity in aquatics. “My thing is that we’re making the whole of swimming more inclusive by creating these safe little spaces, which lead to more people swimming, and that makes swimming, as a whole, more inclusive.”

The success of the programme has relied on Rodrigues and her team confronting the wide range of cultural barriers that keep minorities out of the pool, from having parents who are terrified of water to concerns over feeling out of place, dressing modestly or protecting Black hair.

Other barriers have proven more enduring. “There’s a myth and a stereotype that Black people can’t float and can’t swim,” she said. “It’s not true, but I’ve had to correct two experienced swim teachers who thought that was a thing.”

As summers become hotter across the globe, sending more people into rivers, lakes and pools in search of respite, the imperative has grown to ensure that as many people as possible know how to swim, said Rodrigues.

“It’s the only sport that’s going to save lives,” she said. “If you’ve got water safety knowledge, you could help save someone else’s life as well as your own and your whole family. So this has a knock-off effect on families, on communities and for generations.”

Supreme Court Allows Trump Plan to Restrict Mail-In Voting, for Now

The New York Times August 24, 2026

Supreme Court

Advertisement

Supported by

The administration asked the court to clear the way for President Trump’s order that creates “state citizenship lists” and directs the Postal Service to decide who gets a mail-in ballot.

By Abbie VanSickle and Ann E. Marimow

Reporting from Washington

A divided Supreme Court on Monday allowed the Trump administration to move forward with plans to restrict mail-in voting before the midterm elections.

In an emergency order, the justices said President Trump could proceed with implementing an executive order he had signed, which directed the U. S. Postal Service to help decide which voters should receive mail-in ballots. Under the executive order, the Department of Homeland Security will also create lists of U. S. citizens that the administration believes could be used to monitor voter rolls for noncitizens.

The decision means the administration can move ahead with planning for restricting the use of mail ballots even as a lower court continues to weigh the legality of Mr. Trump’s executive order. But with little more than two months until Election Day — and considerably less before early voting begins in many states — it remains unclear whether the White House’s rules will be in effect for a midterm election in which control of both chambers is at stake.

The order by the court was unsigned, as is typical in such emergency rulings. The majority wrote that it agreed with the government’s argument that it should be able to move forward with its plans, finding that the Trump administration was “likely to suffer irreparable harm” unless the justices lifted a freeze that had been imposed by lower courts.

The three liberal justices dissented, with Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson warning that the majority “needlessly injects chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections.”

The majority said the states that challenged the president’s order could not demonstrate that they were sufficiently harmed by voting rules that had not yet taken effect. The justices cautioned that their order was preliminary and not a final decision about whether the administration’s order “will necessarily be lawful” once the plans are complete. “On that score, time will tell,” the majority said in the 10-page, unsigned order.

That could mean the legal battle will return to the justices, perhaps quickly, as the administration moves to implement the president’s order before the midterms.

Got a news tip about the courts? If you have information to share about the Supreme Court or other federal courts, please contact us.

Mr. Trump signed the executive order in March as part of his broader attempts to curtail voting by mail. It directed federal agencies to create “state citizenship lists” of people who will be 18 or older as of Election Day. Federal officials were then directed to send those names to state election officials, who administer the vote, purportedly so they could use them to purge voter registration lists of anyone who is not a citizen. The order also instructed the Postal Service not to mail ballots on behalf of anyone whose name was not on the approved list.

Several court challenges immediately followed, including a lawsuit in federal court in Massachusetts brought by Democratic state attorneys general. The challengers argued that the president exceeded his authority because the Constitution gives Congress and the states power over elections, not the executive.

In late June, Judge Indira Talwani, a Federal District Court judge in Massachusetts, temporarily blocked the president’s order, finding that it violated the Constitution’s separation of powers. She also determined that Congress had not delegated authority to the Postal Service to determine which voters should receive mail ballots, and that the executive order did not allow enough time before November for the Postal Service to follow the legally required process for agencies when they adopt new rules.

Judge Talwani issued a separate broader ruling in a related case this month, blocking any enforcement of the executive order for the 2026 midterms. She again emphasized that the Constitution does not grant authority over elections to the executive branch. She also noted that, contrary to Mr. Trump’s claims of widespread voter fraud, the government had not provided “evidentiary support of illegal or fraudulent absentee voting.”

A federal appeals court earlier upheld Judge Talwani’s temporary block. At that point, Trump administration lawyers filed an emergency application asking the justices to step in. Several Republican state attorneys general filed a separate, parallel request.

In a brief to the court, the Democratic state attorneys general wrote that the executive order “would allow the federal government to rush out an unprecedented, legally indefensible voter-verification and ballot-interception program that would, among other things, give the U. S. Postal Service far-reaching new powers and responsibilities.”

They also argued that allowing the order to be implemented would mean a chaotic rollout not long before states begin to send out absentee ballots.

And they wrote that voters could be confused and disenfranchised, given that the federal government was likely to make errors in compiling citizen lists and that valid voters would have little time to challenge the government’s determinations.

Chris Cameron contributed reporting.

Abbie VanSickle covers the United States Supreme Court for The Times. She is a lawyer and has an extensive background in investigative reporting.

Ann E. Marimow covers the Supreme Court for The Times from Washington.

Review: Google Pixel 11

Wired August 20, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, when you buy something through our retail links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

8/10

The hot pink Hibiscus color is dazzling, but is Google’s 11th-generation Pixel just another iterative upgrade, or does it dial things up to 11? Diving beneath the surface, we find a slightly better chipset and camera, faster wireless charging, a fresh batch of AI features, and not much else. Don’t get me wrong: This is a slick smartphone, perhaps the best Android phone for folks who are comfortable with Google and Gemini AI, but it’s only a very slight improvement over last year’s Pixel 10.

Although it lands alongside the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL, the Pixel 11 shares more in common with the new Pro Fold (review coming soon). The Pro models' more powerful camera system, with the gimmicky, glowing HiLight LED, is what sets them apart. The base model storage has finally jumped up to a more practical 256 GB, but that means the starting price of the Pixel 11 is $100 more than the 10 at $899 (not technically a price bump since the 256 GB model of the Pixel 10 was the same price).

Refinement has been the pattern in smartphones for the last few years, and the Pixel 11 does nothing to buck that trend. If you’ve got a 3-year-old handset and you’re in the market for a new phone, the Pixel 11 should be in the conversation, but if you’re looking for a justification to upgrade from last year’s Pixel 10, you won’t find it here.

The instantly recognizable design has been slightly refined; most notably, the pill-shaped camera bump is thinner and all-glass. Stick a case on the Pixel 11, and it will lie flat on a desk. It sports the same satin finish on the recycled aluminum frame and gloss finish on the glass back as last year’s phone, but with some fun new colors.

Google Pixel 11

Rating: 8/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

I was delighted to get Hibiscus (otherwise known as hot pink), but there’s also a more subtle Pistachio (warm green), and the usual Frost (white) and Obsidian (black). I’m sad they cut Indigo (surely everyone’s favorite from last year). Like Apple, Google seems to save the fun colors for the regular Pixel, and the Pros look more muted.

Despite a 6.3-inch screen, this is what passes for a small phone nowadays. Switching from last year's Pixel 10 Pro XL, I really appreciated how easy it was to handle the Pixel 11 one-handed. It’s a little thick, but it feels good in hand and has almost the same profile as the Pro, so you can use cases interchangeably. And I do recommend snagging a Pixel 11 case; I already scuffed the paintwork when I dropped it on the beach.

The screen is the same as last year’s: an excellent 6.3-inch OLED display with a 1080 x 2424-pixel resolution and refresh rates of 60 or 120 Hz. It’s a shame Google didn’t upgrade to a variable refresh rate (1 to 120 Hz) since it can save battery life. It also defaults to 60 Hz, and you have to dip into the Display settings to toggle on the smoother 120 Hz. The display is plenty bright with a 3,000-nit peak brightness; I never found myself squinting. Side by side with the Pro, it’s not quite as bright or sharp, and it has larger bezels, but you have to look closely to see the difference.

The fingerprint unlock is as good as any, but Google’s Face Unlock still doesn't work in the dark, which will annoy any iPhone defectors. US buyers will also have to do without a SIM slot, as the Pixel 11 is eSIM-only stateside. Physical SIM cards make switching between phones more straightforward, but phone makers and carriers have made that process smoother with eSIMs than in the past. Sure, it’s much easier to pop a card in than to go through your carrier when traveling abroad, but setting up an international eSIM isn't that complex. Both have benefits, but with US phones and carriers embracing eSIM over the past couple of years, it's become a nonissue.

The new chip, Google’s Tensor G6, is supposed to deliver 20 percent gains in power efficiency, 25 percent faster browsing, and 15 percent faster app loading. The Pixel 11 has 12 GB of RAM and 256 or 512 GB of storage. For everyday use, it feels fast and responsive. I had no issues with loading apps or scrolling web pages, and the camera app feels a bit faster. Compared with my Pixel 10 Pro XL, I also noticed the Pixel 11 notified and loaded video from my Nest video doorbell a second or two faster.

I put it through its paces with the challenging mobile game Wuthering Waves. It was playable, but the action stuttered, and even on the Balanced (graphics and performance) setting, there were dropped frames aplenty during combat. After an hour, the Pixel 11 was warm, and the battery went from 40 to 26 percent. Less demanding games, like Mini Metro and Alto’s Odyssey, were fine, but dedicated gamers should still look elsewhere.

Google Pixel 11

Rating: 8/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The 4,985-mAh battery is a disappointing 15-mAh jump over the Pixel 10, but Google claims battery life has improved 25 percent from 24 hours to 30 hours. I’m not sure it’s quite that much based on my first week of testing, but the Pixel 11 has seen me through very busy days without hitting empty, though I still think daily charging will be the norm for most folks.

The Pixel 11 charges at 30 watts wired (cable but no charger included), but support for Qi2 25W enables faster wireless charging. I recommend buying a Qi2 wireless charger. The magnetic Pixelsnap (Google's version of Apple's MagSafe on iPhones) feels a touch stronger than the one in the 10-series, and it’s such a handy feature that saves you from fumbling with cables. Google has also expanded the screensaver so you can have a multiple swipe function on the nightstand, including clock, weather, photos, charging status, and smart home controls.

Google has also switched to a MediaTek modem in the Pixel 11. I wouldn’t normally mention a modem, but the Samsung variant Google used in last year’s 10 series was prone to draining the battery and not holding a signal terribly well. Anecdotally, the Pixel 11 does better in a few spots where I’ve traditionally had trouble with my Pixel 10 Pro XL, which is great news for when you want to use your phone for calls. Your mileage may vary.

Google’s phones have always been about software over hardware, but the real-world value of AI features comes down to context. If I have to go digging or remember that a feature exists, I probably won’t get much value from it. This is why Google weaves its AI into everything, rather than applying it as a layer on top. The latest Gemini Intelligence features extend Google’s lead in this space.

Google Pixel 11

Rating: 8/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Rambler improves the Pixel’s voice-to-text, cutting ums and ahs and letting you draft messages conversationally. I didn’t like it as much as my colleague, but I’m not really a speech-to-text guy, and I have a Scottish accent that it sometimes picks up wrong. I use the Pixel’s Recorder app a lot and love it for instantly transcribing my interviews, but Rambler doesn’t show the text as you talk like Recorder does; everything pops up after you’re done, which I don’t like as much.

AI overviews pop up right there in the Messages app when someone texts with a meet-up request, and you can add it to your calendar, or if they have a restaurant suggestion, you can tap to open it directly in Maps. Gemini can also dig details like flight numbers out of your Gmail to share via Messages if you let it. This is quite handy.

Fans of Circle to Search will be glad to know you don’t even have to snap a photo anymore; you can open the camera app, hold down the nav bar, and circle anything in the viewfinder to get info on it. You can also get location-based suggestions on the lock and home screen, such as a shortcut to your loyalty card in Google Wallet when you’re in a relevant store or recommendations for what to order at a restaurant from Maps.

There’s nothing groundbreaking here, but features like Call Screen for screening spam calls and Now Playing for surfacing the name of the song you can hear are still there, and those are the kinds of things that I miss when I switch away from a Pixel phone.

AI is firmly embedded in Google’s apps, and there’s no switch to turn it off completely, but you can choose to turn off Gemini, cut its access to apps like Photos and Messages, and turn off features like Circle to Search. Most of the camera app AI options are exactly that: options. But if this all sounds gimmicky and the idea of an AI-infused phone gives you the creeps, the Pixel line is not for you.

The triple-lens rear camera is one of the top reasons to buy the Pixel 11. The camera feels faster, with less processing delay than the Pixel 10, and you can snap a shot and instantly load it into the gallery. Spec-wise, it’s almost identical, with a 48-megapixel main camera, 13-megapixel ultrawide, and 10.8-megapixel telephoto for 5x optical zoom. The main camera sensor is larger, enabling slightly better low-light performance, and the digital zoom capability is up from 20x to 30x. The 10.5-megapixel front-facing camera is the same.

Google Pixel 11

Rating: 8/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Everything works beautifully. Most people probably only ever use the main camera and the selfie camera, and reviewers can get too far into the weeds, but the bottom line is that you don’t need a particularly skilled hand or eye to snap great photos with the Pixel 11. I really appreciate the telephoto lens. I rarely have a use for the ultrawide, but the telephoto is great for zooming in from a distance, and though the 30x zoom is digitally enhanced by combining multiple images, there’s no generative AI at work, so you get a real image.

The camera app is feature-packed if you want to dive in. The most notable new features are the Camera Looks, which are like filters you select before you snap a shot. Phone cameras are typically tuned a certain way—Google’s phones tend to be punchy and high-contrast with realistic colors, while Samsung saturates colors and Apple prefers brighter images—but Camera Looks lets you tweak that to opt for warmer colors or dial up the shadows.

Magic Capture is a clever new feature that lets you hold your phone up at a party or event and record video and select still shots simultaneously, without having to watch through the viewfinder. It’s a nice way to be more in the moment, and a safer way to hand your phone off to Mum and maybe get decent photos back.

No one really needs to upgrade their phone every year or two. It’s only by skipping a few releases that you’ll feel a real difference, and this is especially true for Google's phones because so much of what makes them special is on the software side, and many of those features will make it onto older phones too, though they might take a while.

For slick software features and a camera that’s easy to get great results from, the Pixel 11 is tough to beat in this bracket. If you want performance, both the Samsung Galaxy S26 and the Apple iPhone 17 are superior. Unless you’re a keen photographer, I don’t see a compelling case for paying more to get a Pro model. The Pixel 11 is the value sweet spot in Google’s new lineup, at least until the A-series next year.

The Galaxy’s Fastest Star Could Reveal the Secrets of a Supermassive Black Hole

Wired August 20, 2026

A team of astronomers has just detected the fastest star in the galaxy. Its anomalous speed has a more unsettling explanation: It orbits Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way, the mass of which is equivalent to four million times that of the sun.

S301, as astronomers have named the star, reaches 25,000 kilometers per second (km/s) at its maximum speed and takes 8.7 years to complete one orbit around Sagittarius A*. (By comparison, the sun orbits the center of the galaxy at about 230 km/s.) At its peak speed, S301 moves more than 100 times faster than our star, and reaches 8 percent of the speed of light.

The key to S301’s speed lies in how close it passes to the supermassive black hole. According to the European Southern Observatory (ESO), at its closest approach, the distance between the two is comparable to that between Saturn and the sun.

The enormous gravitational pull of Sagittarius A* accelerates the star as it approaches the black hole. S301, however, does not fall directly into it, but instead follows an extremely elongated orbit around it.

The shape of its orbit also explains why its speed varies so much. At its closest approach, it moves faster, while when it is farther away, it moves more slowly. Something similar happens in the solar system with some comets, such as Halley’s Comet.

S301 is the star with the highest-known orbital velocity in the Milky Way, and also the one that comes closest to Sagittarius A*. It likely did not form where we see it today, and may have lost a companion along the way.

“S301’s orbital properties, and the fact that stars cannot form so close to a massive black hole, indicate that the star was likely part of a binary pair that was torn apart by the tidal forces of Sagittarius A*. In the process, S301 became trapped by the black hole’s gravity while its companion star was kicked out with high velocity, most likely enough to leave the galaxy altogether,” explains the ESO.

Astronomers believe that within 10 years they will be able to determine the rotation of Sagittarius A*. Mass and rotation, or spin, are two of the fundamental properties that scientists use to describe a black hole astrophysically. So far, there are signs that Sagittarius A* is spinning, but it is not yet possible to determine precisely how much or in which direction it is spinning.

According to the theory of general relativity, a rotating black hole drags the spacetime around it along with it. That effect should slightly alter the orbit of S301. If astronomers are able to measure these small deviations over the next few years, they will be able to determine the spin of Sagittarius A*.

A black hole’s spin would warp the fabric of spacetime. Tracking S301 could provide more insight into this phenomenon.

Astronomers first detected S301 in 2023 using GRAVITY, an instrument on ESO’s VLTI in Chile. Since then, they have tracked its movement and, after identifying it, have been able to trace it backward through observations dating back to 2017. By combining this data, they reconstructed its orbit with greater precision and determined that the star passed its closest approach to Sagittarius A* in early 2023. It will approach the black hole again in 2031.

S301 is not the only known star orbiting close to Sagittarius A*. For decades, stars such as S2 have allowed astronomers to determine the black hole’s mass and test predictions of general relativity. The difference is that S301 passes so close to Sagittarius A* that it could allow them to directly measure its spin over the next decade—something that would require several more decades of observations with other stars.

This story originally appeared in WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

If you think that’s a far-fetched scenario, think again. WIRED’s Andy Greenberg got rare access to the closed-door war game and walked away with some disturbing conclusions. This week, Brian Barrett sits down to talk with Andy about Volt Typhoon, the Chinese state-sponsored hacking group that’s spent the past three years pre-positioning itself inside American infrastructure.
